magna-carta-1215.summary: On 15 June 1215, in a meadow at Runnymede between Windsor and Staines, King John sealed a charter of 63 clauses forced on him by his barons. It promised that no free man would be imprisoned, outlawed or exiled except by the lawful judgment of his peers or the law of the land, that justice would not be sold, delayed or denied, and that new taxes needed baronial consent, with a council of 25 barons to hold him to it. Papal annulment came within weeks and war followed, but reissues in 1216, 1217 and 1225 fixed it in English law. Three clauses still stand, and its principle that rulers are bound by law travelled into constitutions far beyond England.

paris-university-statutes-1215.summary: In August 1215 papal legate Robert de Courcon, acting on papal instruction, issued statutes for Paris's masters and students. They set the arts course: no one could lecture before his twenty-first year (an older translation gives twenty) or after fewer than six years of study, theologians needed eight years and age thirty-five, and every student had to have a regular master. They named books to be read, Aristotle's logic among them, and banned his natural philosophy and metaphysics. These statutes gave the university a legal shape, with rights to make its own rules and protect its members, a template later universities copied.

mapungubwe-1220.summary: Around 1220, by Huffman's chronology, Mapungubwe grew into southern Africa's first kingdom, rich on gold sold to Indian Ocean traders. It stood where the Shashe and Limpopo rivers meet in present-day South Africa; Huffman dates its K2 and Mapungubwe sequence to about 1000 to 1300, with Mapungubwe's own phase from about 1220 to 1290. Its rulers lived apart on a sandstone hilltop while commoners farmed and herded below, an early sign of class division in southern Africa. Its capital held about 5,000 people by 1250 and its territory probably covered 30,000 square kilometres, trading gold and ivory toward Indian Ocean ports. Mapungubwe was abandoned around 1300, as power shifted north to Great Zimbabwe.

villard-perpetual-motion-1225.summary: Around 1225 Villard de Honnecourt sketched a wheel he said would turn forever; no such wheel has ever worked. Between about 1225 and 1235 he drew some 250 subjects: church plans and elevations, figures, animals, one water-powered sawmill, one trebuchet and an overbalanced wheel with hinged mallets that he presented as perpetual motion. Whether he was working architect or lay draughtsman is debated.

sultan-han-caravanserai-1229.summary: Seljuk sultan Alaeddin Keykubad I commissions Sultan Han, finished in 1229 by architect Muhammad ibn Khawlan of Damascus, on the road between Konya and Aksaray in central Anatolia. Its walls enclose about 4,900 square metres: an open summer courtyard with a raised kiosk mosque, stables and lodging under arcades, a bath, and a vaulted winter hall lit through a domed oculus. Thirteenth-century Anatolian sultans and viziers endowed dozens of such hans along the routes from the Mediterranean ports to Sivas and Erzurum, spaced roughly a day's caravan march apart, each funded by a waqf so travellers, animals and goods could shelter without charge. Ayşil Tükel Yavuz's 1997 study classifies them by shelter and service spaces. A fire led to rebuilding in 1278.

yam-mongol-postal-relay-1234.summary: In 1234 Ögedei Khan set up relay stations every 25 miles, so messages crossed Eurasia in weeks. Yam stations had permanent staff who supplied remounts and fixed rations to post riders and envoys. Households attached to them were exempt from other taxes but paid a levy in goods to keep them stocked, and Ögedei barred nobles from issuing paizas, tablets that let bearers demand goods and services from civilians. He ordered Chagatai and Batu to run yams in their own domains separately.

mali-empire-1235.summary: Around 1235 Sundiata Keita founded Mali, which held West Africa's gold and made Timbuktu a seat of learning. He defeated Sosso king Sumanguru at Kirina; his empire lasted until about 1610. It grew into West Africa's largest empire, controlling gold fields and trans-Saharan trade and spreading Mandinka language, law and customs. Its wealth became legendary under Mansa Musa, whose pilgrimage to Mecca in 1324 carried so much gold it was noted across the Islamic world. Timbuktu grew into a centre of Islamic learning under Mali's rule.

tripitaka-koreana-1237.summary: From 1237 Korea carved the entire Buddhist canon onto 81,352 woodblocks without a known error. Mongol invaders had burned Goryeo's first set in 1232; King Gojong, whose court had fled to Ganghwa Island, ordered a revised set carved to implore divine help against them. They are kept at Haeinsa temple to this day.

ibn-al-baytar-jami-pharmacopoeia-1240.summary: Diya al-Din Ibn al-Baytar, a Malaga-born herbalist who left Spain about 1220 and collected plants across North Africa, Syria and Anatolia, serves the Ayyubid sultans in Cairo and Damascus as chief of herbalists. In the 1240s he completes Kitab al-Jami li-mufradat al-adwiya wa'l-aghdhiya, an alphabetical guide to roughly 1,400 medicinal substances in 2,324 entries drawn from more than 150 earlier Arabic and Greek authors and his own field observations, with names in Greek, Berber, Persian and Spanish. He dedicates the companion al-Mughni to sultan al-Salih. He dies in Damascus in 1248. Eighty-six manuscript copies survive; Lucien Leclerc's French translation appeared in Paris between 1877 and 1883.

ibn-al-nafis-pulmonary-circulation-1242.summary: In 1242 Ibn al-Nafis worked out pulmonary transit of blood, centuries ahead of Europe. Galen had taught that blood passed from right to left ventricle through pores in their shared wall; Ibn al-Nafis denied such pores exist and reasoned that blood must pass from right ventricle through the lungs, where it mixes with air, into the left. His manuscript stayed unknown to Western scholars until one was found in Berlin in 1924.

qin-jiushao-mathematical-treatise-1247.summary: In 1247 Qin Jiushao published a method for finding a number from its remainders, now used in cryptography. He gave numerical methods for solving polynomial equations up to the tenth degree by nested multiplication, equivalent to what is now called Horner's method, and he applied mathematics to surveying, military matters and rainfall measured with gauges of his own design.

song-ci-forensic-handbook-1235.summary: In 1247 judge Song Ci wrote forensic medicine's first handbook: coroners could read a body for its cause of death. Song Ci, a judge in Southern Song high courts, wrote Collected Cases of Injustice Rectified as a handbook for coroners. It set out how to examine bodies and injuries and distinguish causes of death. Among its cases is a village stabbing of 1235: investigators matched wounds to sickle blades by testing them on animal carcasses, then had villagers lay their sickles in sunlight; flies gathered on just one blade, bearing traces of blood, and its owner confessed. Officials used Song's handbook for centuries, and it was translated into English, German, French and Japanese.

song-ci-forensic-handbook-1235.detail: Song Ci (1186 to 1249) was born into a bureaucrat family in Jianyang, in present-day Nanping, Fujian, and served several terms as presiding judge. While posted to a criminal court in Hunan he examined crime scenes himself whenever a homicide proved difficult. Sickles cut rice at harvest, which pointed suspicion at peasant workers. Generations of forensic scientists drew on his book, and translations extended to other languages beyond those four.

song-ci-forensic-handbook-1247.summary: Song Ci (1186 to 1249), a Southern Song judicial intendant, printed Xi Yuan Ji Lu (Collected Cases of Injustice Rectified, often translated as The Washing Away of Wrongs) in 1247. Written as a guide for magistrates conducting inquests, it tells officials how to examine a corpse, distinguish drowning from strangulation, read wounds to tell a weapon, estimate time of death from decay, and record findings on standard forms. It is the oldest surviving book devoted to forensic medicine. Reissued and expanded for six centuries, it was required reading for Chinese coroners into Qing times; Brian McKnight's English translation appeared from the University of Michigan in 1981.

tusi-couple-1247.summary: In 1247 al-Tusi made a straight line from two circles, a device Copernicus used to move Earth. In his Commentary on the Almagest, Nasir al-Din al-Tusi proposed one small circle rolling inside another of twice its diameter, so a point on its rim swings back and forth along a straight line. He offered it to account for inferior planets' motion in latitude, and later astronomers used it widely in place of Ptolemy's equant, an off-centre point that had troubled them for 1,000 years. Copernicus used this same construction, but no exact route by which it reached him has been identified.

gujarat-block-printed-cottons-fustat-125.summary: Dyers in Gujarat printed cotton with carved wooden blocks, using alum and iron mordants to fix madder reds and blacks, and wax or mud resists to hold whites against indigo vats. Fragments excavated at Fustat (Old Cairo) and Quseir al-Qadim on Red Sea coast, radiocarbon dated from tenth to early sixteenth century, show these cloths sold in Fatimid and Mamluk Egypt as cheap furnishing and dress fabric. Related pieces survived in Sulawesi and Sumatra as heirlooms. This was industrial scale export printing centuries before European calico workshops copied Indian technique, built on chemistry of mordants that European dyers did not master until the 1700s.

land-of-cockaigne-1250.summary: In the 13th century poets described Cockaigne, a land with streets paved with pastry where no one worked. One French fabliau of that century and an English poem surviving in a 14th-century manuscript describe houses made of barley sugar and cakes and shops that give goods away; in English hands it also satirises monastic life. Its fantasy lived on in prints and paintings, including Bruegel's Land of Cockaigne of 1567.

sources.title: Cockaigne - Wikipedia

Pleij, Herman, Dreaming of Cockaigne: Medieval Fantasies of the Perfect Life (Columbia University Press, 2003), ch. 5, pp. 45-54
sources.author: Pleij, Herman
sources.confirms: Cockaigne was a medieval literary land of plenty with rivers of wine, houses of food and a fountain of youth.
sources.qualifies: Pleij's texts are Middle Dutch rhyming versions preserved in 15th-century manuscripts; the fetched chapter does not date the English or French poems.

land-of-cockaigne-1250.verification_note: Pleij (2003) confirms this motif; only its French fabliau is 13th century, while its English Land of Cokaygne survives in a 14th-century manuscript and is undated there.

moai-rapa-nui-1250.summary: From 1250 to 1500 Rapa Nui carved more than 900 moai, up to 80 tonnes each, and moved them without wheels. They were chiefly living faces of deified ancestors. Nearly half remain at Rano Raraku, their main quarry; hundreds were moved from there and set on stone platforms called ahu around the island's shore, gazing inland over clan lands. All had fallen before 1900, toppled in tribal conflicts or after European contact.

sources.title: Megalithic statue (moai) production on Rapa Nui (Easter ...

settlement-of-new-zealand-1250.summary: Around 1250 Polynesian voyagers reached New Zealand by canoe, the last large land on Earth to be settled. Māori oral history describes ancestors arriving from Hawaiki in waka; archaeology traces them to East Polynesia. Radiocarbon dating of rat bones in 2008 put arrival around 1280, and a 2022 study of more than 500 sites found settlement probably occurred in the North Island between 1250 and 1275 and in the South Island between 1280 and 1295. Many Polynesian crops failed in New Zealand's cooler climate, so settlers hunted native birds and sea life, driving some birds extinct.

florin-minted-1252.summary: In 1252 Florence minted its gold florin, a coin so stable in weight that Europe later used it as a common standard for big payments. Florence's florin held 3.5 grams of nominally pure gold and was struck to one standard until 1533; little used even in Florence before 1280, it was accepted across Europe after 1300 for larger transactions, including international trade, as the Byzantine solidus had been.

sources.qualifies: Florence and the 1252 date are supported; the other details are not stated.

sources.author: Locatelli, Stefano

spinning-wheel-reaches-europe-1257.summary: Spinning wheels, which turn a spindle with a hand-driven wheel instead of twirling it by hand, are recorded in Persia by 1257 and in China by 1270; by 1298 Speyer guild laws regulate their use. They multiplied a spinner's output and fed growing wool and linen trades in Europe's cities. Where they were first invented is disputed. Britannica says probably India, reaching Europe through the Middle East. Dieter Kuhn, in a 1979 Early China article, argues from Han stone reliefs that spindle wheels were a Chinese invention of the Warring States period tied to silk reeling. A continuously working flyer wheel appears before 1500, ancestor of Saxony wheels and of Hargreaves's jenny.

sources.title: Kuhn, D., 'The Spindle-Wheel: A Chou Chinese Invention', Early China 5 (1979), 14-24
sources.author: Kuhn, Dieter
sources.confirms: Abstract read: the spindle wheel was a Chinese invention datable to the early Warring States period, linked to silk technology; the flyer spinning wheel was invented in 15th-century Europe.
sources.qualifies: Contradicts the Indian-origin account given by Britannica and the fashion encyclopedia.

sources.title: 'Spinning wheel', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: Probably invented in India; reached Europe via the Middle East; Saxony wheel in the early 16th century.

sources.title: Hochberg, B., 'Spinning', Encyclopedia of Clothing and Fashion (via Encyclopedia.com)
sources.author: Hochberg, Bette
sources.confirms: India about 750; Persia by 1257; China by 1270; Speyer guild laws 1298; flyer illustrated in the Waldburg Hausbuch about 1480.

spinning-wheel-reaches-europe-1257.verification_note: Persia's 1257 date and Speyer's 1298 regulation come from the fashion encyclopedia; place of origin is contested between India (Britannica) and China (Kuhn). approximate_year is set because this wheel's spread cannot be pinned to one year.
spinning-wheel-reaches-europe-1257.detail: Encyclopedia of Clothing and Fashion dates spinning wheels in India to about 750, Persia 1257, China 1270 and its first flyer illustration to Waldburg Hausbuch of about 1480. Kuhn's reconstruction of silk-based origins in China would push invention back more than a thousand years before India's date. Whichever origin holds, wheels reached Europe as Flemish and Italian cloth towns rose, and guild rules such as Speyer's show weavers at first distrusted wheel-spun yarn as weaker than hand-spun thread.

sack-of-baghdad-house-of-wisdom-1258.summary: In 1258 Mongol forces burned Baghdad's libraries, ending 500 years as Islam's seat of learning. Hulegu's army took this Abbasid capital after caliph al-Musta'sim surrendered on 10 February and began looting on 13 February. Estimates of dead range widely, 200,000 among them; Hulegu executed al-Musta'sim on 20 February. Baghdad had been Islam's intellectual capital, with centres of learning including the House of Wisdom; its fall is often said to end the Islamic Golden Age, though historians dispute that, and large libraries reopened within two years. Under Hulegu's Ilkhanate Baghdad prospered but declined relative to Tabriz.

maragheh-observatory-1259.summary: In 1259 Maragheh observatory opened in Persia after three to five years of building. It housed a large collection of astronomical instruments and books and taught students, becoming one of Eurasia's most advanced scientific institutions, and it served as model for Ulugh Beg's observatory in Samarkand, Taqi al-Din's in Constantinople and Jaipur's Jantar Mantar.

mamluk-barid-1260.summary: From 1260 Baybars's relay post across Egypt and Syria brought Damascus news to Cairo in days. This Mamluk sultan, who ruled from 1260 to 1277, folded the barid into his military command. Earlier caliphs had used their barid both to carry official correspondence and as domestic intelligence, reporting on provinces and officials. Couriers on relay horses changed mounts at stations to carry Baybars's messages from Cairo.

sources.author: Silverstein, Adam J.
sources.confirms: The Mamluk Barid was created under Baybars I (r. 1260-77), drawing on earlier caliphal, Byzantine and Sasanid postal traditions as well as the Mongol Yam.
sources.qualifies: Silverstein weighs the Mongol-influence thesis of Sauvaget and Gazagnadou and accepts it only with caveats; Mamluk writers themselves did not credit the Mongols.

yang-hui-triangle-1261.summary: In 1261 Yang Hui drew a number triangle Europe would name after Pascal 400 years later. His book Xiangjie Jiuzhang Suanfa carries China's earliest extant illustration of it. Each number in it is the sum of two above it, giving coefficients for expanding powers of binomials. Yang acknowledged that Jia Xian had invented this method and expounded it around 1100. Yang also worked on magic squares and magic circles.

yang-hui-triangle-1261.verification_note: Needham confirms this 1261 text and its triangle but, with Yang Hui himself, credits Jia Xian about 1100 with its construction.

picture.credit: Yang Hui, in Zhu Shijie's Siyuan Yujian (1303), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

assize-of-bread-and-ale-1266.summary: In 1266 England tied the weight of a farthing loaf to the price of wheat, a consumer law enforced for 600 years. Rather than fixing what a loaf cost, it fixed its weight: a farthing loaf of wastel, finest white bread, had to weigh 6 pounds 16 shillings by money-weight when wheat sold at 12 pence per quarter, and less at each higher price, so buyers paid a farthing whatever wheat cost. Coarser breads had to weigh more than wastel at each step.

roger-bacon-flying-machines-1267.summary: In the 1260s, by convention 1267, Roger Bacon wrote that ships without rowers, carts without horses and flying machines were possible by art, not magic. It argues that nature's powers worked by art can outdo anything claimed for magic, and foresees ships without rowers steered by one man, carriages moving without animals and flying machines with artificial wings: "instruments of navigation without men to row them, as great ships to brooke the sea, only with one man to steer them." It also sets out ways of hiding writing, an early treatment of cryptography.

roger-bacon-opus-majus-1267.summary: In 1267 Roger Bacon told the Pope that knowledge must be tested by experiment. He also described gunpowder in Latin for one of the first times. He sent his Opus Majus to Pope Clement IV at Clement's request. It surveyed learning from languages, optics and mathematics to alchemy and what he called experimental science, meaning that knowledge must be tested by experience. One passage in it, with one in his Opus Tertium, is usually regarded as among Europe's first descriptions of a mixture containing gunpowder's essential ingredients, long after China.

song-shipbuilding-bulkheads-1272.summary: Around 1272 Chinese shipbuilders divided hulls into watertight compartments; Western yards adopted them in the 1800s. A Song-dynasty merchant ship found in Quanzhou Bay in 1973 and excavated in 1974 was divided by 12 bulkheads into 13 compartments, among the strongest physical evidence for Song shipbuilding. Three-masted and about 34.6 metres long, average for long-distance trade of its day, it appears to have been scuttled in shallow water around when Mongols took Quanzhou, with its cargo left aboard. Archaeologists dated it from coins in its hull, latest from 1272.

Needham, Joseph, with Wang Ling and Lu Gwei-Djen, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 4 pt. 3: Civil Engineering and Nautics (Cambridge University Press, 1971)
sources.author: Needham, Joseph; Wang, Ling; Lu, Gwei-Djen
sources.confirms: Transverse watertight bulkheads are the fundamental characteristic of Chinese hull construction and could be made watertight, long before European adoption.
sources.qualifies: Needham's book (1971) predates the 1973-74 excavation of the Quanzhou ship, so that 1272 hull is documented in later archaeology such as Green, IJNA 1983.

sources.title: 'Ship', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page gives no date or facts about a Song dynasty ship excavated at Quanzhou Bay, or 13 compartments. It says the Titanic was built to the “two-compartment standard”;
sources.qualifies: Watertight compartments are discussed, but the Quanzhou ship, 1974 excavation, 1270s date, and 13 compartments are not stated.

song-shipbuilding-bulkheads-1272.verification_note: 1272 comes from its latest coin found aboard, a terminus post quem; this ship sank about 1275 and was built earlier, so its date is approximate. Needham confirms bulkhead construction and its Chinese priority; this Quanzhou wreck's thirteen compartments rest on post-1974 excavation reports.

siege-of-xiangyang-counterweight-trebuch.summary: In 1273 trebuchets hurling stones several feet across broke Xiangyang's walls, and Mongol conquest of China followed. Yuan forces had besieged this Han River city since 1267 without breaching its walls. In 1272 Kublai Khan had Ismail and Al al-Din, engineers sent by Abaqa, Ilkhan of Persia, build counterweight trebuchets, called Muslim trebuchets or hui-hui pao: later accounts credit them with stones of over 300 kilograms thrown some 500 metres with new accuracy, the only artillery able to reach Xiangyang's walls. Lu Wenhuan surrendered on 14 March 1273, which opened the Han and Yangtze rivers to Yuan forces and led to Southern Song's fall.

sources.qualifies: The Song war and 1279 conquest are stated, but the specific Xiangyang claim is not.

mongol-invasions-japan-bombs-1274.summary: In 1274 and 1281 Kublai Khan's fleets hit Japan with gunpowder bombs, after Korea's Goryeo kingdom became his vassal. Mongol troops advanced behind shields and threw paper- and iron-cased explosive bombs, frightening Japanese horses, in one of the earliest cases of gunpowder warfare outside China. Typhoons wrecked both fleets; Japanese called them kamikaze, divine wind. These failures set a limit on Mongol expansion and became nation-defining events in Japan.

ramon-llull-ars-magna-1274.summary: In 1274 Ramon Llull's paper wheels combined ideas into arguments mechanically, an ancestor of computing. He meant it as universal logic to prove Christian doctrine to people of every faith. It assigned letters to God's attributes and other principles, combined them mechanically with diagrams and rotating figures, and tested which statements held, giving it an algebraic cast. Llull refined it for decades, finishing Ars generalis ultima in 1308; later thinkers count it a forerunner of computation theory.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Ramon Llull
Fidora, Alexander and Carles Sierra (eds.), Ramon Llull: From the Ars Magna to Artificial Intelligence (IIIA-CSIC, 2011)
sources.author: Fidora, Alexander; Sierra, Carles; Bonner, Anthony
sources.confirms: Chronology dates Llull's illumination on Mount Randa and the first version of the Art to 1274; rotating figures generated combinations of principles lettered B to K.

sources.title: 'Ramon Llull', Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

ramon-llull-ars-magna-1274.verification_note: Fidora and Sierra's volume confirms 1274 and the combinatorial figures; Bonner says the figures did not determine truth and the aim was conversion of Muslims and Jews.

fabriano-paper-watermark-1276.summary: In 1276 Fabriano in Italy began making paper, with watermarks, earliest of maker's marks pressed into a page. From then onward it earned renown for fine watermarked paper that it keeps today, and paper-making brought it prosperity through late medieval and Renaissance times.

sources.title: Fabriano - Wikipedia
Tsien Tsuen-Hsuin, Science and Civilisation in China, vol. 5 pt. 1: Paper and Printing (Cambridge University Press, 1985)
sources.author: Tsien, Tsuen-Hsuin
sources.confirms: Earliest Italian paper mill was at Fabriano in 1268-76; watermarks with crosses and circles were introduced there in 1282, with animal-glue sizing and metal beaters.
sources.qualifies: Tsien dates the watermark to 1282 and the mill to 1268-76, so 1276 is the mill date, not the watermark date.

sources.qualifies: It supports medieval-era papermaking but does not state that it began around 1276 or that Fabriano introduced watermarks.

fabriano-paper-watermark-1276.verification_note: Tsien dates Fabriano's mill to 1268 to 1276 and first watermarks to 1282; this entry ties watermarks to 1276.

gaocheng-observatory-1276.summary: In 1276 Kublai Khan ordered an observatory built at Gaocheng; its 12-metre gnomon measured the year to within 26 seconds of today's value. Guo Shoujing and Wang Xun designed it to track sun and stars and record time. Its brick-and-stone tower, 9.46 metres high, carries a horizontal bar as gnomon; its noon shadow falls along a 31.19-metre stone scale running north, so solstices and year length could be measured with new precision.

sources.qualifies: It says a Tang Dynasty stele to its south “witnessed the idea of the center of the world.” It does not state 1276, Kublai Khan, the 12-metre or 9.46-metre measurements, 26-second accuracy, or the roles of Guo Shoujing and Wang Xun.

sources.qualifies: The observatory and its astronomical association are stated; the claim’s specific names, date, and measurements are absent.

guo-shoujing-shoushi-calendar-1280.summary: In 1280 Guo Shoujing measured a solar year at 365.2425 days, a figure Europe's Gregorian calendar adopted three centuries later. At Kublai Khan's order, he, Zhang Wenqian and Wang Xun had built 27 observatories across China to gather observations. He also built astronomical instruments, including a simplified armilla and Ling Long Yi.

sources.qualifies: 1280 and the calendar reform are stated; the specific people, measurement, observatories, and Gregorian comparison are absent.

al-mansuri-hospital-1284.summary: In 1284 Cairo built a hospital that treated anyone free. Its building was finished in under six months, speed that drew accusations of forced labour. This hospital was the most lavish of its time, giving sick and poor people drugs, shelter, food and clothing as well as treatment, and it kept treating patients for more than 500 years until demolition in 1910.

al-mansuri-hospital-1284.verification_note: this page is about Mamluk medical patronage, but does not substantiate these specific claims; it states this general fact about Arab hospitals, but not this claim’s specific details

beauvais-cathedral-collapse-1284.summary: In 1284 the tallest Gothic vaults ever built fell in at Beauvais: stone had found its limit. Part of its choir vaulting collapsed; one theory holds it was shaken down by resonant vibration in high winds. Builders rebuilt it at full height but with more columns and six-part vaults. Beauvais stayed incomplete: its nave was never built, and a 153-metre tower added in 1569 fell in 1573.

It does not state that the choir vaults were the tallest ever built, that high winds caused the collapse, or that the vaults were rebuilt at full height with more columns.
sources.qualifies: The page confirms a vault collapse at Beauvais in 1284, but not those additional details.

sources.title: 'Beauvais', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The cathedral dates from the 10th to the 16th century. Its “apse and transept have survived several collapses,” and its choir, at 157 feet (48 metres), “remains the loftiest ever built.” The Romanesque Basse Oeuvre stands in the space planned for the cathedral nave.
sources.qualifies: The choir height and planned nave are consistent; the specific collapse and tower details are absent.

venetian-ducat-1284.summary: In 1284 Venice minted its gold ducat, a coin so trusted it stayed Europe's trade money for 500 years. Venice's Great Council ordered a pure gold coin after Byzantine emperors repeatedly debased their gold hyperpyron, copying size and weight from Florence's florin of 1252: 3.545 grams of 99.47% fine gold, as pure as medieval refining could make it. Ducats circulated beside florins from late medieval times into the 1800s.

sources.author: Day, William R.
sources.confirms: The page identifies the review as Zecca: The Mint of Venice in the Middle Ages and gives its publication date as “1 April 2003” (pages 602-605). It states no facts about a gold ducat, 1284, its purity or weight, the Great Council, the hyperpyron, or its use in trade.
sources.qualifies: The page concerns Venice’s medieval mint, but does not verify the specific claims.

venetian-ducat-1284.verification_note: this page concerns Venice’s medieval mint but does not verify these specific claims

spectacles-italy-1286.summary: Around 1286 a Tuscan made the first eyeglasses, giving scholars and craftsmen decades more working life. Dominican friar Giordano da Pisa said in 1306 that making eyeglasses was discovered about twenty years earlier, placing their first appearance in Pisa or Florence. Earlier readers held magnifying "reading stones" over their books; convex lenses mounted before both eyes corrected presbyopia, farsightedness from stiffening lenses in people past forty. Giordano's colleague Alessandro della Spina made glasses and shared his method openly. Venice became an early manufacturing center using Murano glass, and guild rules governed makers there by 1301.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Glasses
ROSEN, EDWARD, 'The Invention of Eyeglasses', Journal of the History of Medicine and Allied Sciences XI (1956)
sources.author: ROSEN, EDWARD
sources.venue: Journal of the History of Medicine and Allied Sciences
sources.confirms: The page identifies Edward Rosen’s article, “The Invention of Eyeglasses,” published 1 January 1956, in Volume XI, Issue 1, pages 13-46. It says the content is “only available as a PDF” and does not display historical details.
sources.qualifies: The page does not state or confirm the claims about 1286, a Tuscan inventor, Giordano da Pisa’s 1306 statement, or Pisa/northern Italy.

sources.title: The Invention of Eyeglasses
sources.confirms: The page identifies Edward Rosen’s article, “The Invention of Eyeglasses,” published in January 1956, pages 13-46. It does not state when or where eyeglasses were invented, or mention a Tuscan craftsman or Giordano da Pisa.
sources.qualifies: The page confirms the article’s topic, but provides none of the historical dates, places, or figures in the claim.

sources.title: 'Eyeglasses', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: In 1268, Roger Bacon made “the earliest recorded comment” on lenses for optical purposes; magnifying lenses in frames were used in Europe and China “at this time,” and whether East or West learned from the other is disputed.
sources.qualifies: Italy and Florence are stated, but the page does not give 1286, identify Pisa as the invention site, or mention Giordano da Pisa’s 1306 sermon.

spectacles-italy-1286.verification_note: First spectacles were made in central Italy, most likely Pisa or Florence, about 1286 to 1290; Giordano da Pisa's sermon of 23 February 1306 said their art was found 'not yet twenty years' earlier, Venice became a centre later, and Salvino degli Armati's attribution is a known fabrication. Rosen (JHMAS 1956) is that standard study; Britannica places first eyeglasses in Italy, credits Alessandro di Spina of Florence, notes Bacon's 1268 comment on lenses and gives no 1286 date.

picture.credit: Tommaso da Modena, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

three-sisters-agriculture-1070.summary: Around 1070 farmers in eastern North America were once thought to have begun growing maize, beans and squash together; direct dating now places their first co-occurrence in northern Eastern Woodlands in the late 13th century. Cahokia, at its peak from about 1050 to 1200, was fed by maize and Eastern Agricultural Complex crops. Each crop helps its neighbours: cornstalks serve as trellises for climbing beans, beans fix nitrogen in soil and steady maize in wind, and broad squash leaves shade ground, holding moisture and suppressing weeds. This mix gave more energy and protein than any single local crop. Over following centuries it became staple farming for many Indigenous peoples.

sources.title: Three Sisters (agriculture)
The Three Sisters of Indigenous American Agriculture
Hart, John P., 'New Dates from Old Collections: The Roundtop Site and Maize-Beans-Squash Agriculture in the Northeast', North American Archaeologist 21 (2000)
sources.author: Hart, John P.
sources.confirms: The abstract states that Ritchie linked maize, beans and squash at the Roundtop site to a radiocarbon date of A.D. 1070, but AMS dating of the domesticates shows no evidence for the three co-occurring there before A.D. 1300.
sources.qualifies: The A.D. 1070 date behind the record is the Roundtop association this paper overturns.

sources.title: Hart, John P.; Asch, David L.; Scarry, C. Margaret; Crawford, Gary W., 'The age of the common bean (Phaseolus vulgaris L.) in the northern Eastern Woodlands of North America', Antiquity 76 (2002)
sources.author: Hart, John P.; Asch, David L.; Scarry, C. Margaret; Crawford, Gary W.
sources.confirms: The abstract reports AMS dates showing the common bean became archaeologically visible from the Illinois valley to New England only in the calibrated late 13th century AD, 200 to 300 years later than previously thought.
sources.qualifies: Beans, the third sister, arrive in the northern Eastern Woodlands around 1300, not 1070, and Cahokia's peak precedes them.

three-sisters-agriculture-1070.verification_note: AMS dating (Hart 2000; Hart et al. 2002) places first co-occurrence of maize, beans and squash in northern Eastern Woodlands in the late 13th century; an A.D. 1070 date derives from Ritchie's Roundtop association, which direct dating overturned, and Cahokia (peak c. 1050 to 1200) was fed by maize and Eastern Agricultural Complex crops.

timbuktu-manuscripts-1290.summary: After 1200 Timbuktu's scholars filled manuscripts that survive by the hundred thousand. Scribes translated imported works by authors such as Plato, Hippocrates and Avicenna and local authors wrote on history, religion, law, medicine, astronomy and science, in Arabic and in African languages such as Songhay and Fula. During Mali's war of 2012 to 2013 some 4,203 were burned or stolen; about 350,000 were moved to safety in Bamako.

sources.title: Timbuktu Manuscripts - Wikipedia
Hunwick, John O., Timbuktu and the Songhay Empire: Al-Sa'di's Ta'rikh al-Sudan down to 1613 and Other Contemporary Documents (Brill, 2003)
sources.author: Hunwick, John O.
sources.confirms: Timbuktu grew as a scholarly centre under Mali in the fourteenth century, with scholars teaching from their houses and Sankore; it appears on the Catalan atlas by 1375.

verge-and-foliot-clock-1290.summary: Late in the 13th century, clockmakers somewhere in western Europe replace water and sand with a falling weight checked by an escapement: a crown wheel, a vertical verge with two pallets and a horizontal foliot bar whose swing lets that wheel advance one tooth at a time. Britannica calls this escapement the key invention, probably made in 13th-century Europe, and J. D. North's 1975 study ties earliest clocks to monasteries that needed to ring canonical hours. Surviving examples come later: Salisbury's clock of 1386 and Wells's of 1392, now in the Science Museum, were both built with foliots and converted to pendulums after Huygens's invention of 1656. Verge escapements stayed in use for nearly four hundred years.

sources.title: North, J. D., 'Monasticism and the First Mechanical Clocks', in J. T. Fraser and N. Lawrence (eds), The Study of Time II (Springer, 1975), 381-398
sources.author: North, John D.
sources.confirms: Chapter landing page read: scholarly account of the monastic context of the first mechanical clocks, with pages 381 to 398 confirmed.

sources.title: 'Escapement', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: Verge-and-foliot described; the escapement was probably invented in 13th-century Europe.

sources.title: Science Museum Group, 'Wells Cathedral clock, 1392' (object co1347)
sources.author: Science Museum Group
sources.confirms: Clock of 1392 originally regulated by a foliot and converted to a pendulum after 1657.

sources.title: 'Clock', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: Salisbury 1386 and Rouen 1389 among the earliest surviving clocks; Wells clock in the Science Museum.

verge-and-foliot-clock-1290.verification_note: No source names the first clock or its year; 1290 is a placeholder inside the late-13th-century window that Britannica and North give. Dates of surviving clocks are confirmed.
verge-and-foliot-clock-1290.detail: De Vick's clock installed for Charles V in Paris in 1379 is the best documented of early examples and source of most textbook drawings. Astronomical showpieces followed soon after: Richard of Wallingford's clock at St Albans around 1327 and Giovanni de Dondi's astrarium of 1364. A foliot has no natural period of its own, so these clocks drifted by a quarter of an hour or more a day and were reset by sundial; 1656's pendulum cut that error to seconds.

picture.alt: Diagram of the verge and foliot escapement of Henri de Vick's 1379 Paris clock.
picture.credit: Pierre Dubois, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

murano-glass-decree-1291.summary: In 1291 Venice moved all its glass furnaces to Murano, whose guarded secrets made it Europe's glass capital. Venice's Republic ordered this move fearing fire in Venice's mostly wooden buildings.

ram-khamhaeng-inscription-1292.summary: Inscription One, a four-sided stone found at Sukhothai in 1833 by Prince Mongkut, carries a date equivalent to 1292 and describes King Ram Khamhaeng inventing Thai letters in 1283, free trade without tolls, a bell for petitioners and rice fields and fish in rivers. Its script places vowels on one line with consonants, unlike later Thai writing. Michael Vickery and Piriya Krairiksh argued from 1987 that language and palaeography fit a nineteenth-century composition; defenders, including many Thai epigraphers, hold it authentic. Whatever its date, this stone shaped how Thailand narrates its earliest writing and kingship, and UNESCO placed it on Memory of World register in 2003.

sources.title: Vickery, Michael, 'Piltdown 3: further discussion of the Ram Khamhaeng inscription', Journal of the Siam Society 83 (1995)
sources.author: Vickery, Michael
sources.confirms: Linguistic and palaeographic arguments that inscription cannot be 13th or 14th century
sources.qualifies: One side of an unresolved debate

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Ramkhamhaeng'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: 1292 inscription as earliest Thai-language text; reign c. 1279-1298

ram-khamhaeng-inscription-1292.verification_note: Authenticity and date are disputed: Vickery and Piriya argue for a 19th-century origin, while Thai epigraphers and reference works keep 1292. Vickery's article argues one side of that debate.
ram-khamhaeng-inscription-1292.detail: Vickery's 1995 article in Journal of Siam Society restates his case that terms and orthography are anachronistic for thirteenth century. Britannica and most survey histories keep 1292 as a working date. Authenticity is unresolved, and claims about a 1283 alphabet are inscription content rather than established fact.

picture.alt: Ram Khamhaeng inscription stone, Bangkok National Museum, 2024
picture.credit: Paul_012

gaykhatu-paper-money-tabriz-1294.summary: With Mongol herds decimated by cattle plague and his treasury empty, Ilkhan Gaykhatu authorises chav, block-printed paper notes copied from Yuan China, on advice from vizier Sadr al-Din Zanjani and Qubilai's envoy Bolad. First notes circulate in Tabriz on 12 September 1294 by Rashid al-Din's account. They carry Chinese characters, a shahada and Gaykhatu's Buddhist name, in values from a quarter dirham to ten dinars, and refusal is punishable by death. Merchants shut Tabriz's bazaar, prices rise more than tenfold, people flee and commerce halts; his edict is rescinded within about two months. Gaykhatu is overthrown and killed in 1295, and that spring Ghazan orders a consignment of notes bound for Mazandaran burned near Semnan.

huang-daopo-cotton-1295.summary: Returning around 1295 from Yazhou on Hainan, where Li women had long worked cotton, Huang Daopo taught villagers at Wunijing near Shanghai a roller gin for removing seeds, a large bow for fluffing fibre, a three-spindle treadle wheel and patterned weaving. Yuan writers Tao Zongyi and Wang Fengs record her arrival and a shrine raised after her death. Francesca Bray reads this transfer as a turning point that made Songjiang China's cotton cloth centre for five centuries and shifted women's textile labour from silk and hemp to cotton. Later Ming tax and market records show Songjiang cloth sold across north China.

sources.title: Bray, Francesca, Technology and Gender: Fabrics of Power in Late Imperial China (Berkeley: University of California Press, 1997)
sources.author: Bray, Francesca
sources.confirms: Huang Daopo's transfer of Hainan cotton technology to Songjiang and its consequences for women's work

sources.title: Review of Korean Studies 24:2 (2021), article on cotton diffusion in East Asia, pp. 173-204
sources.author: Review of Korean Studies (author not captured from PDF header)
sources.confirms: Huang Daopo returned from Yazhou to Wunijing and introduced ginning and spinning tools

huang-daopo-cotton-1295.verification_note: Biographical dates rest on Yuan notebooks, and 1295 is conventional; Bray's monograph is cited as supporting literature.
huang-daopo-cotton-1295.detail: Her birth date and exact year of return are uncertain; Chinese scholarship places her return between 1295 and 1296 and treats biographical details from Yuan notebooks as thin. A 2021 Korean study of cotton diffusion repeats this chronology. Bray's analysis situates her within Mongol-era movement of people and crops.

picture.alt: Gate of Huang Daopo's tomb and memorial, Xuhui district, Shanghai
picture.credit: Michele

hesdin-automata-park-1299.summary: Before 1300 Count Robert II of Artois filled his park at Hesdin with mechanical monkeys and trick fountains. His master of works Renaud Coignet oversaw this estate from 1292 to 1299. Later owners added mechanical birds and a mechanical king; poet Guillaume de Machaut praised its "engines". Charles V had the town and park destroyed after Hesdin surrendered in 1553.

ottoman-classical-era-1299.summary: Around 1299 Osman I founded the Ottoman state, which ruled three continents for six centuries. The Turkoman tribal leader began with a principality in northwestern Anatolia. His successors conquered most of Anatolia, crossed into Balkan Europe by mid 14th century, and under Mehmed II took Constantinople in 1453, ending Byzantine rule. Selim I's conquests brought Ottoman sultans their title of caliph. Ruled from Constantinople, this empire spanned three continents until its sultanate ended in 1922.

sources.confirms: The page gives no founding or conquest dates.
sources.qualifies: The general rise and regions are mentioned, but the specific dates and claims are absent.

sources.confirms: The page says Osman I founded the dynasty and empire “about 1300,” and describes its beginnings as a “small northwestern Anatolian principality.” The Ottoman period “spanned more than 600 years” and ended in 1922. “Fall of Constantinople” appears as a major event, but the page gives no date for it.
sources.qualifies: The page says about 1300, not specifically 1299, and does not state that Constantinople was taken in 1453.

arte-della-lana-1300.summary: Around 1300 Florence's wool guild put 30,000 to work across the city, a factory without walls. Arte della Lana was one of seven greater guilds that governed trade and shared in ruling the commune. It controlled every stage from baled raw wool to finished cloth, woven on looms scattered through homes across Florence, and coordinated members who rarely owned those means themselves. At its height it employed 30,000 workers directly, kept about a third of Florentines in work and turned out 100,000 lengths of cloth yearly. From 1331 it ran construction of Florence's cathedral.

sources.title: Arte della Lana - Wikipedia
WHY WERE RENAISSANCE FLORENTINE WOOL INDUSTRY COMPANIES SO SMALL? (Quantitative Studies of the Renaissance Florentine Economy and Society, 2019)
sources.venue: Quantitative Studies of the Renaissance Florentine Economy and Society
sources.confirms: The page says Renaissance Florentine wool production used a “putting-out production system organized by a guild.” Its firms were profitable and “by far the largest employer in Florence,” with “dozens of firms” at any given time. It gives no specific year or date for these claims.
sources.qualifies: Guild-organized production is stated; the other details are absent.

sources.title: 'Florence', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page says Florence’s water supply enabled “washing, fulling, and dyeing of cloth.” It dates Orsanmichele’s wheat-market loggia to 1290, its replacement to 1377, and its conversion to a church to 1380. In the early 15th century, major guilds donated its decorations;
sources.qualifies: It does not state that Arte della Lana was one of seven major guilds, employed 30,000 people, or controlled cloth production.

arte-della-lana-1300.verification_note: guild-organized production is stated; other details are absent; it does not state Arte della Lana was one of seven major guilds, employed 30,000 people, or controlled cloth production

baures-fish-weirs-moxos-1300.summary: In Llanos de Moxos, a seasonally flooded savanna of Bolivian Amazonia, communities around Baures laid out low earthen zigzag walls with funnel openings that trapped fish as floodwater drained, alongside straight causeways, canals, forest islands and ponds. Clark Erickson's 2000 survey identified these zigzags as weirs by form, orientation and comparison with weirs still used by local people, and mapped a connected network over 525 square kilometres. Fish, together with raised-field crops and palm groves on artificial mounds, fed dense settlements in a landscape that floods for months each year. Radiocarbon dates from mound settlements elsewhere in Moxos place that culture between about 500 and 1400.

sources.title: Erickson, Clark L., 'An artificial landscape-scale fishery in the Bolivian Amazon', Nature 408 (2000)
sources.author: Erickson, Clark L.
sources.confirms: Zigzag earthworks in Baures identified as fish weirs within a hydraulic network covering 525 square kilometres.
sources.qualifies: Gives no radiocarbon dates for the weirs themselves.

sources.title: Prümers, Heiko et al., 'Lidar reveals pre-Hispanic low-density urbanism in the Bolivian Amazon', Nature 606 (2022)
sources.author: Prümers, Heiko; Betancourt, Carla Jaimes; Iriarte, José; Robinson, Mark; Schaich, Martin
sources.confirms: Casarabe culture of Llanos de Mojos built mounds, causeways and canals between about 500 and 1400, dated by radiocarbon.

sources.title: Erickson, Clark L., 'The Domesticated Landscapes of the Bolivian Amazon', in Balée and Erickson (eds), Time and Complexity in Historical Ecology (Columbia University Press, 2006), ch. 8
sources.author: Erickson, Clark L.
sources.confirms: Synthesis of raised fields, causeways, canals, forest islands and weirs as a built landscape.

baures-fish-weirs-moxos-1300.verification_note: Erickson's Nature paper identifies weirs by form and ethnographic analogy and gives no direct dates; 1300 stands for a span of roughly 500 to 1400 taken from radiocarbon dating of Casarabe mound settlements in Prümers et al. (2022); Baures weirs may be later.
baures-fish-weirs-moxos-1300.detail: Erickson's identification rests on ethnographic analogy with weirs built by Baures and Itonama fishers rather than on direct dating of weir fill. A lidar survey of Casarabe mounds south-west of Baures gives occupation between roughly 500 and 1400, and the Jesuit missionaries who arrived in the 1680s found a reduced population still fishing with weirs. Causeways up to several kilometres long linked mounds and served as dikes.

egypt-sugar-refineries-1300.summary: Sugar cane spread from Lower Egypt into Upper Egypt after 1100, and by around 1300 plantations around Qus, Qift and Asyut fed pressing mills and refineries (matbakh al-sukkar) owned by sultans, amirs and merchant families such as the Kharrubis. In Fayyum a mid-thirteenth-century survey records 1,468 feddans of cane and villages where cotton and rice gave way to sugar. Boiling cane juice in copper vats and draining it in clay cones produced grades from red to white sugar, sold as medicine, festival sweets and an export to Italian merchants. Tsugitaka Sato reconstructed this industry from chronicles, cadastral surveys and al-Nuwayri's encyclopaedia.

sources.title: Sato, Tsugitaka, 'Sugar in the Economic Life of Mamluk Egypt', Mamluk Studies Review 8 (2004)
sources.author: Sato, Tsugitaka
sources.confirms: Spread of cane to Upper Egypt after the eleventh and twelfth centuries; 1,468 feddans of cane in Fayyum; Qift as a production centre; presses in districts surveyed in 1289; sugar as merchandise, medicine and festival goods

sources.title: Sato, Tsugitaka, Sugar in the Social Life of Medieval Islam (Brill, 2015)
sources.author: Sato, Tsugitaka
sources.confirms: Monograph chapters on expansion of cane from Lower to Upper Egypt and on production technology as described by al-Nuwayri

egypt-sugar-refineries-1300.detail: Sato's article lists districts granted after the 1289 cadastral survey whose revenue came from sugar presses, and notes al-sukkar al-Qifti prized for purity. Production contracted after 1400 as Mamluk monopolies, plague mortality and Cypriot and later Atlantic competition cut demand. Egyptian technology, including the use of lime and repeated boiling, passed along trade routes toward China and the Mediterranean. Anchor year 1300 marks a period of large-scale Upper Egyptian production.

picture.alt: Sugar cane growing at Qurna on the west bank of the Nile near Luxor, Upper Egypt
picture.credit: Marc Ryckaert (MJJR)

maori-kumara-storage-pits-1300.summary: Kumara, a tropical perennial, cannot survive a New Zealand winter in open ground. Maori gardeners, within decades of settling Aotearoa about 1250 to 1300, began harvesting tubers each autumn and storing them in rectangular pits (rua kumara) cut into well-drained ground, roofed and sealed to hold temperatures above 10 degrees. Seed tubers kept this way were replanted each spring in mounds, often on soils deliberately modified with added sand, gravel and charcoal to warm them and improve drainage. Excavations at Hokianga and on Banks Peninsula document these made soils and pits down to 43 degrees south, well beyond any other sweet potato cultivation zone of its time.

sources.title: Bassett, Kari N.; Gordon, Hamish W.; Nobes, David C.; Jacomb, Chris, 'Gardening at the edge: documenting the limits of tropical Polynesian kumara horticulture in southern New Zealand', Geoarchaeology 19 (2004)
sources.author: Bassett, Kari N.; Gordon, Hamish W.; Nobes, David C.; Jacomb, Chris
sources.confirms: Modified garden soils with gravel additions at southern limit of kumara cultivation on Banks Peninsula
sources.qualifies: Southern sites may date to late pre-contact centuries

sources.title: Jones, Kevin L., 'Dune soils and Polynesian gardening near Hokianga North Head, North Island, New Zealand', World Archaeology 16 (1984)
sources.author: Jones, Kevin L.
sources.confirms: Dune soils near Hokianga show deliberate sand and charcoal additions for Polynesian gardening
sources.qualifies: Single-site study

sources.title: Furey, Louise, Maori Gardening: An Archaeological Perspective (Department of Conservation, Wellington, 2006)
sources.author: Furey, Louise
sources.venue: Department of Conservation, Science and Technical Publishing
sources.confirms: Synthesis describes rua kumara pits, made soils and garden layouts across New Zealand
sources.qualifies: Grey literature report, not peer-reviewed journal

maori-kumara-storage-pits-1300.verification_note: Pits and made soils are securely documented; a 1300 start is inferred from settlement date and earliest garden deposits rather than a single dated pit.
maori-kumara-storage-pits-1300.detail: Storage pits are among the most common archaeological features in northern New Zealand, often on pa terraces. Garden sites keep borrow pits for gravel and stone-row boundaries alongside storage pits of several forms. At Okuora Farm, geophysics and soil chemistry showed deliberate gravel additions at the southern limit of gardening. These adaptations turned an annual crop cycle into a storable staple that supported dense settlement and later surplus trade with Europeans.

marco-polo-travels-paper-money-1300.summary: Around 1300 Marco Polo's account of China told Europe about paper money and porcelain. Columbus carried a copy. Polo returned to Venice in 1295 after 24 years in Asia and was soon captured by Genoa in its war with Venice. In prison he dictated his travels to cellmate Rustichello da Pisa, producing Europe's first detailed account of Mongol China around 1300, with first Western descriptions of paper money, porcelain and gunpowder. About 150 handwritten copies survive, differing widely because scribes altered text before printing existed. His narrative later inspired Christopher Columbus.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Marco Polo
Yule, Henry and Henri Cordier (eds.), The Book of Ser Marco Polo, 3rd ed. (John Murray, 1903), Book II ch. 24
sources.author: Polo, Marco; Yule, Henry; Cordier, Henri
sources.confirms: Chapter 'How the Great Kaan causeth the bark of trees, made into something like paper, to pass for money' describes Yuan paper currency; Yule dates the dictation at Genoa to 1298.
sources.qualifies: The text was dictated in 1298, two years before the record's 1300.

sources.title: 'Marco Polo', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page states that Marco Polo traveled from Europe to Asia in “1271-95,” spent 17 years in China, and returned to Venice via Hormuz and Constantinople. It does not specify a 1295 return date or state that he was captured by Genoa, dictated his Travels to Rustichello around 1298-1300, or described China’s paper money.
sources.qualifies: The travel period and return to Venice are stated; the other details are absent.

marco-polo-travels-paper-money-1300.verification_note: Primary text confirms Polo's paper-money account; Yule dates its dictation to 1298, so 1300 is a rounded date.

muisca-tunjos-salt-1300.summary: On Colombia's eastern highlands, Muisca communities around Bogotá, Tunja, Zipaquirá and Nemocón ran two linked crafts. Goldsmiths modelled flat figures called tunjos in beeswax, coated them in clay and charcoal, burned out the wax and poured copper-gold tumbaga, leaving casting sprues and rough surfaces because the pieces were offerings for lakes and shrines rather than display. Salt makers at Zipaquirá and Nemocón boiled brine in large ceramic pots, broke the pots and traded hard salt loaves down to Magdalena valley for gold, cotton and shell. Martinón-Torres and Uribe-Villegas's analyses of several hundred tunjos in Bogotá's Museo del Oro show individual makers' habits and deliberate alloy choices across roughly 600 to 1600.

sources.title: Martinón-Torres, Marcos and Uribe-Villegas, María Alicia, 'Technology and Culture in the Invention of Lost-wax Casting in South America: an Archaeometric and Ethnoarchaeological Perspective', Cambridge Archaeological Journal 25 (2015)
sources.author: Martinón-Torres, Marcos; Uribe-Villegas, María Alicia
sources.confirms: Muisca lost-wax casting of tunjos as votive offerings with unfinished surfaces, analysed archaeometrically.

sources.title: Martinón-Torres, Marcos and Uribe-Villegas, María Alicia, 'The prehistoric individual, connoisseurship and archaeological science: The Muisca goldwork of Colombia', Journal of Archaeological Science 63 (2015)
sources.author: Martinón-Torres, Marcos; Uribe-Villegas, María Alicia
sources.confirms: Analysis of individual makers' habits and alloy choices in Muisca tunjos.

sources.title: Uribe Villegas, María Alicia and Martinón-Torres, Marcos, 'Typology, technology, composition and context of Muisca metalwork (Colombia, AD 600-1800): a database', Journal of Open Archaeology Data 1 (2012)
sources.author: Uribe Villegas, María Alicia; Martinón-Torres, Marcos
sources.confirms: Dated corpus of Muisca metalwork spanning 600 to 1800 with compositions and contexts.

muisca-tunjos-salt-1300.verification_note: Goldwork is dated by the Museo del Oro corpus to a span of 600 to 1800, so 1300 is a mid-point. Salt production at Zipaquirá and Nemocón is described by sixteenth-century chroniclers and archaeology; no single foundation date exists.
muisca-tunjos-salt-1300.detail: Spanish chroniclers of 1537 met Muisca markets where salt served as a currency alongside gold discs and cotton blankets. Archaeometric work shows tunjos were rarely polished or depletion-gilded, unlike display pieces from Calima or Quimbaya traditions. Muisca territory had no gold deposits of its own; metal arrived by exchange, with salt and emeralds as principal exports. Chronology spans Early and Late Muisca periods; 1300 is a mid-point, not an event.

picture.credit: Muisca, via Wikimedia Commons

polynesian-navigation-1300.summary: By 1300 Polynesians had settled nearly every habitable Pacific island, steering by stars and swells alone. Archaeologists believe the first settlers reached New Zealand no later than 1300 CE, from a region in East Polynesia later called Hawaiki by Māori.

sources.title: Story: Pacific migrations
J. M. Wilmshurst, A. J. Anderson, T. F. G. Higham and T. H. Worthy, 'Dating the late prehistoric dispersal of Polynesians to New Zealand using the commensal Pacific rat', PNAS 105 (2008), 7676-7680
sources.author: Janet M. Wilmshurst; Atholl J. Anderson; Thomas F. G. Higham; Trevor H. Worthy
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Radiocarbon dating of rat bones and gnawed seeds places human arrival on both main islands of New Zealand at about AD 1280.

sources.title: J. M. Wilmshurst, T. L. Hunt, C. P. Lipo and A. J. Anderson, 'High-precision radiocarbon dating shows recent and rapid initial human colonization of East Polynesia', PNAS 108 (2011), 1815-1820
sources.author: Janet M. Wilmshurst; Terry L. Hunt; Carl P. Lipo; Atholl J. Anderson
sources.venue: Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences
sources.confirms: Settlement of the remote East Polynesian islands, including New Zealand, happened in a rapid pulse around AD 1190-1290.

rapa-nui-lithic-mulch-gardens-1300.summary: Farmers on Rapa Nui (Easter Island) covered large tracts of ground with fist-sized broken basalt, built rock-ringed planting circles (manavai) and dug stone-lined pits to grow sweet potato, taro, yams and bananas on a windswept island with thin, nutrient-poor soils. Satellite mapping in 2013 estimated these rock gardens covered between 2.5 and 12.5 percent of island area. Soil chemistry showed garden plots held higher phosphorus and potassium than adjacent ground, because fresh rock weathering released nutrients while stone cover cut evaporation and wind damage. Lithic mulching let a small population feed its people for centuries on one of Earth's most isolated islands.

sources.title: Ladefoged, Thegn N.; Flaws, Andrew; Stevenson, Christopher M., 'The distribution of rock gardens on Rapa Nui (Easter Island) as determined from satellite imagery', Journal of Archaeological Science 40 (2013)
sources.author: Ladefoged, Thegn N.; Flaws, Andrew; Stevenson, Christopher M.
sources.confirms: Satellite mapping estimates rock gardens cover 2.5 to 12.5 percent of Rapa Nui
sources.qualifies: Range of estimates is wide

sources.title: Ladefoged, Thegn N.; Stevenson, Christopher M.; Haoa, Sonia; et al., 'Soil nutrient analysis of Rapa Nui gardening', Archaeology in Oceania 45 (2010)
sources.author: Ladefoged, Thegn N.; Stevenson, Christopher M.; Haoa, Sonia; Mulrooney, Mara; Puleston, Cedric; Vitousek, Peter M.; Chadwick, Oliver A.
sources.confirms: Garden soils carry higher nutrient levels than non-garden soils
sources.qualifies: Sampling limited to selected plots

rapa-nui-lithic-mulch-gardens-1300.verification_note: Garden chronology is bracketed by settlement around 1200 and forest clearance; 1300 is a rounded approximate start.
rapa-nui-lithic-mulch-gardens-1300.detail: Rapa Nui was settled about 1200 CE; gardens expanded as palm forest cleared in following centuries. These fields supported perhaps 3,000 to 4,000 people and remained productive into European contact in 1722. Rock mulch techniques appear elsewhere in Polynesia and in arid regions worldwide, but Rapa Nui's scale is unusual. Satellite estimates vary widely because scattered stone from natural rockfall is hard to separate from deliberate mulch.

picture.alt: Two stone-walled manavai garden enclosures and a fallen moai at Ahu Te Pa Haha Tea, Rapa Nui, photographed by Mana Expedition in 1914
picture.credit: Unknown author

renaissance-era-1300.summary: From around 1300 Italy's Renaissance revived Greek and Roman learning and put humans at the centre of thought. This name covers Europe's cultural rebirth between late medieval and early modern eras, variously dated 1400s to 1500s or more broadly 1300s to 1600s. Its first traces appear in Italy before 1300 in Dante's writing and Giotto's painting; Florence led, with Italy and then wider Europe following. Its basis was humanism, built on rediscovered Greek philosophy and Roman humanitas. Vernacular writing and metal movable type from late 15th century spread its ideas far beyond Latin readers.

sources.title: Renaissance - Wikipedia
Shapin, Steven, The Scientific Revolution (University of Chicago Press, 1996)
sources.author: Shapin, Steven
sources.confirms: The page gives no Renaissance dates or facts. It refers to the “crucial 17th century” and says “in the 1600s science emerged” from varied beliefs, practices, and influences.
sources.qualifies: It provides 17th-century context but does not establish the claimed 14th-17th-century span, the Italian revival beginning around 1300, human-centered thought, or the broader cultural-rebirth dates.

sources.title: 'Renaissance', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page says the Renaissance is “generally believed to have begun in Italy during the 14th century.” Its “proto-renaissance” preceded it in the “late 13th and early 14th centuries”; Giotto (1266/67 or 1276-1337) and Dante belong to that period.
sources.qualifies: The page does not support spread into the 17th century.

sankore-madrasah-1300.summary: After 1300 Sankoré in Timbuktu drew scholars across the Sahara, and did for 300 years. It was built as Timbuktu took over trans-Saharan trade from declining Walata. Teaching grew around it under Mali and then Songhai rule, peaking in the 15th and 16th centuries under Songhai's Askia dynasty. It was never a centralized university on medieval European lines: individual scholars taught their own students, with some lectures held inside. Learning there declined after Songhai's defeat at Tondibi in 1591.

sources.title: Sankoré Madrasah - Wikipedia
Hunwick, John O., Timbuktu and the Songhay Empire: Al-Sa'di's Ta'rikh al-Sudan down to 1613 and Other Contemporary Documents (Brill, 2003)
sources.author: Hunwick, John O.
sources.confirms: Sankore mosque is associated chiefly with teaching, but there is no evidence of any institution called the University of Sankore; teaching took place in scholars' houses.

sources.title: 'Timbuktu', UNESCO World Heritage Centre
sources.confirms: Sankore Mosque was built in the 14th century and restored by Imam Al Aqib in 1578-1582; he demolished and rebuilt its sanctuary to the dimensions of the Kaaba.
sources.qualifies: It does not say Sankore became a centre of learning in the 14th century or that the peak was “under Songhai.”.

tarascan-copper-bronze-1300.summary: Metalworkers in Michoacán and neighbouring west Mexico, from about 1300, began alloying copper with tin and with arsenic, casting thin-walled bells by lost wax and cold-working tweezers, needles, rings and axe-money. Dorothy Hosler's 1988 studies traced techniques to Ecuador and Colombia carried by sea, then showed west Mexican smiths choosing alloys for sound and colour over hardness: high-tin bronze gave golden bells with a clearer ring, arsenical copper gave silvery sheen. Tarascan rulers at Tzintzuntzan controlled copper ores of Balsas basin and workshops that supplied elites across their state, which Mexica armies never conquered. Spanish records of 1520s list copper tribute and smelting towns.

sources.title: Hosler, Dorothy, 'Ancient West Mexican Metallurgy: South and Central American Origins and West Mexican Transformations', American Anthropologist 90 (1988)
sources.author: Hosler, Dorothy
sources.confirms: Southern origins of west Mexican metallurgy and its transformation into a bronze technology chosen for sound and colour.

sources.title: Hosler, Dorothy, 'Ancient West Mexican Metallurgy: A Technological Chronology', Journal of Field Archaeology 15 (1988)
sources.author: Hosler, Dorothy
sources.confirms: Two-period chronology with bronze alloys appearing in Period 2, about 1200 or 1300 to 1521.

sources.title: Hosler, Dorothy, 'West Mexican Metallurgy: Revisited and Revised', Journal of World Prehistory 22 (2009)
sources.author: Hosler, Dorothy
sources.confirms: Revised dating and ore sources in Balsas basin, Tarascan control of production.

tarascan-copper-bronze-1300.detail: Hosler defines Period 1 (about 600 to 1200) as copper only and Period 2 (about 1200 or 1300 to 1521) as bronze alloys, with mines near Churumuco and Inguarán. Bells carry up to 20 percent tin, far beyond any structural need, which Hosler reads as a cultural choice for tone and colour. Dating comes from stratified finds and radiocarbon at sites such as Tomatlán and Amapa, so 1300 marks an onset, not a single event.

picture.credit: Jaime Rodolfo Sánchez, via Wikimedia Commons

zhu-shijie-jade-mirror-1303.summary: Zhu Shijie, a wandering teacher who had already issued a popular textbook in 1299, printed Siyuan yujian (Jade Mirror of Four Unknowns) in 1303. Its 288 problems in three volumes extend counting-rod algebra to equations with up to four unknowns laid out on a board around a central constant, eliminate variables step by step, and solve polynomial equations to degree fourteen by a method akin to Horner's scheme. He also gives summation formulas for stacked piles and a triangle of binomial coefficients to eighth power. Chinese algebra reached its peak here and then faded until Qing scholars recovered rod methods and Western readers met them through Martzloff and Needham.

sources.title: Martzloff, Jean-Claude, A History of Chinese Mathematics (Berlin: Springer, 2006)
sources.author: Martzloff, Jean-Claude
sources.confirms: Siyuan yujian's four-unknown elimination, polynomial solving and series

sources.title: O'Connor, J. J. and E. F. Robertson, 'Zhu Shijie', MacTutor History of Mathematics Archive
sources.author: O'Connor, J. J.; Robertson, E. F.
sources.confirms: 1303 publication; 288 problems in three volumes; four unknowns; equations to degree 14; 1299 Suanxue qimeng

zhu-shijie-jade-mirror-1303.detail: Jean-Claude Martzloff's history treats Zhu's elimination procedure as a general algebraic technique rather than isolated puzzles. MacTutor's biography summarises content and dating. Zhu's text survived through Korean and later Chinese editions; little is known of his life beyond prefaces.

picture.alt: Page from Siyuan yujian (Jade Mirror of Four Unknowns) by Zhu Shijie, 1303, with a diagram and worked problem
picture.credit: Zhu Shijie, Siyuan yujian (1303)

sea-coal-ban-1306.summary: In 1307 Edward I banned burning sea coal in kilns in London and Southwark because of its smoke, the first recorded air pollution law; by 1321 to 1322 royal palace clerks were ordering coal for their king's own fires. Prelates, magnates and citizens had complained, and commissions had already inquired into lime kilns in 1285 and 1288.

sources.title: Popular Science Monthly/Volume 14/January 1879/Black Diamonds
[PDF] overview by ian williams - University of Southampton
Te Brake, William H., 'Air Pollution and Fuel Crises in Preindustrial London, 1250-1650', Technology and Culture 16 (1975)
sources.author: Te Brake, William H.
sources.confirms: The article (pp. 339-340) documents a royal proclamation of 1307 prohibiting sea coal in kilns, prompted by complaints from prelates, magnates and citizens of London and Southwark, with a commission two weeks later to punish offenders.
sources.qualifies: Te Brake dates the proclamation to 1307 and limits it to kilns; he cites the Calendar of Close Rolls, Edward I (1302-7), p. 537, and mentions no parliamentary petition.

sources.author: Brimblecombe, Peter
sources.venue: Journal of the Air Pollution Control Association
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed study of medieval English responses to coal smoke, including the Edward I commissions and proclamation; bibliographic record confirmed, publisher page blocked.

al-farisi-rainbow-explanation-1309.summary: Kamal al-Din al-Farisi, a student of Qutb al-Din al-Shirazi at Tabriz under Ilkhanid rule, writes Tanqih al-Manazir, a critical revision of Ibn al-Haytham's Optics; an autograph copy is dated Ramadan 708 AH (early 1309). In an appendix on halo and rainbow he treats a raindrop as a transparent sphere, places a water-filled glass globe in a dark chamber with one aperture, and traces sunlight through it. He shows that a primary bow comes from two refractions with one internal reflection and a secondary bow from two reflections between refractions, which also explains its reversed colour order. Theodoric of Freiberg reached identical geometry in Germany within a decade; Descartes repeated this sphere experiment three centuries later. Al-Farisi's account of why colours appear did not hold.

sources.title: Rashed, R., 'Le modèle de la sphère transparente et l'explication de l'arc-en-ciel: Ibn al-Haytham, al-Farisi', Revue d'histoire des sciences 23 (1970), 109-140
sources.author: Rashed, Roshdi
sources.confirms: Analyses al-Farisi's transparent-sphere model for the rainbow and its roots in Ibn al-Haytham's burning sphere.

sources.title: Rashed, R., 'Kamal al-Din al-Farisi', Dictionary of Scientific Biography (Scribner, 1973)
sources.author: Rashed, Roshdi
sources.confirms: Dark chamber with one opening and a water-filled sphere; primary arc from refraction, reflection, refraction; ring from two reflections; Wiedemann dates the final version between 1302 and 1311.
sources.qualifies: Gives Tabriz with a query as place of death in 1320 and dates completion to a range rather than one year.

sources.title: Sabra, A. I., 'Faresi, Kamal-al-Din', Encyclopaedia Iranica
sources.author: Sabra, A. I.
sources.confirms: Correctly accounts for the arc, primary and secondary bows and colour reversal; glass sphere in a dark room with a single aperture; colour explanation unsuccessful.

rashid-al-din-rab-e-rashidi-scriptorium-.summary: Rashid al-Din Fadlallah, physician and vizier to Ilkhanid rulers, signs an endowment deed for his foundation in an eastern suburb of Tabriz on 9 August 1309 (1 Rabi I 709). Rab-e Rashidi holds a mosque, hospital, library, paper mill and book workshop with salaried scribes and painters. A codicil of 1313 to 1314 orders two copies a year of his own works, including Jami al-Tawarikh, one in Arabic and one in Persian, on large Baghdadi paper, collated against a master copy, bound in leather and sent to cities across Ilkhanid lands for anyone to consult or copy against a deposit. Painters cut page sizes and simplified scenes to keep pace. An Arabic copy dated 714 AH (1314) survives split between Edinburgh University Library and Khalili Collections. Rashid al-Din is executed in 1318 and his foundation is looted.

wang-zhen-nong-shu-1313.summary: Yuan dynasty magistrate Wang Zhen (1271 to 1333) completes Nong Shu in 1313 after serving in Jingde, Anhui and Yongfeng, Jiangxi, where he saw northern dry farming and southern rice side by side. The book runs 22 or 37 chapters in three parts: general farming, individual crops, and Nongqi tupu, an illustrated catalogue of 273 tools from ploughs and seed drills to water-powered trip hammers, silk reels and polder fields, each with drawing, verse and notes on use. Bray calls his pairing of text with pictures a new method of encoding technical information, made possible by woodblock printing. He includes Chen Fu's rice methods and aims to carry southern wet-rice technique north and northern tools south.

wang-zhen-nong-shu-1313.detail: Nongqi tupu is the earliest systematic illustrated encyclopedia of agricultural machinery; later Ming compilers including Xu Guangqi copied its plates. An appendix describes wooden movable type Wang devised to print a county gazetteer, first such account anywhere. Wang's drawings of square-pallet chain pump, water-driven blowers and multi-tube seed drill reached Europe in 18th-century Jesuit reports. Some scholars cite 1303 for this treatise; Bray's 2008 and 2020 studies both give 1313.

wang-zhen-wooden-movable-type-1313.summary: In 1313 Wang Zhen set wooden movable type on a revolving table of 60,000 characters, cutting typesetting time. His Nong Shu described the type he had pioneered as magistrate of Jingde in Anhui between 1290 and 1301. Bi Sheng had tried wood in the 11th century and rejected it as unsuitable; Wang added exact methods for cutting and finishing type and locked pieces firmly into one frame with wooden plugs before inking. His main gain was speed: all characters were sorted by tone and rhyme on two revolving tables so one seated compositor could find each piece.

spondent-pariter-alchemy-ban-1317.summary: Around 1317, a conventional date since its decree is undated, Pope John XXII punished alchemists' fraud: they promised gold they could not deliver. His decree Spondent quas non exhibent, sometimes called Spondent pariter, targeted false metal without banning alchemy outright. Anyone making, ordering or selling false alchemical metal to pay debts owed one fine equal to what that weight of true gold or silver would cost, with prison possible. Using such metal to forge coins was condemned too, in a period when papal Avignon was awash in counterfeit currency.

ely-cathedral-tower-collapse-1322.summary: In 1322 Ely Cathedral's tower fell; in its place rose a timber octagon lantern like no other. Rather than rebuild on its old square plan, sacrist Alan of Walsingham's team removed all four tower piers and opened the crossing into one octagon absorbing adjoining bays, perhaps from distrust of soft ground under those piers. Its stone octagon carries timber vaulting and one glazed timber lantern that seems to float on slender struts. How much Walsingham designed remains debated.

mansa-musa-hajj-1324.summary: In July 1324 Mali's king Mansa Musa reached Cairo on his pilgrimage and gave away so much gold that its price fell for a decade. Al-Umari, who visited Cairo soon after, wrote that a mithqal of gold fell from 25 silver dirhams to under 22 and stayed there for at least twelve years. Historian Warren Schultz counters that this lay within normal swings in Mamluk Egypt's gold value. Most of what is known about Musa comes from such Arabic accounts written after his hajj.

ibn-battuta-travels-1325.summary: In 1325 Ibn Battuta left Tangier for Mecca and kept travelling for 30 years across much of Africa, Asia and Iberia, some 117,000 to 120,000 kilometres by different counts, far beyond Marco Polo's 24,000. Near his life's end he dictated his account, A Gift to Those Who Contemplate the Wonders of Cities, known as the Rihla; most of what is known about him comes from it.

tenochtitlan-founded-1325.summary: Around 1325 Mexica settlers founded Tenochtitlan on an island; in 200 years it was among the world's largest cities. Its exact founding date is unclear; 13 March 1325 was chosen in 1925 for 600th anniversary celebrations. Three raised causeways joined it to shore, cut by bridges that let canoes pass and could be pulled up in defense. It became capital of the expanding Aztec Empire and pre-Columbian America's largest city before Tlaxcaltec and Spanish forces captured it in 1521.

milemete-cannon-1326.summary: In 1326 an English manuscript drew Europe's first gun, a vase-shaped pot firing an arrow. It shows a vase-shaped pot-de-fer lying on its table, with one armored man about to touch its vent with red-hot iron. Such "iron pots" were bottles with narrow necks, loaded with powder and an iron-feathered bolt; they replaced spring-powered springalds. Through the 1300s tube-shaped barrels replaced them and grew into bombards.

djinguereber-mosque-1327.summary: In 1327 Timbuktu completed the Djinguereber mosque in mud brick; replastered yearly, it has stood 700 years. It is one of three mosques linked to the city's scholarly community. Ibn Khaldun credited its design to Andalusi scholar Abu Ishaq al-Sahili, reportedly paid 12,000 mithqals of gold dust; recent analyses trace its style instead to Saharan mosques and older African building, treating his influence as myth. Apart from a limestone minaret and some 1960s reinforcement, it is built of earth with straw, fibre and wood. UNESCO listed it in 1988.

wallingford-clock-1327.summary: In 1327 Richard of Wallingford described, in a treatise, a clock to show Moon phases and tides at London Bridge. William of Walsham finished it about 20 years after Richard died in 1336. His design showed mean time in equal and unequal hours and true solar time, lunar phases, positions of lunar nodes and tide height at London Bridge, almost certainly the most complex clockwork then in Britain. It was apparently destroyed when Henry VIII dissolved St Albans Abbey in 1539; modern reconstructions rest on Richard's surviving text.

vijayanagara-era-1336.summary: In 1336 two brothers founded Vijayanagara, which held southern India for three centuries against Deccan sultanates. This Hindu empire came to rule most of southern India, peaking under Krishnadevaraya (1509 to 1529), when it pushed Deccan sultanates north of the Tungabhadra and Krishna rivers. It survived until 1646, though central authority fell sharply after allied Deccan sultanates defeated it at Talikota in 1565.
