vijayanagara-hampi-waterworks-1336.summary: From 1336 Hampi grew on aqueducts and tanks into what was probably India's richest city by 1500. Vijayanagara's rulers made this site on the Tungabhadra River, in today's Karnataka, its capital. Its fortified urban core held roads, an aqueduct, water tanks, gateways, monasteries and markets alongside temples. Persian and Portuguese travellers described prosperity, farms and trading markets; by 1500 it was also the world's second-largest city after Beijing. Armies of allied sultanates conquered, pillaged and destroyed it in 1565, and Hampi stayed in ruins.

bardi-peruzzi-bankruptcy-1344.summary: In the 1340s Florence's two largest merchant-banking companies, Bardi and Peruzzi, collapsed; Britannica dates the Bardi bankruptcy to 1345. Both traded wool cloth, grain, oil and wine between England and Mediterranean ports and lent to governments. Chronicler Giovanni Villani, whose brother held a Peruzzi partnership, blamed England's Edward III for repudiating war loans he put at 900,000 and 600,000 florins. Edwin Hunt (Journal of Economic History, 1990) showed both firms lacked resources to lend on that scale, that Edward never specifically repudiated their debts, and that they may have recovered part of their advances through channels absent from royal ledgers; overextension, including support for Florence's war with Lucca, brought them down. Acciaiuoli, Florence's third great company, failed too.

black-death-1346.summary: From 1346 plague killed a third or more of Europe; scarce labour raised wages for a century. Yersinia pestis bacteria spread mainly by flea bites and, in pneumonic cases, by breath. Its origin is unclear; it reportedly entered Europe in 1347 at Genoa's Crimean port of Caffa under Golden Horde siege, then travelled on rats aboard Genoese ships through the Mediterranean.

egypt-black-death-1348.summary: Plague arrived at Alexandria by ship in autumn 1347 and spread up the Nile through 1348. Al-Maqrizi reports deaths in Alexandria climbing to 200 a day and, at Cairo's peak in late 1348, counts of thousands a day recorded at mosques and city gates. Sultan al-Nasir Hasan and his amirs withdrew to Siryaqus from 25 September to 22 December 1348 while prayers and funeral processions filled Cairo. Michael Dols, working from Arabic chronicles, documented a demographic collapse that recurred with later waves; Stuart Borsch argued that depopulation broke the labour-intensive dyke and canal system of Egyptian agriculture, with consequences lasting into the fifteenth century.

sources.author: Ayalon, Yaron
sources.confirms: Plague reached Alexandria in 1347 and Cairo in 1348; chroniclers reported hundreds of funeral processions daily and deserted villages; Dols suggested a majority of inhabitants of Cairo and Alexandria may have died

egypt-black-death-1348.detail: Dols compared Muslim and Christian responses: Egyptian ulama framed plague as martyrdom for believers rather than divine punishment, and did not endorse flight or contagion theory. Fustat residents nonetheless fled east, leaving quarters in ruins. Borsch's comparison with England found that Mamluk landholding arrangements left Egypt unable to reallocate labour, so output fell while England recovered. Scholars differ on total mortality, often cited as a third of Egypt's population.

black-death-jewish-persecutions-1349.summary: On 14 February 1349 Strasbourg burned 2,000 Jews alive, blamed for a plague that had not yet reached their city. As plague spread, Jewish communities across Europe were accused of poisoning wells, with confessions extracted under torture. Pope Clement VI had issued two bulls in 1348 declaring such accusations the work of "that liar" the devil, to little effect. Some 510 Jewish communities were destroyed between 1348 and 1351, driving large migration to Poland and Lithuania.

sources.qualifies: The general accusations and torture are stated, but the specific Strasbourg claims are absent.

sources.qualifies: The persecution is stated; those specific details are absent.

flagellants-1349.summary: In 1349 flagellants marched from town to town whipping themselves to avert plague; Pope Clement VI condemned them on 20 October that year. Spreading through northern and central Europe during the Black Death, they held plague to be God's punishment for sin; new members pledged thirty-three and a half days of pilgrimage, one for each year of Christ's life, under lay masters who heard confessions and dealt out whippings. France's king barred them on advice from Paris theologians.

charkha-spinning-wheel-india-1350.summary: Isami's 1350 Futuh us-Salatin gives earliest unambiguous Indian reference to a spinning wheel, a hand-cranked wheel driving a spindle through a cord, replacing drop-spindle hand spinning. Irfan Habib argues it arrived from Iran with Turkish rule in thirteenth century and spread through Sultanate towns, multiplying a spinner's output several fold and lowering yarn cost for a cotton industry already dyeing and printing for export. A manuscript illustration of 1468 shows a woman at a wheel. By Mughal period, charkha spinning by women in households fed weaving across Gujarat, Bengal and Coromandel. Gandhi later took this wheel as emblem of self-reliance.

sources.author: Irfan Habib

charkha-spinning-wheel-india-1350.detail: Habib traced textual and pictorial evidence in papers of 1969 and 1978, and he rejects claims of ancient Indian origin. Smith and Cothren argued for earlier Indian use; Habib replies that no pre-Sultanate Indian text or image shows a wheel. Year 1350 marks the earliest secure Indian reference, not first use.

ibn-al-shatir-planetary-models-1350.summary: Ala al-Din Ibn al-Shatir (1305 to 1375), muwaqqit responsible for prayer times at Damascus's Umayyad Mosque, writes Nihayat al-sul fi tashih al-usul, in which every planet, Sun and Moon move on combinations of uniformly rotating circles with no equant point and no eccentric deferent. His lunar model removes Ptolemy's doubling of lunar apparent size, and his Mercury model uses a Tusi couple. His al-Zij al-Jadid turns these models into tables. E. S. Kennedy and Victor Roberts showed in Isis in 1957 and 1959 that Copernicus's lunar and planetary models in his Commentariolus, a century and a half later, are mathematically identical constructions. Ibn al-Shatir also built a sundial for his mosque in 1371 and an astronomical compendium instrument.

sources.title: Kennedy, E. S. and Roberts, V., 'The Planetary Theory of Ibn al-Shatir', Isis 50 (1959), 227-235
sources.author: Kennedy, E. S.; Roberts, Victor

ibn-al-shatir-planetary-models-1350.verification_note: Nihayat al-sul is undated; scholarship places it in mid-fourteenth-century Damascus, so its year is approximate, and his 1371 sundial date comes from Janin (Centaurus 16, 1971).

ife-bronze-heads-1100.summary: Around 1310 to 1350 Ife's artists cast brass heads so lifelike that Europeans later doubted Africans made them. This head was cast in heavily leaded zinc-brass by lost-wax casting, in which wax is modelled, coated in clay, melted out and replaced by molten metal. Museum curators date it to the 14th or early 15th century, while Blier places such heads around 1310 to 1350 on thermoluminescence dates, during Ife's long period as trade and religious centre. Its identity and function remain uncertain; its beaded headdress, possibly representing a crown, suggests association with an Ooni, ruler of Ife, rather than a portrait of one named person.

sukhothai-si-satchanalai-kilns-1350.summary: Along Yom river north of Sukhothai, potters at Si Satchanalai and Sukhothai town built hundreds of brick cross-draft kilns and fired celadon, underglaze-black and brown-glazed stoneware. Thermoluminescence dating by Barbetti and Hein shows stoneware production after about 900, with large-scale output from thirteenth to fifteenth centuries after kilns moved from pits to surface structures. Jars, bowls and figurines from these kilns turn up in shipwrecks and burial sites from Philippines to Indonesia, filling demand when Ming export restrictions cut Chinese supply. Production declined in sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, and UNESCO listed Sukhothai and Si Satchanalai towns in 1991.

sources.title: Barbetti, Mike and Don Hein, 'Palaeomagnetism and high-resolution dating of ceramic kilns in Thailand: a progress report', World Archaeology 21 (1989)
sources.author: Barbetti, Mike; Hein, Don
sources.confirms: Stoneware after c. 900; large-scale production 13th to 15th centuries; decline 16th to 17th

sukhothai-si-satchanalai-kilns-1350.detail: Earlier Thai tradition credited Chinese potters brought by Ram Khamhaeng; excavation and dating instead show local evolution over centuries. Kiln counts exceed 200 at Ban Ko Noi alone. Shipwreck cargoes dated by Chinese coins and ceramics anchor export phase to fourteenth and fifteenth centuries.

picture.credit: sailko

yuan-paper-money-inflation-1350.summary: In 1350 Mongol China printed money backed by nothing; and the hyperinflation that followed helped end Mongol rule. Paper money under Jin and Song had already run through cycles of overprinting, inflation and public flight to silver. Mongol rulers issued their own notes from 1227, first backed by silk; Kublai Khan's Zhongtong and Zhiyuan notes in turn suffered devaluation and hyperinflation. In 1350 Yuan's court issued its final series, Zhizheng Jiaochao, as pure fiat money, and people widely refused it. Marco Polo's chronicler, William of Rubruck and Ibn Battuta all described China's paper currency to outsiders.

statute-of-labourers-1351.summary: In 1351 England's first national labour law froze wages at pre-plague levels and barred moving for better pay. Parliament enacted the Statute of Labourers under Edward III in response to labour shortages after the Black Death. It set maximum wages at levels paid before plague, specifically those of 1346, and restricted labourers from moving to seek better conditions.

It says the statute forbade hiring by the day instead of by the year or “other usual terms,” while its next two clauses set maximum day-work and piece-work rates.

taghaza-salt-mines-1352.summary: Ibn Battuta left Sijilmasa on 13 February 1352 and after 25 days reached Taghaza, a mining settlement deep in the western Sahara where houses and a mosque were built of salt blocks roofed with camel skins. Enslaved Masufa workers cut rock salt into slabs; each camel carried two, and caravans hauled them south to Walata and Mali, where a load fetched 20 to 40 mithqals of gold against 8 to 10 at Walata. Nothing grew at Taghaza, so food came in from the south and water from brackish wells. His account is the earliest eyewitness description of this trade that underwrote Mali's gold exports.

sources.author: Ibn Battuta; Gibb, H. A. R. (tr.)
sources.confirms: Departure from Sijilmasa 1 Muharram 753 (13 February 1352); 25 days to Taghaza; houses and mosque of salt blocks roofed with camel skins; Masufa slaves dig salt; a camel carries two slabs; prices of 8-10 mithqals at Walata and 20-40 at Mali

sources.author: McDougall, E. Ann
sources.venue: International Journal of African Historical Studies
sources.confirms: Scholarly study of Saharan salt deposits including Taghaza and their place in trans-Saharan trade
sources.qualifies: JSTOR landing page shows title and citation only

taghaza-salt-mines-1352.detail: Taghaza supplied salt to Sahelian markets until Moroccan forces seized it in the sixteenth century and mining shifted to Taoudenni. E. Ann McDougall's work on Saharan salts traces how control of these deposits shaped relations between Saharan nomads, Mali and Songhay, and later Morocco's 1591 invasion. Ibn Battuta's travel narrative, dictated to Ibn Juzayy after his return, survives in manuscripts edited and translated in the nineteenth and twentieth centuries.

strasbourg-clock-rooster-1354.summary: In 1354 Strasbourg's cathedral clock was finished with a crowing rooster, made about 1349 and installed about 1352, the West's oldest surviving automaton. Its centerpiece was a gilded mechanical rooster of iron, copper and wood, taken as a symbol of Christ's Passion. At noon it flapped its wings, spread its feathers, opened its beak, put out its tongue and crowed through bellows and reed. Reused in Strasbourg's second clock, it survives in that city's Museum of Decorative Arts and is held to be the oldest surviving automaton in the West.

firuz-shah-yamuna-canals-1355.summary: Sultan Firuz Shah Tughlaq ordered canals from Yamuna and Sutlej rivers in 1355 to carry water to his new town Hisar-i Firuza and to dry tracts of Haryana. Engineers dug channels roughly 150 kilometres long with fall graded for gravity flow, and Firuz levied a water tax (haqq-i shurb) on irrigated fields. Contemporary chroniclers Barani and Afif report rising revenue, two crops a year and new villages along canal banks. A rebuilt line of his Yamuna canal became Mughal Nahr-i Bihisht to Delhi and then British Western Jumna Canal, making this one of South Asia's longest-lived irrigation works.

Welch and Crane's Muqarnas study examines Firuz's building programme including Hisar and canal-linked hunting palaces. huolongjing-gunpowder-manual-1360.summary: Around 1360 Ming general Jiao Yu wrote the Fire Dragon Manual's earliest edition, finished by 1375, drawing on a now-lost illustrated text; its preface appeared only in Nanyang's edition of 1412. It guides use of gunpowder "fire weapons" China had used from the 1280s to 1350s: land mines, cast-bronze "eruptor" cannon about 130 centimetres long and fire arrows launched from hollow tubes, early rockets.

de-dondi-astrarium-1364.summary: In 1364 Giovanni de' Dondi finished a 107-gear clock that tracked the Sun, Moon and five planets on a tabletop. He, a scholar and physician, named it astrarium. Its 107 wheels and pinions combined timekeeping and calendar functions with displays of mean and sidereal time and of Sun, Moon and five then-known planets, following Ptolemy's Earth-centered model. Historians Bedini and Maddison call it the earliest astronomical clock with near-complete description and firm documentation. Its original was lost, perhaps in Mantua's sack of 1630, but de' Dondi's detailed account survives and has guided reconstructions.

ming-era-1368.summary: In 1368 the Ming expelled Mongol rulers and ruled China for 276 years, sending fleets to Africa, then turning in. This dynasty, officially Great Ming, ruled until 1644, China's last imperial dynasty ruled by Han Chinese. Founder Hongwu sought self-sufficient rural communities in fixed order. Yongle moved his capital to Beijing, built its Forbidden City, restored China's Grand Canal and sent eunuch Zheng He on seven Indian Ocean voyages. Beijing fell in 1644 to rebel Li Zicheng; Southern Ming remnants held out until 1662.

It gives no information about 1368, Mongol expulsion, the dynasty’s duration or end, fleets to Africa, or Hongwu’s policies.

haijin-sea-ban-1371.summary: In 1371 Ming rulers banned private sea trade; China turned from the ocean as Europe took to it. Founder Zhu Yuanzhang limited legal foreign trade to official tribute missions and placed overseas commerce under government monopoly. It answered Japanese piracy amid anti-Ming insurgency, but proved unenforceable: trade continued as smuggling, and piracy became endemic in waves, much of it by Chinese dispossessed by this policy. Piracy fell to negligible levels once this ban ended in 1567. It also slowed growth of China's domestic trade.

da-ming-baochao-1375.summary: In 1375 the Ming issued paper money declared valid forever and printed too much of it; within a century these notes were worthless. A note of 1 guàn nominally equaled one thousand bronze coins. They had no backing in metal reserves, and officials set no limit on printing. Overprinting plus government reluctance to accept its own notes destroyed trust, driving silver's price upward. Later emperors abolished issue; by 1535 one guàn of paper was worth 0.28 of a coin. Qing rulers took that lesson and long avoided paper money.

sources.title: Great Ming Treasure Note - Wikipedia

sources.confirms: The page identifies a chapter, “Paper Money from the Yüan Dynasty to the End of the Ch’ing Dynasty,” on pages 62-70. It states none of the specific claims about Ming notes, including the 1375 date, overprinting, depreciation, guàn-to-coin value, metal backing, or issuance limits.

ibn-khaldun-muqaddimah-1377.summary: In 1377 Ibn Khaldun's Muqaddimah explained why states rise and fall by social forces, not God or chance. He wrote it as introduction and first book of his planned world history, Kitab al-ʿIbar. It proposed ʿilm al-ʿumrān, a new science of human society and its changes through history, ranging over historiography, economics, political theory and ecology. Its best-known idea is ʿasabiyyah, group cohesion: ruling houses rise on the edges of empires through strong solidarity, lose it in power and comfort, and fall to groups with stronger bonds. Many modern thinkers count it the first work of sociology.

sources.title: Muqaddimah - Wikipedia
Chapter 3 Ibn Khaldun the Statesman (Ibn Khaldun, 2010)
sources.confirms: The page identifies this as Chapter 3, “Ibn Khaldun the Statesman,” in a 2010 book (pp. 60-96).
sources.qualifies: The page does not state that he completed a draft in 1377, describe the Muqaddimah as the introduction and first book of Kitab al-ʿIbar, or mention ʿilm al-ʿumrān.

sources.title: 'Ibn Khaldūn', Encyclopaedia Britannica

It does not explicitly say he completed it in 1377.
sources.qualifies: The other elements are supported, but completion in that year is not stated.

jikji-metal-type-1377-1377.summary: In 1377 Korean monks printed Jikji with movable metal type, 78 years before Gutenberg's Bible. This anthology of Zen Buddhist teachings, compiled by monk Baegun, was printed at Heungdeok Temple in Cheongju, three years after his death. His students Seoksan and Daldam, with Myodeok, published it in two volumes. Only its second metal-type volume survives, held in France's National Library. UNESCO confirmed it in 2001 as the world's oldest extant book printed with movable metal type.

It does not state that it was printed at Heungdeok temple.
sources.qualifies: The page supports the year, Korea, Buddhist subject matter, and metal-type claim, but does not name Heungdeok temple.

ragusa-quarantine-1377.summary: On 27 July 1377 Ragusa's Great Council, ruling a trading republic on the Adriatic (now Dubrovnik), decreed that people and ships arriving from plague-infected places could not enter until they had spent a month on Mrkan islet or at Cavtat. This law, recorded in Ragusa's Liber Viridis, was the first municipal isolation rule of its kind; Venice set up a lazaretto in 1423 and stretched it to forty days, a wait from which quarantena takes its name. Ragusa followed with a permanent Health Office in 1390 and built its Lazareti outside its eastern gate in the 1620s. Trentino, this thirty-day rule, worked without any knowledge of plague's cause, by matching isolation to how long an infected traveller took to fall ill.

ciompi-revolt-1378.summary: In 1378 Florence's wool workers, with no guild and no vote, ran Florence's government for six weeks. These unrepresented labourers were called Ciompi; belonging to no guild, they had no voice in government yet owed heavy taxes. After minor guilds demanded more office in June, the Ciompi took up arms on 22 June and on 21 July seized government, forcing the Signoria to create three new guilds with political office. Their government fell late in August 1378; a regime after 1382 repealed its reforms and dissolved those new guilds.

salisbury-cathedral-clock-1386.summary: Around 1386 Salisbury Cathedral's clock began running; it still does and is said to be Earth's oldest working clock, though its dating and that claim are both disputed. Two descending stone weights power it, one for its going train, regulated by verge-and-foliot escapement of the earliest mechanical type, another for its striking train. Its usual date rests on a 1386 document naming a clock keeper; specialists dispute whether the surviving frame, identified by Howgrave-Graham in 1929, is that clock or a later one.

sources.title: Salisbury Cathedral clock
Howgrave-Graham, R. P., 'A Great Cathedral Clock Rediscovered', Practical Watch and Clock Maker (1929) 445-447
sources.author: Howgrave-Graham, R. P.
sources.venue: Practical Watch and Clock Maker (Antiquarian Horological Society document archive)
sources.confirms: Howgrave-Graham reports the rediscovery of the Salisbury Cathedral clock mechanism, a clock documented at the cathedral in 1386, and describes the foliot escapement later replaced by an anchor.
sources.qualifies: He treats the identification of the surviving mechanism with the 1386 clock as an inference from documents, not an established fact.

sources.title: Church of England, 'Salisbury Cathedral', Church Heritage Record 12031
sources.author: Church of England
sources.confirms: The heritage record lists the cathedral clock as dating from about 1386 and among the oldest working clocks.

salisbury-cathedral-clock-1386.verification_note: A 1386 document naming a clock keeper, not the surviving mechanism, supplies its date; Howgrave-Graham identified that mechanism in 1929, and specialists still dispute whether its frame is the clock of 1386 or a later one.
salisbury-cathedral-clock-1386.detail: Set aside in 1884 when its successor was installed, it was rediscovered in 1928 in Salisbury's central tower, by then fitted with a pendulum in place of verge and foliot. Restoration in 1956 gave it reproduction verge and foliot; it now stands in Salisbury's north nave aisle near its west front. Its original bell tower was demolished in 1790. Rival claimants to oldest working clock include Beauvais Cathedral's clock in France, said to date from 1305 and entirely preserved in its frame, Chioggia's clock tower in Italy and Comayagua Cathedral's clock in Honduras, said to be Moorish work of the 12th century though records are lost.

picture.alt: Iron frame of Salisbury Cathedral's clock mechanism, dated about 1386, photographed in the cathedral nave.
picture.credit: Arpingstone (Adrian Pingstone), Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

dai-viet-firearms-1390.summary: In 1390 Vietnamese forces on Luoc river fired guns into Cham king Che Bong Nga's flagship and killed him, ending two decades of Cham raids on Thang Long. Sun Laichen traces how handguns and cannon moved from Ming China into Dai Viet in late fourteenth century through border trade and captured arms, then onward to Lan Xang, Lan Na and Ayutthaya during Ming occupation of Vietnam (1407-1427) and after. Vietnamese smiths adapted Chinese designs so well that Ming armies later copied Vietnamese guns. Tonio Andrade places this diffusion within a wider East Asian gunpowder age that predates Portuguese arrival.

sources.title: Sun, Laichen, 'Military technology transfers from Ming China and the emergence of northern mainland Southeast Asia (c. 1390-1527)', Journal of Southeast Asian Studies 34 (2003)
sources.author: Sun, Laichen
sources.confirms: Chinese gunpowder technology spreads to Dai Viet and mainland Southeast Asia from c. 1390

dai-viet-firearms-1390.detail: Sun's reading of Vietnamese annals, Ming Shilu and Burmese chronicles gives 1390 as earliest reliable firearm use in Southeast Asia. Portuguese chroniclers found guns already in Melaka in 1511. Sun stresses overland and riverine transfer rather than maritime European routes.

kingdom-of-kongo-1390.summary: Around 1390 the Kingdom of Kongo arose in Central Africa; a century on it exchanged ambassadors with Portugal. It began with marriage between Nima a Nzima of Mpemba Kasi and Lukeni lua Nsanze of Mbata; their son Lukeni lua Nimi began its expansion. Ruled by its Manikongo, it stretched from Atlantic shores to the Kwango River. Portuguese explorer Diogo Cão arrived in 1483, and in 1491 King Nzinga a Nkuwu was baptised as João I. Kongo stayed independent until 1862, then served intermittently as Portugal's vassal until Portugal abolished its monarchy in 1914 after crushing one revolt.

stromer-paper-mill-nuremberg-1390.summary: On 24 June 1390 Nuremberg merchant Ulman Stromer starts making paper at Gleissmuhle mill on the Pegnitz, first paper mill in German lands, with Italian workmen he had hired and sworn to secrecy. His own chronicle records it: »Ich Ulman Stromer, hub an mit dem ersten papir zu machen zu sant johanns tag und der Clos Obsser war der erst der zu der arbait kam«. Paper had reached Europe through Xativa in Muslim Spain around 1100 and Fabriano in Italy by the 1270s; Stromer's mill carried papermaking north just as demand from chanceries, merchants and, sixty years later, Gutenberg's press began to climb. It appears in Schedel's Nuremberg Chronicle of 1493.

sources.author: Stadtarchiv Nurnberg

stromer-paper-mill-nuremberg-1390.detail: Lore Sporhan-Krempel's 1954 article in Archivalische Zeitschrift remains the standard archival study of that mill, and Wolfgang von Stromer's 1970 Business History Review article sets Stromer family businesses inside Nuremberg's late-medieval trading economy. Stromer's account survives in his Puchel von meim geslechet und von abentewr, a family chronicle begun in 1360, which also records that he made his Italian workers swear not to teach papermaking to anyone outside his mill.

chaucer-treatise-astrolabe-1391.summary: Geoffrey Chaucer writes A Treatise on the Astrolabe in Middle English for a ten-year-old, opening “Litell Lowis my sone, I have perceived wel by certeyne evidences thyn abilite to lerne sciencez touchinge noumbres and proporciouns”. Its worked examples are fixed to a date: “the yeer of oure lord 1391, the 12 day of March at midday, I wolde knowe the degree of the sonne”. It is English's earliest technical manual and shows how far an Islamic instrument had travelled: a Latin tradition descending from Arabic texts, now put into English for a London household. A 15th-century copy survives as British Library Sloane MS 314, and 14th-century English-made astrolabes survive in Cambridge's Whipple Museum.

chaucer-treatise-astrolabe-1391.detail: Walter Skeat edited it for the Early English Text Society in 1872 and again in Clarendon Press's Complete Works of 1900, quoted here. Chaucer worked from a 12th-century Latin translation of Messahala's Arabic astrolabe text. It explains its parts first and then gives forty short conclusions, each a procedure such as finding daytime hours or an ascendant at a given moment, so a child could follow it with astrolabe in hand.

joseon-era-1392.summary: In 1392 a new dynasty, Joseon, took Korea and ruled for 505 years, creating Korea's alphabet along the way. Taejo founded it after overthrowing Goryeo, moving his capital in 1393 to today's Seoul. His kingdom lasted until the Korean Empire replaced it in 1897. It pushed its northern border to the Amnok and Tuman rivers, made Neo-Confucianism state ideology while discouraging Buddhism, and saw classical Korean culture, trade, literature, science and technology reach their height. Failed Japanese invasions in 1592 and 1598, then Manchu invasions, severely weakened it.

ho-quy-ly-paper-money-1396.summary: In 1396 Vietnam issued its first paper money, Thông bảo hội sao, and made people hand in copper coins the state needed for weapons. Hồ Quý Ly, a Trần court official who held power behind the throne under king Trần Thuận Tông, ordered those notes on Vương Như Chu's proposal. They came amid his run of reforms after old king Nghệ Tông died in 1395: examinations for scholars and low officials, translation of Confucian classic Book of Documents into Nôm script, rules on official dress and, in 1397, a new capital in Thanh Hóa. In 1400 he deposed Trần rule and took power himself, founding his short-lived Hồ dynasty.

medici-bank-1397.summary: In 1397 the Medici Bank opened in Florence, a date usually taken as its founding, and became its century's most powerful bank. Its Rome branch handled Church deposits; further branches followed across Italy and Europe, and it improved general-ledger accounting through double-entry tracking of debits and credits. It became Europe's largest and most respected bank, and under Cosimo from 1434 its wealth made his family unofficial rulers of Florence. Branches collapsed with Medici political power in 1494.

akan-goldweights-1400.summary: Akan communities in what is now Ghana and Côte d'Ivoire weighed gold dust on balances against small cast-brass weights, geometric at first and later shaped as animals, tools and proverb scenes. Timothy Garrard showed that their weight series derives from Islamic standards, the mithqal and the Islamic ounce, reaching Akan gold producers along Mande trade routes from Jenne and Begho. Akan smiths adopted this metrology about 1400 and used it until British colonial currency displaced gold dust around 1900. Hundreds of thousands of weights survive in museums, each a record of lost-wax casting skill and of a market system that priced gold against cloth, salt and later European goods.

sources.title: Garrard, Timothy F., 'Myth and Metrology: The Early Trans-Saharan Gold Trade', Journal of African History 23 (1982)
sources.author: Garrard, Timothy F.
sources.confirms: Akan made the Islamic weight standard the basis of their weight system from about 1400 to 1900; demolition of claims of a Roman-era trans-Saharan gold trade

akan-goldweights-1400.detail: For his 1980 book Akan Weights and the Gold Trade, Garrard used metrological analysis of more than 8,000 weights to overturn earlier claims of Egyptian or Portuguese origin, and in 1982 he demolished the myth that Roman-era caravans supplied Mediterranean gold. Weights also served as teaching objects: figurative types encode sayings used in dispute and ceremony. Dating of adoption is inferred from weight standards and trade history rather than excavated contexts, so the year is approximate.

picture.credit: Unknown author

kohala-dryland-field-system-hawaii-1400.summary: On Hawai'i Island's leeward Kohala slopes, farmers laid out a grid of earth and stone embankments and trails covering about 60 square kilometres, planting sweet potato and dryland taro without irrigation. Mapping of walls from aerial photographs and GIS shows expansion from about 1400 CE, with subdivision of fields intensifying through 1600 and 1700s. Dating of residential complexes found household numbers grew in step with new field walls. Kohala fed a growing population and supplied surplus for chiefs during Hawai'i's transition to archaic states under rulers such as 'Umi and later Kamehameha, who was born in Kohala around 1758.

kohala-dryland-field-system-hawaii-1400.detail: Embankments ran across slope to trap moisture and wind-blown soil; trails ran upslope dividing land units. Rainfall and soil age bounded field extent, with older, leached soils excluded. Later soil studies showed Hawaiian farmers targeted soils of intermediate age with the best nutrient supply. Production probably peaked around 1700 and declined after contact in 1778 as population collapsed from introduced disease.

madhava-kerala-school-1400.summary: Around 1400 Madhava in Kerala found infinite series for pi, 250 years before Newton. He is credited with deriving infinite series for π and for sine, cosine and arctangent, centuries before comparable work in Europe, and with correction terms that improve truncated series. Most of his writings are lost; later Kerala scholars, especially Nilakantha around 1500, name him as source, so attribution of some results is debated. His dates rest on circumstantial evidence from pupils' works.

madhava-kerala-school-1400.verification_note: Madhava is dated only circumstantially (about 1340 to about 1425), so 1400 is a conventional placeholder, and attribution of specific series is debated, some appearing only in Jyesthadeva's Yuktibhasa; MacTutor and Photoniques give his dates as about 1350 to 1425 and place his series around 1400, against a birth year of 1340.

mixtec-tomb-7-goldwork-1400.summary: Mixtec workshops in Oaxaca cast gold and tumbaga pectorals, rings, lip plugs and bells whose fine threads imitate wirework, using lost-wax moulds in which wax threads were laid over clay cores. Alfonso Caso's 1932 excavation of Tomb 7 at Monte Albán, a Zapotec tomb reopened by Mixtec nobles in Late Postclassic times, yielded more than 120 gold objects alongside turquoise mosaics, carved bones, rock crystal and silver. Ceramic mould fragments from Mixtec sites show a two-part casting technique distinct from South American practice. Spanish conquerors melted most Mesoamerican gold; Tomb 7 survives as the largest intact set of Mixtec metalwork.

sources.title: Levine, Marc N., 'Ceramic Molds for Mixtec Gold: a New Lost-Wax Casting Technique from Prehispanic Mexico', Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory 26 (2019)
sources.author: Levine, Marc N.
sources.venue: Journal of Archaeological Method and Theory
sources.confirms: Ceramic mould fragments show a distinct Mixtec lost-wax casting technique for gold.

sources.author: Ortega-Avilés, M.; Tenorio-Castilleros, D.; Segura-Venzor, I.L.

mixtec-tomb-7-goldwork-1400.detail: Caso dated Tomb 7's reuse to about 1300 to 1500 by associated Mixteca-Puebla polychrome pottery; Jansen and Pérez Jiménez read its carved bones as a genealogical record of a Mixtec lady. Mould fragments come from Yucundaa and other Mixteca Alta sites and show goldsmiths pressing wax into fired clay matrices before investing, which allowed repeated motifs. A 2020 analysis of silver-gold foils from Tomb 7 found hammered, annealed sheets.

moa-extinction-new-zealand-1400.summary: Within roughly 100 to 150 years of Polynesian arrival in Aotearoa around 1280, every species of moa, flightless birds standing up to 3.6 metres, was gone. A 2000 population model showed a few thousand hunters taking eggs and adults could achieve this quickly. A 2014 study assembled 270 radiocarbon dates from moa bones and eggshell in archaeological middens and found hunting peaked within decades and ended by about 1400 to 1450. A genetic study that year estimated a human population below 2,500 at peak exploitation. Moa loss removed New Zealand's largest herbivores and a major protein source, pushing Maori economies toward kumara gardening, fishing and fern root.

sources.title: Perry, George L. W.; Wheeler, Andrew B.; Wood, Jamie R.; Wilmshurst, Janet M., 'A high-precision chronology for the rapid extinction of New Zealand moa (Aves, Dinornithiformes)', Quaternary Science Reviews 105 (2014)

moa-extinction-new-zealand-1400.detail: Moa-hunter sites such as Wairau Bar and Shag River Mouth contain remains of thousands of birds, often with only legs taken. Habitat burning of eastern South Island forest compounded hunting. Earlier scholars argued for extinction spread over several centuries; high-precision dating has narrowed it. Some bone dates still carry old-carbon problems, so exact end dates vary by region, with southern populations perhaps surviving a few decades longer.

soroban-abacus-1400.summary: Around 1400, by one speculation, Chinese abacuses reached Japan as the soroban, merchants' calculator into the computer age. Smith and Mikami report historians usually assigning its importation to late sixteenth century, with Mori Kambei Shigeyoshi its first great teacher under Hideyoshi; merchants may have known its parent suanpan under Ashikaga shoguns. Early sorobans kept two upper and five lower beads per rod, as on the suanpan; Japanese makers cut them over time to a single five-bead above and four unit beads below, each rod holding one digit. Merchants used it from its arrival, but wide use came only after 1600, when mathematicians such as Seki Kōwa studied it and refined both device and methods. It is still taught in Japan.

sources.title: Soroban
Chen, Mark Yu-Shan, 'Mechanical Numeracy: Thinking With the Soroban Abacus in Modern Japan', IEEE Annals of the History of Computing 47 (2025)
sources.author: Chen, Mark Yu-Shan
sources.venue: IEEE Annals of the History of Computing
sources.confirms: The page calls the soroban “a traditional arithmetic tool” in modern Japan and says it persisted in households, businesses, and bureaucracy. It gives the publication date as 23 September 2024 and journal issue as Jan.-March 2025.
sources.qualifies: The page supports the soroban’s role in Japan but does not verify the origin, date, route, or design claims.

sources.author: Smith, David Eugene; Mikami, Yoshio
sources.confirms: States that the importation and improvement of the Chinese suan-pan as the soroban is usually assigned to the close of the sixteenth century, names Mori Kambei Shigeyoshi as its first great teacher, and argues merchants may have known it earlier during the Ashikaga shogunate.
sources.qualifies: Places the soroban's arrival at the end of the sixteenth century, not around 1400, and traces it to direct China-Japan trade rather than Korea.

soroban-abacus-1400.verification_note: Chen (IEEE Annals 2025) treats abacus lineage without stating a 1400 arrival in Japan, a conventional date; Smith and Mikami (1914) report that historians usually assign soroban's importation to late sixteenth century, with Mori Kambei Shigeyoshi as its first great teacher under Hideyoshi, and only speculate that merchants knew suan-pan earlier under Ashikaga shoguns, so about 1400 and a route through Korea sit at an early edge of that speculation.
soroban-abacus-1400.detail: Around 1850 its upper pair of beads lost one member, and this Japanese configuration ran alongside the suanpan until Meiji times, after which suanpan use faded. In 1891 Irie Garyū removed one earth bead, giving today's pattern, reintroduced in 1930 and popular from the 1940s. Rods come in odd numbers, never fewer than seven; basic models have thirteen, practical ones 21, 23, 27 or 31. On 11 November 1946 in Tokyo, Kiyoshi Matsuzaki's soroban beat an electric calculator operated by US Army Private Thomas Nathan Wood 4 to 1 on speed and accuracy across all four arithmetic operations.

taino-conuco-cassava-1400.summary: Across Hispaniola, Cuba, Puerto Rico and Jamaica, Taíno communities planted bitter cassava cuttings in conucos, knee-high mounds of loosened earth that drained heavy rain and eased harvesting of tubers. Women grated roots on boards set with stone chips, squeezed out prussic acid in woven tube presses, then baked flat bread on clay griddles called burenes, producing a food that kept for months. Fields also carried sweet potato, beans, maize, peppers and cotton; fish weirs, corrals for hutia and sea turtle completed the diet. Irving Rouse's synthesis and Newsom's analysis of plant remains describe this system supporting towns of several thousand when Columbus arrived in 1492.

sources.title: Rouse, Irving, The Tainos: Rise and Decline of the People Who Greeted Columbus (Yale University Press, 1992), ch. 1
sources.author: Rouse, Irving
sources.confirms: Conuco mound cultivation, cassava processing with graters, presses and griddles, and Taíno subsistence at contact.

sources.title: Newsom, Lee A., Native West Indian plant use (PhD dissertation, University of Florida, 1993)
sources.author: Newsom, Lee A.
sources.confirms: Archaeobotanical evidence for cassava, maize, sweet potato and other cultigens in Caribbean sites.

sources.author: Keegan, William F.; Hofman, Corinne L.

taino-conuco-cassava-1400.verification_note: Conuco agriculture is documented archaeologically from about 600 onward and in Spanish accounts after 1492; 1400 stands for the mature Taíno system at contact. Population figures for Hispaniola in 1492 are disputed across sources, so none is given.
taino-conuco-cassava-1400.detail: Las Casas and Oviedo, writing in the 1520s to 1550s, describe conuco mounds and cassava bread in detail; Spanish colonists adopted cassava bread as ship's biscuit. Archaeobotanical evidence from Puerto Rico and Hispaniola adds maize, yams and arrowroot. Griddle sherds and grater chips are common finds from about 600 onward, so 1400 marks the mature late Taíno system rather than an origin.

yap-rai-stone-money-palau-1400.summary: Men from Yap in western Micronesia sailed to Palau's limestone Rock Islands, negotiated quarry rights with Palauan clans, and carved aragonite and calcite disks with a central hole, some over three metres wide, using shell and stone tools. Finished rai were rafted and towed home behind outrigger canoes across roughly 400 kilometres of open sea. Survey and excavation of Omis Cave in 2001 gave radiocarbon dates showing quarrying by about 1400 CE, with far larger output after iron tools and European ships arrived in the 1870s. Rai value depended on size, quality and the story of each disk's voyage; ownership changed by public agreement while stones stayed in place.

sources.author: Fitzpatrick, Scott M.

sources.qualifies: Earliest quarrying dates have wide intervals

sources.author: Fitzpatrick, Scott M.; McKeon, Stephen

sources.qualifies: Analogy with cryptocurrency is interpretive

yap-rai-stone-money-palau-1400.verification_note: Fitzpatrick's dates indicate quarrying by at least 1400 CE; some sources place beginnings earlier, so year is approximate.
yap-rai-stone-money-palau-1400.detail: Scott Fitzpatrick and Stephen McKeon draw an analogy between rai ownership records, held in oral memory across a community, and distributed ledgers behind cryptocurrencies, while cautioning that rai were not currency in a strict sense. Omis Cave preserved unfinished disks, tool fragments and hearths. Captain David O'Keefe's trade in the 1870s enabled thousands of large stones, which deflated older values. Several thousand rai remain on Yap today.

zawar-zinc-smelting-1400.summary: By 1400 smelters at Zawar in Rajasthan made zinc by the ton, a method Europe did not master until the 1700s. Debris dates to the second millennium AD, with scale-up by 1300 to 1500. Zinc is hard to smelt because its ore, once reduced, leaves furnaces as vapour rather than molten metal. Zawar's answer was distillation: ore balled with organic matter went into clay retorts fitted with condenser tubes, set mouth-down in brick furnaces over water-filled vessels, where zinc vapour condensed and dripped down.

act-against-multipliers-1404.summary: In 1404, in a parliament that met that January (regnal year 1403 to 1404), Henry IV made it a felony to multiply gold or silver by alchemy; the crown feared cheap gold more than it wanted it. It forbade "multiplying" gold or silver, meaning transmuting base metals, since such metal could feed counterfeit coin and debase currency, weakening royal authority. Four decades later Henry VI issued licences exempting alchemists from it in hopes of paying for wars. Robert Boyle lobbied for repeal, which came in 1689 with the Royal Mines Act of 1688.

city-of-ladies-1405.summary: In 1405 Christine de Pizan's City of Ladies argued that women lacked learning only because they were denied it. She wrote it in French as her formal reply to Jean de Meun's popular Roman de la Rose. It opens with Christine despairing over Matheolus's Lamentations and their claims about women; Reason, Rectitude and Justice then appear and help her build an allegorical city whose walls and houses are famous women, each adding to her case that women are valued members of society who should be educated as men are.

zheng-he-treasure-voyages-1405.summary: From 1405 to 1433 China's treasure fleets sailed as far as Africa; after 1433 no more were sent. Zheng He, a Muslim-born eunuch who had helped the Yongle Emperor seize his throne, commanded them under Yongle and his successor Xuande. Yongle meant them to establish a Chinese presence over Indian Ocean trade, impress foreign rulers and extend his tributary system; preparation included so many interpreters that Nanjing opened a language institute.

yongle-encyclopedia-1408.summary: In 1408 Ming China completed its Yongle Encyclopedia in 11,095 volumes, a reference work unmatched in size until Wikipedia. The Yongle Emperor had commissioned this classified compendium of existing writings in 1403. Xie Jin's first version by 100 scholars was rejected as too small, and by 1405 some 2,169 scholars were gathering books across China. Never printed, it survived only as a 1562 to 1567 manuscript copy; most of that was lost in late 19th-century upheavals, leaving fewer than 400 volumes.

age-of-discovery-era-1418.summary: From 1418 Portuguese ships worked down Africa's coast, beginning voyages that joined every continent by sea. From about 1418 to 1620 seafarers from European states explored, colonised and conquered regions across the globe. Portugal began with Atlantic islands and West Africa's coast, reaching India by sea under Vasco da Gama in 1498; Spain backed Columbus's Atlantic crossings from 1492 and the Magellan-Elcano voyage that first circled the Earth in 1522. These routes spurred global trade and the Columbian exchange of plants, animals, peoples, including enslaved people, and diseases between hemispheres, and built European colonial empires with new centres of power beyond Europe.

ulugh-beg-observatory-1420.summary: In 1428 Ulugh Beg's Samarkand observatory charted stars better than anyone since Ptolemy. Its main instrument was a huge marble meridian arc, partly cut into rock so its building need not be tall, which measured solar altitude, star positions, year length, planetary periods and eclipses. Astronomers including Jamshid al-Kashi and Ali Qushji worked there and compiled Zij-i Sultani, tables and star catalogue listing about 1,000 stars, published in 1437. After Ulugh Beg's son had him murdered in 1449 this observatory was destroyed; its remains were found in 1908.

al-kashi-decimal-fractions-1427.summary: In 1427 al-Kashi used decimal fractions as routine, 150 years before Europe adopted them. Working at Ulugh Beg's observatory, he finished his Miftāḥ al-ḥisāb, Key of Arithmetic, that year. In it he used decimal fractions and base-sixty fractions with equal ease, a century and a half before Simon Stevin's De Thiende of 1585 made decimals common practice in Europe. The book also solves triangles from given sides and angles, so that in France the law of cosines is called al-Kashi's theorem. In 1424 he had computed 2π to 16 decimal places, unmatched for 180 years.

jang-yeong-sil-jagyeongnu-1434.summary: In 1434 Korea's Jang Yeong-sil completed the Jagyeokru, a water clock that struck the hours unattended. King Sejong, hearing of self-striking clocks abroad, had set his court technician to build one; after early failures Jang studied Chinese designs. Water rising in its lower vessel lifted floating rods that tipped small iron balls down pipes to release larger balls, which struck bell, gong and drum to sound each hour. Joseon used it as its standard of time. It did not survive; reconstructions follow written descriptions.

inca-chasqui-relay-1438.summary: From 1438 Inca relay runners carried messages and knotted records along 40,000 kilometres of road, covering 240 kilometres a day. Fresh runners at each station let a message travel up to 300 kilometres in one day. Chronicler Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa credited the service to Pachacuti, who began his reign about 1438 and wanted daily reports from his growing provinces; Juan de Betanzos credits his predecessor Viracocha Inca, and Martín de Murúa his son Topa Inca Yupanqui.

sources.confirms: The page says the Inca built a vast road network with two north-south routes: one along the coast for about 2,250 miles (3,600 km), the other inland along the Andes for a comparable distance. A relay service carried messages as knotted cords called quipu at “150 miles (241 km) a day”;

inca-empire-1438.summary: From 1438 Inca rulers under Pachacuti built an empire run by roads, storehouses and knotted cords, with no writing. He reorganized his Kingdom of Cusco into Tawantinsuyu, Realm of the Four Parts. Through conquest and peaceful assimilation he and his son Topa Yupanqui brought most of today's Peru under Inca rule; by 1533 their empire ran from Ecuador to Chile, pre-Columbian America's largest, built, as anthropologist Gordon McEwan notes, without wheel, draft animals, iron or writing. Spanish conquest began in 1532.

sources.title: Inca Empire - Wikipedia

sources.author: Ogburn, Dennis E
sources.confirms: The article gives no specific year for Pachacuti’s expansion and does not mention roads, storehouses, knotted cords, or Tawantinsuyu. It says dates from Chamical suggest Inca expansion north began “1 to 2 decades earlier” than the traditional chronology, and recommends building the timeline from 14C dates.
sources.qualifies: It discusses Inca expansion and challenges the traditional chronology, but does not confirm the claim’s specific date or details.

sources.qualifies: The page supports expansion beginning in 1438 and reaching Quito, but does not provide the claimed 1533 extent or administration detail.

inca-empire-1438.verification_note: Ogburn, Radiocarbon 2012: Inca imperial expansion began one to two decades earlier than traditional 1438 chronology drawn from Cabello Valboa.

inca-road-system-1438.summary: From 1438 Inca rulers ran an empire on 40,000 kilometres of road, without wheels or horses. As conquest spread from Cusco, they claimed exclusive right over routes many built centuries earlier by Wari and Tiwanaku peoples. They extended them into a single network of some 40,000 kilometres. Two north-south trunk roads, along the coast and through mountains, carried many branches, with paving where needed, stairways, retaining walls, drainage and bridges. Without wheels, these roads moved information, goods, soldiers and people across nearly 2,000,000 square kilometres holding about 12 million people.

quipu-1438.summary: From 1438 Inca officials kept census, taxes and stores on knotted cords called quipus, governing without writing. Specialists called quipucamayocs read these cords of cotton or camelid fibre. Pendant cords hang from one main cord; colour, order and knot type carry categories, while knots placed in decimal positions record numbers. Quipus appear in archaeological finds from the first millennium CE, probably under the Wari, and some features are thought to encode non-numeric information that remains undeciphered.

sources.title: Quipu - Wikipedia
Urton, Gary, Inka administration in Tawantinsuyu by means of the knotted-cords (The Cambridge World History, 2015)
sources.author: Urton, Gary
sources.confirms: The page describes “knotted-cord records” and says it investigates them using the Khipu Database.
sources.qualifies: Knotted-cord records are mentioned, but the claim’s specific historical details are absent.

sources.qualifies: The reader’s title is missing.

quipu-1438.verification_note: knotted-cord records are mentioned, but this claim’s specific historical details are absent; the reader’s title is missing
quipu-1438.detail: After 1532 Spanish officials accepted quipucamayocs' readings as evidence in tribute disputes. Just under 1,400 pre-Columbian quipus survive.

picture.alt: Inca khipu of knotted cotton cords, made between about 1400 and 1532, used for recording counts and accounts.
picture.credit: Peru, Inca Period, 15th-16th Century, CC0, via Cleveland Museum of Art

inca-stonecutting-sacsayhuaman-1440.summary: From Pachacuti's rebuilding of Cusco around 1440, Inca masons quarried andesite at Rumiqolqa and Huaccoto and limestone at Sacsayhuamán, dragged blocks on ramps and dressed them with river-cobble hammers of increasing fineness until each face met its neighbours with joints too tight for a blade. Jean-Pierre Protzen's experiments in the 1980s at Inca quarries showed a single worker shaping a block in hours by pounding and repeatedly test-fitting, with bedding joints cut concave to lock stones. Sacsayhuamán's zigzag terrace walls hold blocks weighing over 100 tonnes. Cieza de León, writing in 1553, recorded that twenty thousand workers served by rotation in its construction.

sources.title: Protzen, Jean-Pierre, 'Inca Quarrying and Stonecutting', Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians 44 (1985)
sources.author: Protzen, Jean-Pierre
sources.venue: Journal of the Society of Architectural Historians
sources.confirms: Experimental reconstruction of Inca quarrying and hammerstone dressing at Rumiqolqa and Kachiqhata.

sources.title: Protzen, Jean-Pierre, 'Inca Stonemasonry', Scientific American 254 (1986)
sources.author: Protzen, Jean-Pierre
sources.confirms: Fitting by repeated test-fitting and pounding; block sizes at Sacsayhuamán.

sources.title: Protzen, Jean-Pierre, Inca Architecture and Construction at Ollantaytambo (Oxford University Press, 1993)
sources.author: Protzen, Jean-Pierre
sources.confirms: Quarry ramps, block transport and construction sequence at Ollantaytambo.

inca-stonecutting-sacsayhuaman-1440.verification_note: Cusco's rebuilding is dated to Pachacuti's reign (about 1438 onward) from chronicle testimony; Sacsayhuamán's construction spans several reigns into early 1500s. Cieza's workforce figure is a chronicler's report, not a count.
inca-stonecutting-sacsayhuaman-1440.detail: Protzen found no evidence for metal tools or abrasives; hammerstone pitting on finished faces and on quarry rejects matched his experimental marks. Blocks were moved by ropes over prepared ramps whose traces remain at Ollantaytambo's Kachiqhata quarry. Cusco's polygonal and coursed masonry served palaces, Qorikancha temple and kallanka halls; Sacsayhuamán's construction continued under Tupac Inca Yupanqui and Huayna Capac into early 1500s.

walls-of-benin-1440.summary: Around 1440 Benin City was rebuilt to a plan, with earthworks that grew into history's largest made before machines. Its inner earthwork ran about 12 kilometres, and in places a 17-metre drop separated rampart top from ditch floor, every basket of it dug and piled by hand. Villages across Ewuare's kingdom had been raising such banks since the seventh century; this whole network, estimated at 16,000 kilometres enclosing 6,500 square kilometres, holds a Guinness record as the longest earthwork built before machines.

sources.qualifies: Only Ewuare’s broad chronology and late-fifteenth-century dating are supported.

cheugugi-rain-gauge-1441.summary: In 1441 Korea set standard rain gauges in every province, the earliest known national rainfall records. On 18 August 1441, by the lunar calendar, King Sejong ordered his Gwansanggam observatory to set an iron cylinder, two cheok tall and eight chon across, on a stone stand to catch rain; the Sejong Sillok credits this idea to his Crown Prince, later King Munjong. In 1442 dimensions were revised and standard procedure fixed, so provincial offices kept identical cheugugi and reported comparable totals.

sources.title: Ch'ŭgugi - Wikipedia
측우기 (Cheugugi), National Institute of Korean History
Hong, Jinkyu et al., 'Precipitation data in Seoul, Korea during 1778-1907', Scientific Data 11 (2024), 566
sources.author: Hong, Jinkyu
sources.confirms: States that King Sejong and his scholars invented the Cheugugi rain gauge in 1441, that King Yeongjo restored the observation system in 1770, and that palace records ran until a modern gauge replaced it in 1907.

sources.author: National Palace Museum of Korea

cheugugi-rain-gauge-1441.verification_note: Dates are split: this gauge was built in the 8th lunar month of 1441; a standardized nationwide system was ordered in 1442 (5th month). Title says 'standardizes' but year is 1441. Either year 1442 or retitle to its 1441 invention (recommended).
cheugugi-rain-gauge-1441.detail: Under that 1442 procedure, offices measured depth with a ruler, recorded when rain began and ended, and reported totals. King Yeongjo revived this system in 1770, and surviving gauges date from then.

picture.alt: Stone pedestal for a cheugugi rain gauge from Changdeokgung palace, displayed at National Palace Museum of Korea.

bahmani-cannon-deccan-1442.summary: Persian chronicler Shihab Hakim's Ma'asir-i Mahmud Shahi describes cannon (top) and gunpowder in Bahmani campaigns against Vijayanagara and Malwa from 1442, earliest clear textual evidence for firearms used in Indian warfare. Iqtidar Alam Khan's reading shows Deccan sultanates and their rivals acquired artillery through Persian Gulf and Red Sea trade and foundries staffed by Turkish and Persian gunners, decades before Babur's field guns at Panipat (1526). Gun founding then spread to Gujarat, Vijayanagara and Bengal. Surviving Deccan bronze guns at Bidar and Bijapur, including later Malik-i Maidan (1549), show large castings in copper alloy, a craft tied to local bell and icon metallurgy.

sources.title: Iqtidar Alam Khan, 'Early Use of Cannon and Musket in India: A.D. 1442-1526', Journal of the Economic and Social History of the Orient 24 (1981)
sources.author: Iqtidar Alam Khan
sources.confirms: 1442 Bahmani evidence as earliest clear cannon use; diffusion to 1526

sources.title: Iqtidar Alam Khan, Gunpowder and Firearms: Warfare in Medieval India (Oxford University Press, 2004)
sources.author: Iqtidar Alam Khan

bahmani-cannon-deccan-1442.verification_note: Khan 1981 abstract read. Monograph confirmed through publisher listing and reviews; not read to page.
bahmani-cannon-deccan-1442.detail: Khan's JESHO article dates earliest Indian cannon and musket use between 1442 and 1526 and his OUP monograph widens evidence to Gujarat and Bengal. Earlier claims of thirteenth or fourteenth century Indian gunpowder weapons rest on ambiguous terms for fire-projectors and are treated as unproven.

picture.credit: Santoshsmalagi

hangul-promulgation-1443.summary: In 1443 King Sejong gave Korean its own alphabet of 28 letters, so simple a reader could learn it in a morning. His court had been forcing Korean into Chinese characters built for another tongue. Each letter marks one sound, and five basic consonants are drawn as tongue, lips or throat making it, so a 1446 handbook could promise a sharp reader the whole set in a morning and a slow one in ten days. Officials kept writing Chinese for another four and a half centuries; in 1894 Korea's government made Hangul its preferred script for state papers, and both Koreas write with 24 of those original letters today.

sources.title: Hangul
Ramsey, S. Robert, 7. THE INVENTION OF THE ALPHABET AND THE HISTORY OF THE KOREAN LANGUAGE (The Korean Alphabet, 1997)
sources.author: Ramsey, S. Robert
sources.confirms: The page gives no year for Sejong’s invention and states no alphabet letter count or “learn it in a morning” claim. It says Sejong’s alphabet recorded Korean with “consonant clusters and a complex system of tones”;
sources.qualifies: Sejong’s invention is stated, but the claimed date, 28 letters, ease of learning, and specific letter-sound details are absent.

sources.title: 'Hangul', Encyclopaedia Britannica

sources.qualifies: The page does not specifically state that all 28 letters were created in 1443.

hangul-promulgation-1443.detail: Elites looked down on it for centuries, and it gained wide acceptance only in the late 19th century.

picture.credit: Government of Joseon, public domain, via Kyujanggak Institute (mirrored on Wikimedia Commons)

nezahualcoyotl-dike-1449.summary: After floods in 1449 inundated Tenochtitlan, Mexica ruler Moctezuma Ilhuicamina asked Nezahualcoyotl, ruler of Texcoco, to design a remedy. Workers from allied cities drove twin rows of stakes across Lake Texcoco, packed them with stone and earth, and built a dike of about 16 kilometres from Atzacoalco to Iztapalapa, with sluices that let water pass. It separated brackish eastern water from fresh western water fed by springs, protected chinampa fields and the city's causeways, and kept lake levels workable for canoe traffic. Chroniclers Alva Ixtlilxóchitl and Torquemada describe its construction; archaeology and colonial maps confirm its line. Spanish forces breached it in 1521 and colonial Mexico City flooded repeatedly afterward.

sources.title: Cordova, Carlos E., 'Late Aztec Settlement, Hydraulic Management, and Environment', in The Lakes of the Basin of Mexico (Springer, 2022), ch. 13
sources.author: Cordova, Carlos E.
sources.confirms: Nezahualcoyotl's dike within Aztec hydraulic management of Lake Texcoco, with length and function.

sources.title: Candiani, Vera S., Dreaming of Dry Land: Environmental Transformation in Colonial Mexico City (Stanford University Press, 2014), ch. 1
sources.author: Candiani, Vera S.
sources.confirms: Prehispanic dikes and causeways as inherited infrastructure that colonial drainage projects replaced.

sources.title: Milhauser, John K., 'Aztec Use of Lake Resources in the Basin of Mexico', in Oxford Handbook of the Aztecs (Oxford University Press, 2016)
sources.author: Milhauser, John K.
sources.confirms: Dike separating saline and fresh water and its role for chinampa agriculture and lake transport.

nezahualcoyotl-dike-1449.verification_note: Construction date of 1449 or 1450 comes from chroniclers writing after 1600 (Alva Ixtlilxóchitl, Torquemada); length is given as 12 to 16 kilometres across sources.
nezahualcoyotl-dike-1449.detail: Palerm's 1973 survey of prehispanic hydraulic works and Cordova's 2022 synthesis treat the dike as part of a Basin-wide system with Chapultepec aqueducts, Coyoacán aqueduct and smaller dikes at Mexicaltzingo. Length estimates range from 12 to 16 kilometres. Chroniclers writing a century later give its date as 1449 or 1450; no contemporary record survives.

bigo-earthworks-uganda-1450.summary: South of Katonga river in western Uganda, a community cut more than ten kilometres of ditches through laterite, some four metres deep, enclosing pasture and a central mound complex now called Bigo bya Mugenyi. It is one of about fifteen earthwork sites between the Katonga and Lake Albert; Munsa and Kibengo are next in size. Peter Robertshaw's radiocarbon and luminescence dates place digging at Munsa and Kibengo in the fifteenth or sixteenth centuries and Bigo at about the same time or a century earlier. He reads them as capitals of three contemporary polities built by cattle-keeping elites, not as evidence of a Cwezi empire of oral tradition.

sources.title: Robertshaw, Peter, 'The ancient earthworks of western Uganda: capital sites of a Cwezi empire?', Uganda Journal 48 (2002)
sources.author: Robertshaw, Peter
sources.confirms: Radiocarbon and luminescence dates place Munsa and Kibengo ditches in the fifteenth or sixteenth centuries, Bigo the same age or a century older; earthworks read as capitals of three contemporary polities rather than a Cwezi empire

sources.title: Robertshaw, Peter and Taylor, David, 'Climate change and the rise of political complexity in western Uganda', Journal of African History 41 (2000)
sources.author: Robertshaw, Peter; Taylor, David
sources.confirms: Palaeoecological and archaeological evidence linking earthwork construction at Munsa to climate shifts and growing political complexity

bigo-earthworks-uganda-1450.verification_note: Bigo's own dates are inferred from Munsa and Kibengo; Robertshaw allows a range from 1300s to 1500s.
bigo-earthworks-uganda-1450.detail: Merrick Posnansky excavated Bigo in 1960 and reported occupation debris, cattle bones and roulette-decorated pottery. Robertshaw's later fieldwork at Munsa linked earthwork construction to a period of drier climate and competition over grazing, and to a shift toward centralized power that preceded Bunyoro and Buganda. Dating of Bigo rests on few samples, and 1450 is a midpoint estimate.

picture.credit: Aishablue

chan-chan-chimu-1450.summary: Around 1450 Chan Chan, Chimu capital in northern Peru's Moche valley, was the largest mud-brick city on Earth, about 20 square kilometres fed by canals; the Incas took it within decades. Nine large rectangular compounds, independent units often called citadels or palaces, stand behind high thick earthen walls decorated with friezes, each holding temples, dwellings, storehouses, reservoirs and burial platforms. Moche valley canals irrigated its fields; an 80-kilometre canal meant to bring Chicama river water was abandoned unfinished.

chan-chan-chimu-1450.detail: Around those nine compounds lay thirty-two smaller compounds and four craft sectors. Earthen walls make Chan Chan vulnerable to El Niño rains.

gutenberg-press-1450.summary: By 1450 Gutenberg was printing with cast metal type; in 50 years Europe had 20 million books. His press printed from type cast in quantity, so a page could be set from reusable metal letters rather than carved or copied by hand. Movable type already existed in East Asia; his system joined type cast from a lead, tin and antimony alloy in his hand mould, oil-based ink and a wooden press adapted from screw presses used for wine and oil. Gutenberg, a goldsmith who had experimented with printing in Strasbourg during the 1430s, was funded by moneylender Johann Fust with 800 guilders; a second loan of 800 financed his 42-line Bible, completed in 1455 in about 180 copies, which showed the method working at scale.

sources.title: Wikipedia: Johannes Gutenberg
Fust and Gutenberg (Gutenberg, 2020)
sources.confirms: The page describes Gutenberg’s system: texts were broken into the Latin alphabet’s 26 letters, “cut and cast in metal once” and reused to print different texts, unlike copying whole texts by hand or carving them into wood. It identifies the Gutenberg Bible as dated 1454.
sources.qualifies: Reusable metal type is described; the other specifics are not stated.

sources.title: 'Johannes Gutenberg', Encyclopaedia Britannica
