By 1450, his “printing experiments” had reached “a considerable degree of refinement.” The page says his method used movable type and likely involved a readily melting, quickly cooling metal alloy, “oil-based ink,” and a press likely adapted from presses for wine, oil, or paper.
sources.qualifies: Hand mould and the specific timing/location are not stated).

gutenberg-press-1450.verification_note: reusable metal type is described; other specifics are not stated; hand mould and specific timing/location are not stated

henry-the-navigator-caravel-1450.summary: Around 1450 Portugal refined the caravel, a ship that could sail into the wind and so come home from Africa. Prince Henry the Navigator, needing better ships for Atlantic and West African exploration, gathered experts in mapmaking, navigation, astronomy and ship design at Sagres. Their caravel, a small decked vessel descended from Iberian fishing craft, was rigged with triangular lateen sails or lateen and square sails together. Unlike square-rigged barcas and oared ships then standard, it could beat to windward and handle open ocean, and was easier to steer. Diogo Cão, Bartolomeu Dias and later Columbus sailed caravels, opening routes for Iberian spice trade.

sources.title: Caravel - Wikipedia
Unger, Richard W., Portuguese Shipbuilding and the Early Voyages to the Guinea Coast (The European Opportunity, 2019)
sources.author: Unger, Richard W.
sources.confirms: The page identifies a chapter titled “Portuguese Shipbuilding and the Early Voyages to the Guinea Coast,” by Richard W. Unger, first published in 1995.
sources.qualifies: The topic matches, but the claim’s specific details are absent.

sources.title: 'Caravel', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page describes the caravel as a 15th-, 16th-, and 17th-century ship used for long voyages, and says it is thought to have been developed by the Portuguese to explore Africa’s coasts, encouraged by Prince Henry the Navigator. Its ability to sail “to windward” helped sailors return despite opposing winds and currents;
sources.qualifies: Those details are missing.

henry-the-navigator-caravel-1450.verification_note: Unger (2019) and Britannica confirm Portuguese caravel development under Henry; a Sagres school of experts is a legend not stated in either.

inca-andenes-moray-terraces-1450.summary: During 15th-century expansion, Inca state labor builds stone-walled andenes that turn steep slopes into level, irrigated fields with drainage layers of gravel and sand, and at Moray near Cusco cuts concentric terraces with radii of 45 to 65 meters and walls 3 to 5 meters high. Microclimate gradients measured between top and bottom of Moray bowls support reading Moray as a space for adapting potato, oca, quinoa and maize to altitude bands. Potatoes freeze-dried into chuno stocked state warehouses. Terraces let the Inca feed several million people on mountain land Spanish observers later judged unfarmable, and many near Cusco remain in use.

sources.title: Esenarro, D., Hidalgo, C. and Vilchez Cairo, J., 'Microclimates, Geometry, and Constructive Sustainability of the Inca Agricultural Terraces', Heritage 9:2 (2026), 56
sources.author: Esenarro, Doris; Hidalgo, Celeste; Vilchez Cairo, Jesica
sources.confirms: Measures Moray terrace radii of 45 to 65 metres, wall heights of 3 to 5 metres, drainage construction and temperature gradients between terrace levels.
sources.qualifies: Treats Moray's role as an agricultural experiment site as an interpretation supported by microclimate data, not as documented Inca intent.

sources.title: BBC Travel, 'The innovative technology that powered the Inca'
sources.author: BBC Travel
sources.confirms: Describes andenes construction, drainage layers and continued use of Inca terraces near Cusco.

sources.title: Peru Ministry of Foreign Trade and Tourism (MINCETUR), tourism inventory record for Moray
sources.author: MINCETUR
sources.confirms: Official description of Moray's concentric terraces and depth.

inca-andenes-moray-terraces-1450.verification_note: Construction dates for Moray and most andenes are inferred from Inca expansion under Pachacuti and successors; no written date exists. Experimental-station reading is interpretation.
inca-andenes-moray-terraces-1450.detail: Andenes reduce erosion, store daytime heat in stone and lengthen growing seasons. Moray's purpose as experimental station is inferred from microclimates and geometry rather than from Inca records, which were oral and knotted in quipu. Terrace building predates Inca rule by centuries; they scaled and standardized it with mit'a labor service under Pachacuti and his successors after about 1438. Spanish chroniclers recorded state granaries holding years of reserves, and terrace walls still stand after five centuries of earthquakes.

picture.alt: Concentric Inca terraces at Moray near Cusco, Peru
picture.credit: Kenneth Moore, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

machu-picchu-1450.summary: Around 1450 Inca builders raised Machu Picchu with drains so good it has stood without mortar since. Its dry-stone walls and engineered terraces drained excess water and limited erosion.

sources.title: Machu Picchu - Wikipedia
Burger, Richard L., 'New AMS dates for Machu Picchu: results and implications', Antiquity 95 (2021)
sources.author: Burger, Richard L.; Salazar, Lucy C.; Nesbitt, Jason
sources.confirms: The page says Machu Picchu was occupied “from c. AD 1420-1532,” with activity beginning two decades before textual sources linking it to Pachacuti’s rise in AD 1438.
sources.qualifies: It does not state that the site was built around 1450 as a royal estate, or mention mortar, dry-stone walls, drains, terraces, or erosion.

sources.title: 'Machu Picchu', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page says Machu Picchu’s dwellings were “probably built and occupied from the mid-15th to the early or mid-16th century”; it gives no specific construction date of around 1450.
sources.qualifies: Royal-retreat/palace evidence and terraces are stated; the precise date and drainage, mortar, and erosion claims are not.

machu-picchu-1450.verification_note: Burger and colleagues (Antiquity 2021) report AMS dates showing occupation from about AD 1420 to 1532, two decades earlier than a 1438-based chronology, so around 1450 is a late estimate.

picture.alt: Terraces and stone buildings of Machu Picchu, built about 1450 under Pachacuti, photographed in 2009.
picture.credit: Martin St-Amant (S23678), CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

yemen-sufis-coffee-drinking-1450.summary: By mid-fifteenth century Sufi circles in Aden, Zabid and Yemen's highlands drink qahwa brewed from roasted coffee beans during dhikr, their long night litanies. Arabic accounts collected by Abd al-Qadir al-Jaziri in the 1550s credit Jamal al-Din al-Dhabhani, a jurist and Sufi of Aden who died in 1470 to 1471, with adopting this drink after seeing it in Ethiopia and finding it drove off fatigue. Ralph Hattox, reviewing every early source in 1985, concludes coffee entered common urban use in Yemen in the mid-1400s and no earlier reference exists. From Yemen both habit and commercial planting spread to Mecca by about 1500 and to Cairo soon after, and Yemeni terraces supplied almost all coffee sold worldwide for two centuries.

sources.title: Hattox, R. S., Coffee and Coffeehouses: The Origins of a Social Beverage in the Medieval Near East (University of Washington Press, 1985), ch. 2
sources.author: Hattox, Ralph S.
sources.confirms: Coffee came into general use in Islamic lands in the mid-fifteenth century among Yemeni Sufis; al-Dhabhani died 875 AH (1470-71).

sources.title: Hattox, R. S., Coffee and Coffeehouses, full text (Internet Archive)
sources.author: Hattox, Ralph S.
sources.confirms: Translates Ibn Abd al-Ghaffar's account of Sufi use in Yemen and al-Dhabhani's Ethiopian journey; conclusion that adoption by Sufi groups in Yemeni cities dates to the mid-fifteenth century.
sources.qualifies: Hattox treats the Ethiopian journey as legend and allows that others may have used coffee in Yemen slightly earlier.

yemen-sufis-coffee-drinking-1450.verification_note: No contemporary fifteenth-century text survives; dating rests on sixteenth-century Arabic accounts analysed by Hattox, who gives mid-fifteenth century. A 1454 date often quoted is unconfirmed.

picture.alt: View of Mocha, Yemen's coffee port, from Olfert Dapper's 1680 description of Arabia
picture.credit: Olfert Dapper / Jacob van Meurs, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

hwacha-rocket-launcher-1451.summary: In 1451 King Munjong of Korea ordered stronger hwachas, carts firing up to 200 rocket arrows at once; Korean scientists including Yi To and Ch'oe Haesan had built the first in 1409. His Munjong hwacha, purportedly designed by king and brother together, had interchangeable modules firing 100 rocket arrows or 200 darts from 50 barrels. Fifty units guarded Seoul and 80 its northern border. In the 1590s, 40 hwachas helped 3,400 Koreans repel 30,000 Japanese at Haengju.

sources.title: Hwacha - Wikipedia
Cho, Sung-Jin, 'Lessons Learned: An Analysis of the Combat Effectiveness of the Joseon Singijeon Using a Ballistic Model', Journal of the KNST 9 (2026)
sources.author: Cho, Sung-Jin; Jung, Se-Youn
sources.confirms: The page states that the Joseon-era Singijeon was mounted on a Hwacha and could launch multiple projectiles simultaneously. It gives no date of 1451, no mention of King Munjong, and no figure of 100 or 200 rockets.
sources.qualifies: The launcher and simultaneous launches are stated; the claimed date, king, and rocket counts are not.

sources.title: 'Rocket and missile system', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page gives 1232 for Chinese defenders using weapons described as “arrows of flying fire,” but says there is “no explicit statement that these arrows were rockets.” It provides no information about Joseon, hwachas, Yi To, Ch’oe Haesan, King Munjong, 1409, 1451, or carts firing 200 rocket arrows.
sources.qualifies: It mentions an early rocket-related claim, but does not confirm the Korean names, dates, or figure.

hwacha-rocket-launcher-1451.verification_note: Cho, Journal of the KNST 2026, confirms singijeon mounted on a hwacha fired many projectiles at once; its 1451 date and 100-rocket count were not stated.

picture.alt: Reconstructed hwacha cart with its rack of launching tubes for singijeon rocket arrows, later photograph of a museum reconstruction.
picture.credit: Josh Berglund, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

fall-of-constantinople-orban-cannon-1453.summary: In 1453 Ottoman cannon brought down Constantinople's walls, which had resisted attack for 800 years. Sultan Mehmed II's army took the city after a 53-day siege. About 7,000 defenders held twelve miles of fifth-century Theodosian wall. Mehmed brought some 70 large guns from Edirne plus bombards cast on site, among them Hungarian engineer Orban's 8.2-metre "Basilica", which threw a 270-kilogram stone ball over a mile but took hours to reload. Repeated heavy shot opened breaches that infantry stormed.

sources.title: Fall of Constantinople - Wikipedia
Philippides, Marios, The Siege and the Fall of Constantinople in 1453 (Routledge, 2017)
sources.author: Philippides, Marios; Hanak, Walter K.
sources.confirms: The page identifies the book as about “The Siege and the Fall of Constantinople in 1453.” It gives no details about cannon, Sultan Mehmed II, the siege’s duration, defenders, or the city walls.
sources.qualifies: The year 1453 is stated; the other claim details are absent.

sources.title: 'Fall of Constantinople', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page states the city fell on May 29, 1453, after a 55-day siege. Ottoman cannon bombardment began April 6 and “brought down a section of the wall”;
sources.qualifies: Cannon support and the fall are confirmed; the siege duration differs from 53 days, and the other claims are not stated.

fall-of-constantinople-orban-cannon-1453.verification_note: Philippides and Hanak (2011) and Britannica confirm its fall on 29 May 1453 after bombardment; Britannica gives a 55-day siege and land walls of 6.5 km, against 53 days and twelve miles in other accounts.

picture.alt: Dardanelles Gun, bronze bombard cast in 1464 on pattern of Orban's siege guns of 1453, photographed at Fort Nelson, Hampshire.
picture.credit: Tim Sheerman-Chase, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

gutenberg-bible-1454.summary: In 1454 Gutenberg put the first printed Bibles on sale in Mainz; a book that took a scribe a year could be made by the hundred. Preparation probably began soon after 1450; his first precisely datable printing is a 31-line indulgence that existed by 22 October 1454. In March 1455 Enea Silvio Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II, wrote that he had seen pages displayed in Frankfurt and that all copies, 158 or 180, were already spoken for. Some sold for 30 florins, about 100 grams of gold. Forty-nine copies survive in substantial part.

sources.title: Gutenberg Bible - Wikipedia
The Gutenberg Bible (B 42) of 1454 (Gutenberg, 2020)
sources.confirms: The page identifies “The Gutenberg Bible (B 42) of 1454” and describes Gutenberg’s “master work of 1,282 pages - the Latin Bible.” It says he used the Vulgate, St Jerome’s “late-4th-century translation of the Septuagint,” in a Rhineland textual variant of a 13th-century Parisian revision.
sources.qualifies: Those claims are absent.

sources.title: 'Gutenberg Bible', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page says Gutenberg “completed it about 1455” at Mainz, Germany. It describes a three-volume Latin Bible printed in 42-line columns, with six compositors working simultaneously in its later stages.
sources.qualifies: The page gives about 1455, not 1454, and does not provide the other claimed details.

gutenberg-bible-1454.verification_note: A Brill chapter titles this Bible 'B42 of 1454' with 1,282 pages; Britannica gives completion about 1455, so 1454 marks when sales began and not completion.

picture.alt: Library of Congress's vellum Gutenberg Bible, printed in Mainz about 1454 to 1455, photographed on display in 2015.
picture.credit: MC BSU, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

bereguardo-canal-pound-locks-1458.summary: Bertola da Novate, ducal engineer to Francesco Sforza from 1451, completes a 19 km canal from Abbiategrasso to Bereguardo near Milan with 18 pound locks dropping 24 metres, Europe's first canal with a series of chambered locks. A single pound lock had been tried on the Naviglio Grande in 1438, and a lock at Vreeswijk in Holland in 1373 is probably Europe's first. China had built its first pound lock on the Grand Canal in 984, as Joseph Needham showed in a 1963 Newcomen Society paper. Milanese canals continued: Martesana in 1470, and in 1497 Leonardo da Vinci, as ducal engineer, fitted San Marco lock with the first mitre gates, V-shaped pairs still used on canals today.

sources.title: Needham, J., 'China and the Invention of the Pound-Lock', Transactions of the Newcomen Society 36 (1963), 85-107
sources.author: Needham, Joseph
sources.confirms: Landing page read: paper on the 10th-century Chinese pound lock and its European successors, read at the Science Museum on 1 April 1964; pages 85 to 107 confirmed, full text not opened.

sources.title: 'Bereguardo Canal', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: First European canal with a series of pound locks; 1438 lock on the Naviglio Grande; Bertola da Novate engineer from 1451, canal stopped at Bereguardo in 1458; 19 km, 24 m fall, 18 locks; Martesana 1470; Leonardo's San Marco lock 1497 with first mitre gates.

sources.title: 'Canals and inland waterways', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: Vreeswijk lock of 1373 the probable first pound lock in Europe.

picture.alt: Remains of an old lock on the Naviglio di Bereguardo near Milan.
picture.credit: Yorick39, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

chapultepec-aqueduct-1449.summary: In 1466, under Moctezuma I, Tenochtitlan's new aqueduct had two channels, so water flowed while one was cleaned. Its two stone-masonry troughs kept water flowing while one was being maintained.

sources.title: Chapultepec aqueduct - Wikipedia
Solis Olguin, Felipe, 'Chapultepec, espacio ritual y secular de los tlatoani aztecas', Arqueologia Mexicana 57 (2002) 36-40
sources.author: Solis Olguin, Felipe
sources.confirms: Solis describes the Chapultepec aqueduct built in 1466 during the reign of Moctezuma I, with two channels so one could be cleaned while the other carried water, a design attributed to Nezahualcoyotl.
sources.qualifies: Solis dates the aqueduct to 1466, not 1449.

sources.title: Castaneda Gonzalez, Rocio, 'Water and the Aztec Empire', in Water Management in the Valley of Mexico (Springer, 2024) 3-16
sources.author: Castaneda Gonzalez, Rocio
sources.confirms: The chapter describes the aqueduct from the Chapultepec springs as the main fresh water supply of Tenochtitlan.
sources.qualifies: The chapter does not give a construction date.

chapultepec-aqueduct-1449.verification_note: Solis dates this Chapultepec aqueduct to 1466 in Moctezuma I's reign, with two channels and a design attributed to Nezahualcoyotl; an earlier aqueduct is sometimes placed in the 1420s or 1440s, and no peer-reviewed source gives 1449.

inca-qollqa-storehouses-1470.summary: Along Qhapaq Ñan roads and above provincial centres, Inca administrators built rows of round and rectangular stone storehouses, qollqa, on cool, windy hillsides. Floors raised on gravel and ventilation ducts kept chuño (freeze-dried potato), maize, quinoa, dried meat, cloth and weapons dry for years. At Hatun Xauxa in Peru's Mantaro valley, D'Altroy and Earle counted more than 2,000 qollqa with over 170,000 cubic metres of capacity; Cotapachi in Bolivia held about 2,400. Khipu keepers recorded contents. Stored staples fed armies, labour drafts under the mit'a system and relief after frost or drought, and Spanish armies in the 1530s lived off these stores for years.

sources.title: D'Altroy, Terence N. and Earle, Timothy K., 'Staple Finance, Wealth Finance, and Storage in the Inka Political Economy', Current Anthropology 26 (1985)
sources.author: D'Altroy, Terence N.; Earle, Timothy K.
sources.confirms: Counts and capacity of qollqa at Hatun Xauxa and the staple-finance model of Inca storage.

sources.title: LeVine, Terry Y. (ed.), Inka Storage Systems (University of Oklahoma Press, 1992)
sources.author: LeVine, Terry Y.
sources.confirms: Regional surveys of storehouse architecture, ventilation and contents across Inca provinces.

sources.title: Earle, Timothy, 'Staple Finance, Wealth Finance, and Storage in the Inka Political Economy', in Bronze Age Economics (Routledge, 2018), ch. 10
sources.author: Earle, Timothy
sources.confirms: Reprint and reassessment of the storage model.

inca-qollqa-storehouses-1470.detail: D'Altroy and Earle's 1985 model distinguishes staple finance (bulk food and cloth stored locally) from wealth finance (prestige goods moved to Cusco). Terry LeVine's 1992 volume gathers surveys of storage at Huánuco Pampa, Pumpu and Cuzco. Chuño production, freezing potatoes overnight at altitude and trampling out water, long predates the Inca but reached state scale in these depots. Construction dates follow Inca conquest of each province, roughly 1460 to 1530.

picture.alt: Row of stone qollqa storehouses on a hillside at Ollantaytambo, Peru; modern photograph
picture.credit: D. Gordon E. Robertson, via Wikimedia Commons

inca-tin-bronze-1470.summary: As Inca armies and administrators extended Tawantinsuyu under Pachacuti and Tupac Inca Yupanqui, they replaced local arsenical copper with tin bronze for chisels, axes, tumi knives, crowbars, mace heads and tupu pins, drawing tin from cassiterite deposits of Bolivia's altiplano. Heather Lechtman's 1984 analysis in Technology and Culture argued that Inca state policy, not metallurgical advantage alone, drove this shift: tin bronze cast well and could be standardised, and its distribution marked imperial reach. Sites from Ecuador to northwest Argentina show tin bronze appearing with Inca ceramics. Earlier Andean metallurgy had prized colour and surface; Inca practice added uniform alloy for utilitarian objects.

sources.title: Lechtman, Heather, 'Andean Value Systems and the Development of Prehistoric Metallurgy', Technology and Culture 25 (1984)
sources.author: Lechtman, Heather
sources.confirms: Inca adoption of tin bronze as an imperial standard and its contrast with earlier Andean emphasis on colour and surface.

sources.title: Lechtman, Heather, 'Andean Metallurgy in Prehistory', in Roberts and Thornton (eds), Archaeometallurgy in Global Perspective (Springer, 2014)
sources.author: Lechtman, Heather
sources.confirms: Chronology of arsenical and tin bronzes in the Andes and Inca-period distribution.

sources.title: Shimada, Izumi and Merkel, John F., 'Copper-Alloy Metallurgy in Ancient Peru', Scientific American 265 (1991)
sources.author: Shimada, Izumi; Merkel, John F.
sources.confirms: Arsenical bronze tradition on the north coast that Inca tin bronze displaced.

inca-tin-bronze-1470.detail: Lechtman's samples from Machu Picchu and provincial centres showed tin contents clustered around 5 to 8 percent, consistent with controlled alloying. Tin bronze had existed since Tiwanaku times around Lake Titicaca; Inca expansion from the 1460s made it empire-wide. Gold and silver remained state monopolies for cult and display, worked at Cusco by specialists drawn from conquered Chimú workshops after 1470.

picture.alt: Inca cast bronze tumi knife with figures on its handle, Metropolitan Museum of Art
picture.credit: This file was donated to Wikimedia Commons as part of a project by the Metropolitan Museum of Art. See the Image and Dat, via Wikimedia Commons
picture.changes: resized to 1200 px long edge; converted to JPEG

venetian-patent-statute-1474.summary: In 1474 Venice passed the first patent law: register a new device, get ten years' sole right. Its Senate's statute was Europe's first statutory patent system, possibly the world's earliest codified one. Its text argues that clever men gather in Venice and would invent more if others could not copy their works and take their honor. Anyone who perfected "any new and ingenious device, not previously made" in Venetian lands was to register it with the Provveditori di Comun; for up to ten years nobody else could make one without its inventor's consent. Some historians see it as codifying existing custom rather than founding modern patent law.

sources.title: Venetian Patent Statute - Wikipedia
Kostylo, Joanna, 'Commentary on the Venetian Statute on Industrial Brevets (1474)', in Primary Sources on Copyright (1450-1900), eds. L. Bently and M. Kretschmer (2008)
sources.author: Kostylo, Joanna
sources.confirms: Venetian Senate passed the first general patent law on 19 March 1474, requiring registration of new and ingenious devices with the Provveditori di Comun for ten years of protection.
sources.qualifies: Kostylo frames the statute as codifying earlier Venetian custom rather than as the start of modern patents.

sources.title: Long, Pamela O., 'Invention, Authorship, "Intellectual Property," and the Origin of Patents: Notes toward a Conceptual History', Technology and Culture 32 (1991), 846-884
sources.author: Long, Pamela O.
sources.confirms: Peer-reviewed conceptual history of invention and patents in the special issue on patents and invention; the abstract frames the Venetian origin of patents within earlier craft and guild practice rather than as a clean founding.

sources.title: Nard, Craig A. and Andrew P. Morriss, 'Constitutionalizing Patents: From Venice to Philadelphia', Review of Law and Economics 2 (2006)
sources.author: Nard, Craig A.; Morriss, Andrew P.
sources.confirms: Abstract names the Venetian patent statute of 1474 as the first of three events that constitutionalized patent law.

venetian-patent-statute-1474.verification_note: Primary-source commentary confirms this 19 March 1474 statute and its terms; Kostylo cautions it codified existing practice.
venetian-patent-statute-1474.detail: Infringers faced a fine of 100 ducats and destruction of their copy. Venice granted about 2,000 patents under this statute by 1788.

picture.alt: Manuscript text of Venetian Senate's patent statute of 19 March 1474, from Archivio di Stato di Venezia.
picture.credit: Senate of Venice, public domain, via Archivio di Stato di Venezia (mirrored on Wikimedia Commons)

caxton-press-westminster-1476.summary: In 1476 William Caxton opened England's first press at Westminster, and his choices helped fix English spelling. Earlier, in 1473 or 1474, he had printed his own translation of the Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye, the first book printed in English. Heavy demand for it prompted his Westminster venture, where his first known book was Chaucer's Canterbury Tales. Printing in London's dialect across many works, he is credited with helping standardise written English.

sources.title: William Caxton - Wikipedia
CAXTON AT WESTMINSTER. A.D. 1476, 1491 (The Life and Typography of William Caxton, England's First Printer, 2014)
sources.venue: The Life and Typography of William Caxton, England's First Printer
sources.confirms: The page identifies Chapter VI as “CAXTON AT WESTMINSTER. A.D.
sources.qualifies: The chapter title gives 1476-1491, but the other claims are not stated.

sources.title: 'William Caxton', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page says Caxton set up a press in Brugge “about 1474”; The Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye was published there in 1475 as “the first book printed in English.” Toward the end of 1476 he returned to England and established his press at Westminster.
sources.qualifies: Westminster and 1476 are supported; the Recuyell’s stated year and location differ.

caxton-press-westminster-1476.verification_note: this chapter title gives 1476-1491, but other claims are not stated; Westminster and 1476 are supported; Recuyell’s stated year and location differ

picture.alt: Opening of William Caxton's Recuyell of the Historyes of Troye, printed in Bruges 1473 to 1474, two years before he set up his Westminster press.
picture.credit: William Caxton, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

ottoman-printing-ban-1483.summary: From 1483, by a tradition André Thevet first recorded in his 1580s writings, Ottoman sultans barred printing in Arabic script; no decree survives, though the Muslim world went without a press for 250 years. Later writers had Bayezid II and his successors enforcing it on pain of death; no documentary evidence supports such a ban. Printing in other scripts went on: Jewish presses from 1493 in Constantinople, and Greek, Armenian and other Christian presses in Salonica, Bursa, Belgrade and Smyrna. Arabic-script printing by non-Muslims began in Aleppo in 1706. In 1727 Sultan Ahmed III licensed the first Muslim-run press for secular Arabic-script works, religious texts still excluded, yet printing did not take off until the 19th century.

sources.title: Global spread of the printing press - Wikipedia
K. A. Schwartz, 'Did Ottoman Sultans Ban Print?', Book History 20 (2017), 1-39
sources.author: Kathryn A. Schwartz
sources.confirms: Extant documentary evidence does not support the claim that Ottoman sultans banned print; the story derives from Andre Thevet in the 1580s and no edict survives.

sources.title: Coşgel, M. M., Miceli, T. J. and Rubin, J., 'The political economy of mass printing: Legitimacy and technological change in the Ottoman Empire', Journal of Comparative Economics 40 (2012), 357-371
sources.author: Coşgel, Metin M.; Miceli, Thomas J.; Rubin, Jared
sources.confirms: The Ottomans waited almost three centuries to sanction printing in Arabic characters and relaxed the restriction in 1726 by granting Müteferrika exclusive rights.
sources.qualifies: These authors accept that sultans banned Arabic-script printing, which Schwartz disputes, and date the licence to 1726 rather than 1727.

ottoman-printing-ban-1483.verification_note: Schwartz (Book History 2017) finds no documentary evidence for a sultanic ban on print in 1483 or 1485 and no surviving firman, tracing that story to André Thevet's writings in 1580s France; Coşgel, Miceli and Rubin (Journal of Comparative Economics 2012) treat such a ban as fact, explain it by political economy and say Ottomans relaxed it for Arabic characters in 1726 with exclusive rights to Ibrahim Müteferrika, where other accounts give 1727. Scholarship is divided on whether any ban existed; this entry follows Schwartz.

malleus-maleficarum-1486.summary: In 1486 the Hammer of Witches was printed, and print spread a manual that fed two centuries of witch trials. Heinrich Kramer, a Dominican inquisitor expelled from Innsbruck in 1484 after failing to prosecute alleged witches there, published his Malleus Maleficarum in Speyer. It argued that witchcraft existed and denying it was error, classed sorcery as heresy for secular courts to prosecute, held that practitioners were more often women than men, and recommended torture to obtain confessions and death as its sure remedy. Printing carried it widely: 28 editions by 1600, used by Catholic and Protestant courts in witch trials.

sources.title: Malleus Maleficarum - Wikipedia
Levack, Brian P., Heinrich Kramer: Malleus Maleficarum, 1486 (The Witchcraft Sourcebook, 2015)
sources.author: Levack, Brian P.
sources.confirms: The page identifies “Heinrich Kramer: Malleus Maleficarum, 1486” and lists Brian P. Levack as author.
sources.qualifies: The title supports the 1486 association; the other claims are not stated.

sources.title: 'Malleus maleficarum', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page dates the work to “c. 1486” and says it went through 28 editions between 1486 and 1600.
sources.qualifies: It identifies Heinrich (Institoris) Kraemer as a Dominican inquisitor, but does not state he was expelled from Innsbruck or that the book was printed there in 1486. It also does not specifically describe the printing press as the means of its spread.

malleus-maleficarum-1486.verification_note: its title supports the 1486 association; other claims are not stated; it identifies Heinrich (Institoris) Kraemer as a Dominican inquisitor, but does not state he was expelled from Innsbruck or that this book was printed there in 1486. It also does not specifically describe the printing press as means of its spread
malleus-maleficarum-1486.detail: Cologne's theology faculty condemned it for recommending illegal procedures. Jacob Sprenger was credited as co-author from 1519, a claim scholars dispute.

picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, CC BY 4.0, via Wellcome Collection

ibn-majid-navigation-manual-1490.summary: Ahmad ibn Majid, born about 1432 in Julfar on a Gulf coast now part of Ras al-Khaimah and heir to a family of pilots, finishes his prose manual Kitab al-Fawaid fi usul ilm al-bahr wa'l-qawaid about 1490. Its chapters set out a 32-point sidereal compass rose, stellar altitude measured in finger-widths with a kamal, latitude sailing, monsoon seasons, and routes and landfalls from East Africa to Sumatra. He wrote some forty works, most in verse for memorising. A Meccan writer later claimed he piloted Vasco da Gama from Malindi to India in 1498; G. R. Tibbetts, who translated this manual in 1971, and later scholars reject that story, since Portuguese accounts name a Gujarati pilot and Ibn Majid was then in his sixties. A manuscript of his collected treatises is held by the Library of Congress.

sources.title: Tibbetts, G. R., Arab Navigation in the Indian Ocean before the Coming of the Portuguese, being a translation of Kitab al-Fawa'id of Ahmad b. Majid (Royal Asiatic Society, 1971)
sources.author: Tibbetts, Gerald Randall
sources.confirms: Full translation with study of navigation techniques; rejects the da Gama pilot story as unreliable.

sources.title: Ibn Majid, Kitab al-fawa'id fi ma'rifat ilm al-bahr wa-al-qawa'id, manuscript (Library of Congress, Near East Section)
sources.author: Ibn Majid, Ahmad
sources.confirms: Collection of eight treatises on seafaring assembled in 1490, covering routes, harbours and landfalls of the Indian Ocean, Red Sea and Gulf.
sources.qualifies: The catalogue summary repeats the belief that da Gama consulted him.

taxis-imperial-post-1490.summary: In 1490 the Taxis family began an imperial relay post, the seed of Europe's first public mail. Innsbruck was its hub; its first main route ran to Mechelen in present-day Belgium. Stations about 15 km apart, with inns and stables, let riders and horses change without delay, raising travel speed from roughly 25 to 166 km a day. Meant for official traffic, it soon carried private letters, and the Taxis family ran posts for about 400 years.

columbian-exchange-1492.summary: After 1492 maize and potatoes crossed to feed Eurasia and smallpox crossed to empty the Americas, some transfers deliberate, many unintended. Maize, potatoes, tomatoes, cassava, chili peppers and tobacco spread across Africa, Asia and Europe and supported population growth there; wheat, rice, sugar cane, horses, cattle, pigs and sheep went westward. Old World diseases cut Indigenous American populations by an estimated 80 to 95 percent and nearly wiped out Caribbean peoples. Millions of Africans were carried across in slavery.

sources.qualifies: The population-loss claim is overstated; intent is unspecified).

columbus-first-voyage-1492.summary: On 12 October 1492 Columbus landed on a Bahamian island, and two worlds unknown to each other were joined for good. Christopher Columbus made landfall on an island its people called Guanahani, having sailed west from Spain on 3 August in search of a sea route to Asia's spices. A Genoese navigator, he reckoned Japan lay about 2,400 nautical miles west of the Canaries, roughly a quarter of its true distance, and Spain's Catholic Monarchs backed him. Believing he had reached Asia's Indies, he returned on 4 March 1493; Caribbean islands are still called the West Indies.

columbus-first-voyage-1492.detail: Palos de la Frontera supplied two caravels under royal order. After Guanahani he explored Cuba and Hispaniola, where his flagship Santa María wrecked on 25 December.

trithemius-in-praise-of-scribes-1492.summary: In 1492 Abbot Trithemius argued that monks should keep copying books by hand because parchment outlasts paper, an argument he had printed. He sent it with a dedication letter to Abbot Gerlach of Deutz. It argued that copying books by hand remained useful work for monks, disciplining mind and body and preserving texts. In this dispute between scribes and printers he took a middle position: keep old practice and allow new. After months of stylistic revision he had it printed in 1494 by Peter von Friedberg in Mainz, which later writers have treated as a curiosity.

constantinople-hebrew-press-arbaah-turim.summary: Brothers David and Samuel ibn Nahmias, Sephardic refugees who left Spain after its 1492 expulsion and gathered type and paper in Naples, set up a press in Constantinople under Bayezid II. Their colophon dates completion of Jacob ben Asher's legal code Arbaah Turim, more than 800 folio pages, to 4 Tevet 5254, 13 December 1493, and blesses their sultan. Printing in Arabic script remained closed to Muslims, so for two centuries Hebrew, then Armenian (1567) and Greek (1627) presses carried this technology in Ottoman lands. Nahmias family members printed until 1518; Hebrew presses in Constantinople issued over 100 titles by 1530, more than Müteferrika's Arabic-script press produced in its eighteenth-century run. Bibliographers long doubted 1493; Adri Offenberg's 1969 study of colophon and paper confirmed it.

aldine-press-1494.summary: In 1494 Aldus Manutius founded his Venice press, whose first dated book appeared in 1495, and went on to print cheap pocket-sized classics; books became companions to carry as well as consult. He hired Francesco Griffo to cut type: a roman face first used in Pietro Bembo's De Aetna in 1496, then a cursive variant designed to save paper, used in his 1501 Virgil, the first book printed in italic. From April 1501, with that Virgil, he issued small octavo books sized for portability. Venice granted him sole right to print Greek, but counterfeits from Lyon undercut him abroad.

pacioli-double-entry-1494.summary: In Venice in 1494 Franciscan mathematician Luca Pacioli publishes Summa de arithmetica, geometria, proportioni et proportionalita, whose section Particularis de computis et scripturis gives the first printed account of double entry as Venetian merchants used it: journal, ledger, debit matched to credit, and a trial balance. Pacioli codified rather than invented double entry. Alan Sangster's 2016 article in The Accounting Review traces its emergence to early 13th-century Italy, most likely a Florentine bank answerable to Florence's bankers' guild. Print turned a craft passed between counting houses into a teachable technique, and translations spread it across Europe. Internet Archive holds a digitised 1494 copy.

leonardo-robot-knight-1495.summary: Around 1495 Leonardo drew a mechanical knight that sat and waved, the first humanoid robot. No complete drawing survives, but scattered sketches show pulleys driven through worm gears in its chest moving its arms, an external crank and cables working hips, knees and ankles, and a hinged jaw on its flexible neck, all hidden under German-Italian armour. Several researchers have since built working versions.

kano-indigo-dye-pits-1498.summary: At Kofar Mata inside Kano's city wall, Hausa dyers sank deep clay-lined pits in which indigo leaves, ash and potash ferment for weeks before cloth is dipped and beaten to a glossy blue-black. Dyers' guild tradition dates these pits to 1498, and Marisa Candotti's study of Hausa textile origins traces dyeing and weaving in Kano to this period of growth under Sarkin Kano Muhammad Rumfa. Dyed cloth and turbans moved by caravan to Tuareg and Kanuri buyers and across the Sahara, making Kano a textile capital that Heinrich Barth in 1851 saw clothing people from Timbuktu to Lake Chad. More than a hundred pits once worked at Kofar Mata; a few still do.

Candotti argues that textile production in Hausaland grew from local cotton cultivation, Islamic dress norms and trans-Saharan demand rather than from imported technique. swahili-mtepe-sewn-ships-1498.summary: When Vasco da Gama's fleet anchored at Mozambique Island in March 1498, its chronicler described local vessels whose planks were stitched together with coconut-fibre cord instead of nails, with sails woven from palm matting. These were mtepe, sewn-plank ships that Swahili and Bajuni mariners sailed between Lamu, Zanzibar, Kilwa and Sofala, carrying mangrove poles, grain and goods for Indian Ocean exchange. Erik Gilbert traced this craft's survival into the twentieth century; a last mtepe left Lamu waters around 1935. In 2003 shipwrights in Zanzibar built a reconstruction, Shungwaya, documented by Bojakowski, Sarathi and Berrocal.

swahili-mtepe-sewn-ships-1498.detail: Sewn boats had worked this coast since at least AD 100, as Periplus of the Erythraean Sea records. Mtepe hulls flexed over coral and could be unstitched and repaired, suiting shallow creeks and beach landings. Their square matting sail and curved stem carved with eyes made them distinctive to European observers. Metal fastenings and dhow types from Arabia and India gradually replaced them under British colonial regulation.

vasco-da-gama-calicut-1498.summary: On 20 May 1498 Vasco da Gama reached India by sea, breaking Venice's hold on spices and opening Asia to Europe. He landed at Kappadu near Kozhikode, later called Calicut; the spice trade had reached Europe overland, largely through Venice. Bartolomeu Dias had rounded Africa's Cape of Good Hope in 1488, and spies sent via Egypt had scouted India's markets; da Gama's fleet joined those pieces. Sailing from Lisbon in 1497, he swung wide through the South Atlantic, worked up East Africa, and at Malindi hired a Gujarati pilot who used the monsoon winds to cross to India in 23 days.

atlantic-slave-trade-1500.summary: After 1500 Europeans began shipping enslaved Africans to the Americas, about 12.5 million embarked over four centuries by SlaveVoyages' estimate, with scholarly totals from 11.1 million to 15.4 million. Up to 2 million died at sea; most came from West and Central Africa. Europeans had bought enslaved people on Africa's coast since the 15th century; in American colonies, Indigenous workers were dying from overwork, disease and maltreatment, and colonists wanted labour for sugar, coffee, tobacco, cocoa and cotton plantations and for mines. Some voyages ran a triangular route whose middle leg, the Middle Passage, carried captives west.

hawaiian-fishponds-1500.summary: By 1500 Hawaiians farmed fish in walled sea ponds, the Pacific's most developed fish farming; some still work. Heʻeia pond on Oʻahu is roughly 600 to 800 years old. Seawater ponds enclosed shallow reef flats behind low lava-rock walls, up to 1,920 metres long and cemented with coralline algae, which let water through but held fish. Keepers grew algae for mullet and other species to graze, and wooden grates in channels let small fish in while keeping mature ones from leaving. When James Cook arrived there were at least 360 ponds yielding some 2,000,000 pounds of fish a year.

little-ice-age-1500.summary: From around 1500 the Little Ice Age cooled the North Atlantic world for three centuries. IPCC reviewers read it as largely independent regional changes with at most modest Northern Hemisphere cooling, no ice age of global extent. Convention dates it between 1500 and 1900; some experts prefer about 1300 to about 1850, and there is no consensus on its start. Proposed causes include low solar output, volcanic eruptions, ocean circulation shifts and population collapse.

little-ice-age-1500.detail: NASA notes three cold intervals beginning about 1650, 1770 and 1850. Cold European summers drove Alpine glaciers forward, with advances peaking around 1380 and again around 1590.

maori-pa-fortifications-1500.summary: From about 1500 CE, Maori began cutting ditches and banks across ridge spurs and headlands, terracing slopes and raising palisades of split timber to create pa. Roughly 6,000 to 7,000 pa sites survive, concentrated in North Island areas with kumara gardens. A reassessment of marine-shell radiocarbon dates put earliest defended sites near 1500, later than once believed. Archaeologists at Pouerua in Northland studied obsidian flows into a fortified volcanic cone to test whether population pressure explained fortification. Pa protected stored kumara in pits, served as refuges and statements of mana, and later in 1840s and 1860s evolved into gunfighter pa with trenches and bunkers that absorbed British artillery.

sources.title: Schmidt, Matthew, Radiocarbon Dating New Zealand Prehistory Using Marine Shell, BAR International Series 842 (Archaeopress, 2000)
sources.author: Schmidt, Matthew
sources.confirms: Re-evaluated radiocarbon dates place earliest pa around 1500
sources.qualifies: Marine shell dates require reservoir corrections

Pa design used natural slopes, with ditches up to several metres deep and fighting stages above palisades. Ruapekapeka and Gate Pa in 1845 and 1864 showed engineering adapted against muskets and cannon. Dating pa remains difficult because many were reoccupied and rebuilt over generations.

pounamu-greenstone-industry-1500.summary: Pounamu, nephrite jade from rivers such as Arahura and Taramakau on Te Tai Poutini (South Island's West Coast), is among Earth's toughest stones. Maori workers sawed boulders with sandstone and quartz sand, ground blanks for days on wet grinding stones (hoanga), and drilled holes with cord-driven stone-tipped spindles. Chapman's 1891 account to Otago Institute recorded these methods from Maori informants. Archaeological reviews show nephrite use rising sharply after about 1500, as earlier basalt and argillite adze sources fell from use. Pounamu toki (adzes), mere (clubs) and hei-tiki travelled by foot and canoe to every part of Aotearoa, carrying mana and genealogy with them.

pounamu-greenstone-industry-1500.verification_note: Archaeology dates a marked increase in pounamu working to after about 1500; some use goes back to moa-hunter sites, so 1500 marks intensification rather than beginning.
pounamu-greenstone-industry-1500.detail: Nephrite occurs only in a few South Island districts; its spread to northern North Island sites demonstrates exchange networks spanning 1,000 kilometres. Ngai Tahu controlled main sources and crossing routes over Southern Alps passes. Today ownership of pounamu is vested in Ngai Tahu under a 1997 settlement. Chapman also described Te Koroka inland source near Lake Wakatipu, named in Ngai Tahu tradition, which later geologists confirmed.

spread-of-printing-1500.summary: By 1500 presses in 236 European towns, by Febvre and Martin's count, had printed some 20 million books for 70 million people. Before the press a book had to be copied by hand. After Gutenberg lost a lawsuit to his investor Johann Fust, his monopoly ended and his method ceased to be secret; emigrating German printers, then foreign apprentices, carried it outward: Cologne 1466, Rome 1467, Venice 1469, Paris 1470, Buda and Kraków 1473, London 1477. By 1481 the Netherlands had shops in 21 towns, Italy and Germany about 40 each; Buringh and van Zanden put 220 presses and about 8 million books by 1500, and output rose tenfold in the sixteenth century.

nilakantha-tantrasangraha-1501.summary: In 1500, by his pupil's dating, Nilakantha in Kerala had planets circle a mean Sun, which in turn circled Earth, a model like Tycho Brahe's a century later. His Tantrasangraha, A Compilation of the System, covers planetary motion, eclipses, trigonometry and their underlying mathematics in 432 Sanskrit verses, drawing on Sangamagrama Madhava's work. In it he revised Aryabhata's model for Mercury and Venus; according to George G. Joseph, his equation of centre for those planets stayed most accurate until Johannes Kepler after 1600. Jyeshtadeva's Yuktibhāṣā commentary, around 1550, worked out its proofs. Western scholars learned of it through C. M. Whish's paper of 1835.

His Tantrasamgraha, written in 1501, comprises “432 Sanskrit verses divided into 8 chapters” and is “based on the epicyclic and eccentric models of planetary motion.” It covers planetary motions and longitudes, eclipses, and other astronomy topics.
sources.qualifies: The stated date, verse count, planetary motion, and eclipses are supported; the inner-planet claim is absent.

aztec-sun-stone-1502.summary: Between 1502 and 1521 Mexica sculptors carved their 24-tonne Sun Stone, a calendar now Mexico's national symbol. Moctezuma II's name glyph on its central disc dates it to his reign. It is 3.6 metres across, 98 centimetres thick and weighs 24,590 kg, cut from olivine basalt of Xitle volcano. Rings of day signs and glyphs for four earlier suns, or eras, surround a central deity; it uses calendar glyphs to express cyclical time rather than working as a calendar, and archaeologists now think it served as an altar for sacrifices.

sources.qualifies: The page does not state carving dates, identify Mexica sculptors or Moctezuma II’s glyph, call it a national symbol, give its thickness or exact weight, or specify “oli.” Its approximate size and weight differ from the claim’s figures.

aztec-sun-stone-1502.detail: Its basalt block was probably dragged up to 22 kilometres by thousands of people. Buried after Spanish conquest, it was rediscovered on 17 December 1790 beneath Mexico City's main square.

leonardo-codex-flight-1505.summary: In 1505 Leonardo filled a notebook with how birds fly and how a person might; he never flew, but he drew the problem correctly. Applying mechanics to observation, he compared wing to wedge and tail to rudder, used laws of equilibrium to explain how birds balance in air, studied air resistance, currents and wind, and sketched joints for an artificial wing. Smithsonian curators count among its notes early concepts that reappeared in successful airplanes four centuries later.

javanese-jong-1511.summary: When Portuguese fleets reached Melaka in 1511, they met Javanese jong: ships with hulls of three or four planking layers fastened by wooden dowels, two to four masts carrying lug sails, twin quarter rudders and cargo capacity that Portuguese observers put at several hundred tons, larger than their own carracks. Pierre-Yves Manguin's reading of Portuguese, Chinese and Javanese sources shows a Southeast Asian shipbuilding tradition that linked Java, Melaka, Pegu and Maluku in pepper, rice and cloth trade. Shipowners from Japara, Gresik and Tuban sent fleets to attack Portuguese Melaka in 1513. Within a century jong gave way to smaller hybrid vessels as Portuguese artillery and later Dutch monopolies changed Indonesian seas.

sources.title: Manguin, Pierre-Yves, 'The Southeast Asian ship: an historical approach', Journal of Southeast Asian Studies 11 (1980)
sources.author: Manguin, Pierre-Yves
sources.confirms: Jong construction, size and trade role as described in early 16th-century sources

javanese-jong-1511.verification_note: Abstract and chapter metadata confirmed; tonnage estimates derive from Portuguese observers and Manguin treats them with caution.
javanese-jong-1511.detail: Manguin cautions that Portuguese tonnage figures may exaggerate and that no jong hull has been excavated intact. Archaeological wrecks in Gulf of Thailand show related lashed-lug and dowelled construction. His later chapter, 'The vanishing jong', traces decline through sixteenth and seventeenth centuries.

picture.alt: Ship relief at Borobudur, Java, showing an outrigger vessel of an earlier Javanese tradition
picture.credit: Andreas Sihono

piri-reis-map-1513.summary: In 1513 the Ottoman admiral Piri Reis, at Gallipoli, mapped the Americas from captured Spanish charts. He presented it to Sultan Selim I after Egypt's conquest in 1517. About one third survives, its western part, on gazelle-skin parchment roughly 90 by 63 cm, showing Atlantic coasts of Europe, Africa and South America. It is a portolan chart: compass roses and radiating bearing lines for navigation by dead reckoning rather than a latitude and longitude grid, with long notes in Ottoman Turkish. Found at Topkapı Palace in 1929, it drew worldwide attention because its Caribbean copies a lost map by Christopher Columbus.

more-utopia-1516.summary: In 1516 Thomas More's Utopia, an island without property, named every later ideal society. The London lawyer, on embassy in Flanders, wrote it in Latin and had it printed by Dirk Martens in Leuven in December. It is framed as dialogue: More and his host Pieter Gillis meet a talkative Portuguese traveller, Raphael Hythlodaeus, whose name means roughly "peddler of nonsense", which let More disown his boldest claims. Hythlodaeus describes an island society holding goods in common, without money or gold, with religious freedom, a six-hour working day and no lawyers. More had called it Nusquama, Latin for "nowhere"; Erasmus suggested Greek coinage Utopia, "no place". Its title named a literary genre.

luther-95-theses-printing-1517.summary: In 1517 Luther sent out his Ninety-five Theses, and the press spread them across Germany. Luther, professor of moral theology at Wittenberg, had grown alarmed when parishioners returned from buying Johann Tetzel's indulgences believing they no longer needed to repent. The Theses argued that repentance was inward and lifelong, and that indulgences led Christians away from it and from works of mercy.

It gives no details about printing or circulation, Luther’s 1517 actions or position, Tetzel’s indulgences, or parishioners’ beliefs.
sources.qualifies: The title includes 1517; the other claim details are absent.

luther-95-theses-printing-1517.detail: Printed forms included a four-page Latin pamphlet in Basel, placards in Leipzig and Nuremberg, several hundred copies across Germany that year, and Kaspar Nützel's German translation. Dispute with Johann Eck followed, then the 1519 Leipzig Debate.

fugger-charles-v-election-1519.summary: In 1519 Jakob Fugger lent 543,000 guilders to buy Charles V the empire: money, with dynastic politics, chose an emperor. When Emperor Maximilian I died, seven prince-electors chose his successor: three archbishops, Bohemia's king, and Palatinate's, Brandenburg's and Saxony's rulers. Francis I of France had already secured Trier and Palatinate and offered 300,000 guilders; Henry VIII and Frederick of Saxony also stood. Jakob Fugger of Augsburg, whose loans to Maximilian tied his fortune to Habsburg success, backed Maximilian's 19-year-old grandson Charles with more than 850,000 guilders transferred to electors. Charles was elected unanimously as Charles V, for political and dynastic reasons as much as for money, Cohn argues.

magellan-elcano-circumnavigation-1519.summary: In September 1522 one ship and 18 men returned to Spain from humanity's first voyage around Earth. Juan Sebastián Elcano brought Victoria home three years after leaving with Ferdinand Magellan's five ships and some 270 men. Magellan, a Portuguese sailor in Spanish service, had set out on 20 September 1519 to reach the Moluccas, or Spice Islands, by sailing west. After mutinies and wintering on Patagonia's coast, his fleet entered the strait now named for him on 1 November 1520 and crossed an ocean he named Mar Pacifico in 98 days; Magellan was killed in the Philippines in April 1521.

magellan-elcano-circumnavigation-1519.detail: During that Pacific crossing men died of scurvy and ate sawdust and rats. Magellan's ships reached those islands in November 1521.

smallpox-tenochtitlan-1520.summary: In 1520 smallpox reached Tenochtitlan and killed perhaps 40 percent of its people in months. It arrived while Hernán Cortés rebuilt his alliances after being driven out. Spanish sources trace it to Francisco de Eguía, an enslaved African in Narváez's force left ill at Cempoala. Smallpox had been endemic in Spain for centuries, so Spaniards had acquired immunity; Mexica had none. It broke out in Tenochtitlan in late October 1520 and ran about sixty days, until early December. Ruler Cuitlahuac died after eighty days in office. Historians count it as decisive in the 1521 siege.

No page numbers for those claims are visible.

smallpox-tenochtitlan-1520.detail: Tlaxcalan chieftain Maxixcatl, Spain's ally, also died, but losses fell hardest inside crowded Tenochtitlan, where the Florentine Codex records people too sick to seek food.
