afonso-kongo-letters-1526.summary: Mvemba a Nzinga, baptised Afonso I, ruled Kongo from 1506 to about 1542 and ran a written diplomacy with Portugal through dozens of Portuguese-language letters drafted at his court in Mbanza Kongo. He asked Manuel I for ships, masons, carpenters, physicians and teachers, sent sons and nephews to study in Lisbon, and built a Kongolese church under his own authority. In letters of 1526 to João III he protested that Portuguese traders and their Kongolese partners were seizing free subjects, including nobles, and demanded that trade pass through his officials. John Thornton's work established the letters as a record of a literate African state negotiating with Europe on its own terms.

sources.title: Thornton, John K., 'Early Kongo-Portuguese Relations: A New Interpretation', History in Africa 8 (1981)
sources.author: Thornton, John K.
sources.confirms: Afonso I (Mvemba a Nzinga, r. 1506-1543) requested ships, firearms, masons and carpenters from Portugal; letter of 14 October 1514 to Manuel I

sources.title: Thornton, John K., Afonso I Mvemba a Nzinga, King of Kongo: His Life and Correspondence, tr. Luís Madureira (Hackett, 2023)
sources.author: Thornton, John K.; Madureira, Luís (tr.)
sources.confirms: Reign 1506-1542; letters on sovereignty, Kongolese Christianity and control of the slave trade; education and literacy campaigns and apprenticeships in carpentry, masonry and medicine
sources.qualifies: Publisher page does not date the slave-trade complaints to 1526

afonso-kongo-letters-1526.verification_note: Thornton gives Afonso's death as 1543 in 1981 and 1542 in 2023. The 1526 date for the slave-trade letters follows standard editions of the correspondence.
afonso-kongo-letters-1526.detail: Thornton's 1981 reinterpretation of early Kongo-Portuguese relations and his 2023 biography with Luís Madureira's translations show Afonso pursuing education and literacy campaigns, apprenticeships in carpentry, masonry and medicine, and control of the slave trade rather than its abolition. His letters survive in Lisbon's Torre do Tombo and in copies. Afonso's successors continued this correspondence with Rome and Lisbon for two centuries.

picture.alt: Mbanza Kongo (São Salvador), capital of Kongo, in an engraving published by Astley in 1745
picture.credit: Thomas Astley

first-battle-of-panipat-1526.summary: In 1526 Babur's 12,000 men with guns beat an army five times larger: gunpowder took India. He met Delhi Sultan Ibrahim Khan Lodi at Panipat, north of Delhi. Ibrahim reportedly fielded 50,000 to 70,000 men and 1,000 war elephants but no gunpowder arms; Babur had about 12,000, some with matchlock muskets, 15 to 20 cannons, and cavalry fighting as horse archers. Behind a line of tied wagons, musket and cannon pinned Ibrahim's centre while horse archers struck flanks and rear, and cannon noise panicked his elephants. Ibrahim and some 20,000 men died, opening Mughal rule in India.

sources.title: First Battle of Panipat - Wikipedia
Davis, Paul K, Panipat 21 April 1526 (100 Decisive Battles, 2001)
sources.author: Davis, Paul K
sources.confirms: The page dates the chapter “Panipat” to 21 April 1526 and says Babur’s invasion of northern India began “in the 1520s.” It also states that Timur looted India in 1398 and that Babur sought to assert his right to rule from Samarkand.
sources.qualifies: The page does not state the armies’ sizes, weapons, elephants, or the battle’s outcome.

sources.title: 'Battles of Panipat', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Dates: April 20, 1526 (some scholars say April 21). Location: Panipat, about 50 miles (80 km) north of Delhi.
sources.qualifies: The page does not give Babur’s force as 12,000, say his army was outnumbered five to one, identify this as among India’s earliest gunpowder battles, or state that gunpowder “took India.” It does support the use of guns and a larger Lodi force.

first-battle-of-panipat-1526.verification_note: Page says one of the earliest Indian battles using gunpowder arms, not the first. || Davis (2001) and Britannica confirm Babur's use of artillery and matchlocks at Panipat on 20 or 21 April 1526; the five-to-one ratio and 12,000 figure are not stated.
first-battle-of-panipat-1526.detail: Babur tied 700 wagons in line with breastworks for musketeers between them and left gaps for cavalry sorties. He anchored one flank on Panipat town and dug a trench on the other, so Ibrahim's wider army could not deploy against that front.

picture.alt: Mughal painting from an Akbarnama of about 1596 showing Babur receiving booty and Humayun's salute after defeating Sultan Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526.
picture.credit: Mughal India, court of Akbar (reigned 1556 to 1605), CC0, via Cleveland Museum of Art

mughal-empire-era-1526.summary: In 1526 Babur founded the Mughal Empire with cannon and muskets, and it ruled most of India for two centuries. This Timurid prince from Central Asia's Fergana Valley had ruled Kabul since 1504 and sought lands to its southeast. With assistance from Safavid and Ottoman empires, his outnumbered army used firearms and cannon to defeat Delhi Sultan Ibrahim Lodi at Panipat in 1526, then swept down northern India's plains. Conventionally that victory marks Mughal founding, though historians sometimes date its imperial structure to about 1600 under his grandson Akbar. Reduced to Delhi's surroundings by 1760, it was formally dissolved by Britain after 1857.

sources.title: Mughal Empire - Wikipedia
Davis, Paul K, Panipat 21 April 1526 (100 Decisive Battles, 2001)
sources.author: Davis, Paul K
sources.confirms: The page dates the chapter “Panipat 21 April 1526” and says Babur’s invasion of northern India began “in the 1520s.” It states Timur had looted India in 1398 and that Babur later sought to assert his right to rule from Samarkand.
sources.qualifies: The battle date and invasion are supported; the other details are absent.

sources.title: Khan, Iqtidar Alam, 'Early Use of Cannon and Musket in India: A.D. 1442-1526', Journal of the Economic and Social History of the Orient 24 (1981), 146-164
sources.author: Khan, Iqtidar Alam
sources.venue: Journal of the Economic and Social History of the Orient
sources.confirms: Traces gunpowder weapons in India from 1442 up to Babur's campaign of 1526, the firearms and cannon behind the Panipat victory; opening page read through OpenAlex, JSTOR and Brill pages blocked.

mughal-empire-era-1526.verification_note: battle date and invasion are supported; other details are absent
mughal-empire-era-1526.detail: At its height under Aurangzeb it stretched from Afghanistan to Bengal and into the Deccan.

picture.alt: Page from a Babur-nama of about 1590 showing Babur meeting Sultan Ali Mirza at the Kohik River.
picture.credit: India, Mughal school, 16th century, CC0, via Cleveland Museum of Art

paracelsus-1500.summary: In 1527 Theophrastus von Hohenheim, called Paracelsus, became town physician and medical lecturer at Basel and taught that disease is chemical and should be treated with chemical remedies. He is believed to have taken his doctorate at Ferrara in 1516 (Britannica). At Basel he lectured and wrote in German rather than Latin so people outside universities could follow, and on 24 June 1527, in front of Basel's university, he reportedly burned books of Avicenna and Galen, pillars of academic medicine. He prepared remedies containing mercury, sulfur, iron and copper sulfate, uniting medicine with chemistry, and declared that what sickens in large doses can cure in small ones. Charles Webster (Social History of Medicine, 1995) shows how his medical system, first set out in full around 1531, was bound up with his theology and his attack on miraculous healing by saints.

sources.title: Paracelsus - Wikipedia
WEBSTER, CHARLES, 'Paracelsus Confronts the Saints: Miracles, Healing and the Secularization of Magic', Social History of Medicine 8 (1995)
sources.author: WEBSTER, CHARLES
sources.confirms: The page identifies Paracelsus as “Theophrast von Hohenheim, 1493-1541” and says his De causis morborum invisibilium followed Opus Paramirum (1531). It discusses his views on miraculous healing and secularizing magic.
sources.qualifies: Name and lifespan match; the other claims are not stated.

sources.title: 'Paracelsus', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Paracelsus was a German-Swiss physician and alchemist. The page says he helped establish “the role of chemistry in medicine” and used remedies containing mercury, sulfur, iron, and copper sulfate.
sources.qualifies: “illness is chemical” is not stated; the doctorate year differs.

paracelsus-1500.verification_note: Corrected in November 2026: date fixed at Paracelsus's Basel year, 1527, since 1500 was no event (he was born 1493); his Ferrara doctorate now reads 1516 and his book burning 24 June after Britannica, with Webster (Social History of Medicine, 1995) for his medical system.
paracelsus-1500.detail: His chemical and mineral remedies entered official pharmacopoeias; London's first Pharmacopoeia of 1618 records them. Students came from across Europe to hear him at Basel, and his quarrels with faculty and city drove him out within months.

picture.alt: Woodcut portrait of Paracelsus by Augustin Hirschvogel, 1538, made in physician's lifetime.
picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, Public Domain Mark, via Wellcome Collection

yuktibhasa-1530.summary: Between about 1500 and 1530 (Singh and MacTutor give about 1500, Divakaran the early 1500s) Jyeṣṭhadeva wrote out proofs of Kerala's infinite series in Malayalam, the first to prove them. It consolidates discoveries of Madhava of Sangamagrama, Nilakantha Somayaji and others, and mainly supplies rationale for results in Nilakantha's Tantrasamgraha, giving proofs and derivations where earlier texts stated rules. Its topics include infinite series for π, sine, cosine and arctangent, techniques predating Newton and Leibniz by about two centuries, though it never unified them around derivative and integral. Written in a local language, it went largely unnoticed outside India until modern times.

sources.title: Yuktibhāṣā - Wikipedia
'Jyesthadeva (1500 - 1575) - Biography - University of St Andrews', MacTutor History of Mathematics
sources.confirms: The page says Jyesthadeva wrote the Yuktibhasa in Malayalam; it calls it “written in 1501” and says the treatise is half astronomy and half mathematics.
sources.qualifies: Malayalam, the proofs, and the connection to Madhava and Nilakantha are supported; the date and “first” claim are not.

sources.title: Divakaran, P. P., 'The First Textbook of Calculus: Yuktibhasa', Journal of Indian Philosophy 35 (2007) 417-443
sources.author: Divakaran, P. P.
sources.confirms: Divakaran presents Jyesthadeva's Yuktibhasa as a Malayalam text of the Kerala school that gives proofs of the infinite series for pi and the trigonometric functions, and calls it the first textbook of calculus.
sources.qualifies: Divakaran places the text in the early sixteenth century rather than at 1530.

sources.title: Singh, Avinash, 'India and the Calculus of Trigonometric Functions', arXiv:2304.03684 (2023)
sources.author: Singh, Avinash
sources.confirms: Singh describes the Yuktibhasa as the Kerala school's prose treatise that proves the series for sine, cosine and arctangent.
sources.qualifies: Singh dates the Yuktibhasa to about 1500, not 1530.

yuktibhasa-1530.verification_note: Scholars date Yuktibhasa between about 1500 and 1530: Singh and MacTutor give about 1500 or 1501, Divakaran places it early in that century, and 1530 is that range's latest end.
yuktibhasa-1530.detail: It also gives second and third order approximations of sine and cosine.

iwami-ginzan-silver-1533.summary: In 1533 merchant Kamiya Jutei brought two refiners from Korea to Iwami Ginzan in western Honshu, where they introduced haifuki, a cupellation process that smelts silver ore with lead and then oxidises lead away on an ash bed. Output from Iwami and later Ikuno and Sado rose so sharply that Kobata Atsushi estimated Japan supplied up to a third of world silver in late sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries. Portuguese and Chinese traders carried this silver to Ming China in exchange for silk, feeding Ming tax reforms and Manila galleon commerce. UNESCO listed Iwami Ginzan in 2007 as a mining landscape worked from sixteenth to twentieth centuries.

sources.title: Kobata, Atsushi, 'The production and uses of gold and silver in sixteenth- and seventeenth-century Japan', Economic History Review 18 (1965)
sources.author: Kobata, Atsushi
sources.confirms: Haifuki introduction at Iwami 1533; Japanese silver output and export to China

sources.title: UNESCO World Heritage Centre, 'Iwami Ginzan Silver Mine and its Cultural Landscape'
sources.author: UNESCO World Heritage Centre
sources.confirms: Mining and refining from 16th to 20th centuries; scale of silver production and trade

iwami-ginzan-silver-1533.detail: Kobata's 1965 article remains a base reference for production and export figures, though later work by Yamamura and Kamiki revised volumes. Daimyo and then Tokugawa shogunate controlled Iwami directly; thousands of shafts and settlements remain in forested hills. Haifuki came from Korean practice, with Chinese roots.

picture.alt: Ryugenji mabu, a tunnel of Iwami Ginzan silver mine, Shimane
picture.credit: Wakuwaku99

casa-de-moneda-mexico-1535.summary: In 1535 Spain opened a mint in Mexico City, America's first; its silver pesos served world trade as its coin for three centuries. It was built over Moctezuma's Casa Denegrida, his black house of meditation. Its silver coins of eight reales, and their successor, Mexico's silver peso, circulated widely across America and Asia well past 1800 and underlay several modern currencies, including the United States dollar, Japanese yen and Chinese yuan. Casa de Moneda still operates as Mexico's national mint, oldest in the Americas.

sources.title: Mexican Mint - Wikipedia
Castañeda, Carlos E., 'The Coinage of the First Mint of the Americas at Mexico City, 1536-1572', Hispanic American Historical Review 38 (1958)
sources.author: Castañeda, Carlos E.
sources.confirms: The page’s book title identifies the “First Mint of the Americas at Mexico City” and gives the years 1536-1572. The book was published in 1955 and reviewed on August 1, 1958.
sources.qualifies: The page does not state that the mint opened in 1535, describe the pesos or their trade role, or mention Moctezuma’s Casa Denegrida.

sources.title: MendozaAntonio de Mendoza
sources.confirms: The page states that Charles I appointed Mendoza viceroy in 1535 and that he governed for 15 years. It does not state that a mint opened in Mexico City in 1535 or mention the Casa de Moneda, silver pesos, eight-reales coins, Moctezuma’s Casa Denegrida, or a world trade coin.
sources.qualifies: 1535 appears as Mendoza’s appointment year, not as a mint-opening date; the other mint claims are absent.

casa-de-moneda-mexico-1535.verification_note: Nesmith's 1955 monograph on Mexico City's mint, 1536 to 1572 (reviewed in HAHR 1958), dates its operation from 1536; Britannica gives 1535 only as Mendoza's appointment year, so 1535 marks its founding order and not its first coinage.

paracelsus-homunculus-1537.summary: In 1537 a text under Paracelsus's name gave a recipe for growing a tiny human in a glass, a dream of made life. A homunculus is an artificial miniature human that alchemists believed could be made. De natura rerum, dated 1537 in its text and of disputed authorship, gives this method: human semen sealed in a glass vessel and left forty days in venter equinus, warm fermenting horse dung, until something transparent and manlike forms; fed with human blood and kept at that even heat for forty weeks, it grows into a living child, like one born of a woman but much smaller.

sources.title: Homunculus - Wikipedia
Newman, William R., Promethean Ambitions: Alchemy and the Quest to Perfect Nature (University of Chicago Press, 2004), ch. 4
sources.author: Newman, William R.
sources.confirms: The Paracelsian school asserted an artificial human, the homunculus, could be made; sixteenth-century debate over its status is treated in chapter 4.

sources.title: Newman, William R., 'The Homunculus and His Forebears: Wonders of Art and Nature', in Natural Particulars: Nature and the Disciplines in Renaissance Europe, eds. Anthony Grafton and Nancy Siraisi (MIT Press, 2000), pp. 295-320
sources.author: Newman, William R.
sources.confirms: Scholarly chapter on the homunculus recipe in De natura rerum and its medieval antecedents; the landing page confirms the bibliographic data.

paracelsus-homunculus-1537.verification_note: Newman and Sudhoff treat De natura rerum as of uncertain, possibly pseudo-Paracelsian, authorship, and its 1537 date is stated in the text rather than securely established.
paracelsus-homunculus-1537.detail: Such beings were credited with secret knowledge of their art. Later writers compared them to Jewish folklore's golem.

picture.alt: Woodcut portrait of Paracelsus printed in 1540, three years after De natura rerum described his recipe for a homunculus.
picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, Public Domain Mark, via Wellcome Collection

mexico-city-printing-press-1539.summary: In 1539 the Americas' first printing press opened in Mexico City, a century before any in English America. Juan Cromberger, a Seville printer, had decided in 1536 to open a printing house in Mexico and sent Giovanni Paoli, a Lombard known as Juan Pablos, to run it. Pablos left Seville on 12 June 1539, reached Mexico City in October and set up shop in Cromberger's house. That year Pablos printed America's first known published book, Bishop Juan de Zumárraga's Breve y mas compendiosa doctrina Christiana, in Spanish and Nahuatl. After Cromberger died in 1540 Pablos secured permission to run his press as his own, printing at least 37 books and training Mexico's next printers.

sources.title: Juan Pablos - Wikipedia
De la Torre Villar, Ernesto, 'Clive Griffin. The Crombergers of Seville. The History of a Printing and Merchant Dynasty', Estudios de Historia Novohispana 12 (1992)
sources.author: De la Torre Villar, Ernesto
sources.confirms: The page identifies a review of The Crombergers of Seville. The History of a Printing and Merchant Dynasty, published in Oxford in 1988;
sources.qualifies: The printing-dynasty topic is present, but the claim’s details are not stated.

sources.title: RESEÑAS
sources.confirms: The page says the Crombergers’ workshop influenced “el establecido por Juan Pablos en México en 1539” and discusses “las relaciones entre el Bresciano, Pablos, y los Cromberger” (p. 249).
sources.qualifies: It does not state that 1539 was the first press in the Americas, compare it with English America, give a 1536 decision, or say that Juan Cromberger sent Giovanni Paoli.

mexico-city-printing-press-1539.verification_note: this printing-dynasty topic is present, but this claim’s details are not stated; it does not state 1539 was the Americas' first press, compare it with English America, give a 1536 decision, or say that Juan Cromberger sent Giovanni Paoli
mexico-city-printing-press-1539.detail: Cromberger's name appeared on all its early books until 1545, though he never crossed the Atlantic.

ardabil-carpet-woven-1540.summary: A knotted inscription on a pair of carpets made for Safavid shah Tahmasp's dynastic shrine at Ardabil records completion in 946 AH (1539 to 1540) as work of 'a servant of the court, Maqsud Kashani'. Each measures about ten by five metres, with wool pile in ten colours on a silk warp and weft, averaging 5,300 asymmetric knots per square decimetre; a single carpet holds roughly 26 million knots. A central sunburst medallion with two hanging lamps floats over a blue field of scrolling blossoms, a design shared with Tabriz manuscript illumination. Shrine authorities sold both carpets in 1888 through Ziegler and Company of Manchester to pay for earthquake repairs. London's South Kensington Museum bought one in 1893 for 1,750 pounds on William Morris's advice; its twin, trimmed to patch the first, reached Los Angeles County Museum of Art in 1953.

sources.title: Victoria and Albert Museum, 'The Ardabil Carpet', museum number 272-1893, collections record
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
sources.confirms: Inscription dated 946H with Maqsud Kashani's name; 340 knots per square inch; wool pile on silk; bought 1893 for 1,750 pounds after Morris's advice; twin sold 1892 and given to LACMA 1953; Ziegler bought from shrine 1888.

sources.title: Melville, C., 'The Ardabil Carpets in Context', Muqarnas 37 (2020), 1-41
sources.author: Melville, Charles
sources.confirms: Places the carpets' commission within Tahmasp's patronage of the Ardabil shrine and discusses the dating and inscription.

ardabil-carpet-woven-1540.verification_note: Place of weaving is not recorded; Tabriz and Kashan are both proposed in scholarship.

picture.alt: The Ardabil Carpet, dated 946 AH (1539-40), Victoria and Albert Museum
picture.credit: Unknown weaver, Victoria and Albert Museum, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

maize-west-africa-1540.summary: Maize crossed the Atlantic with Portuguese ships and by about 1550 was growing from Gambia's river to São Tomé and Congo's estuary, according to accounts that Marvin Miracle assembled in 1965. West African farmers folded it into existing systems: planted on cleared forest plots alongside yams, harvested early to bridge hungry months, and ground or roasted in ways borrowed from sorghum cooking. James McCann describes this as maize's 'invention' in West Africa, since Akan and Yoruba growers selected flinty, early-maturing types and gave it local names and ritual places. Maize spread inland slowly: it was unknown in Buganda in 1861.

sources.title: Miracle, Marvin P., 'The Introduction and Spread of Maize in Africa', Journal of African History 6 (1965)
sources.author: Miracle, Marvin P.
sources.confirms: Maize grown from the Gambia to São Tomé and the Congo mouth in the sixteenth century; Portuguese role undocumented; unknown in Buganda in 1861

sources.title: McCann, James C., 'Maize's Invention in West Africa', in Maize and Grace: Africa's Encounter with a New World Crop, 1500-2000 (Harvard University Press, 2005), ch. 3
sources.author: McCann, James C.
sources.confirms: Chapter on West African adoption and adaptation of maize
sources.qualifies: Chapter landing page gives title and pages; text not opened

maize-west-africa-1540.detail: Miracle found no documentary proof of Portuguese introduction and warned that early European observers often confused maize with sorghum. McCann's Maize and Grace follows the crop from coastal gardens to its twentieth-century dominance in eastern and southern African diets, when hybrid seed and colonial maize boards made it a staple. Provisioning of slave ships with maize meal tied it to Atlantic slaving. Anchor year 1540 is a midpoint of first reports.

picture.alt: Maize for sale at Sawla market, Northern Region, Ghana
picture.credit: CIAT

copernicus-de-revolutionibus-1543.summary: In 1543 Copernicus published a book that moved Earth from the universe's centre to orbit around the Sun. Nicolaus Copernicus's De revolutionibus orbium coelestium was printed in Nuremberg just before his death. He had sketched this system in his Commentariolus, a manuscript circulated to friends by 1514, but hesitated to publish for decades. In 1539 young Wittenberg mathematician Georg Joachim Rheticus came to study with him, printed a summary, Narratio Prima, in 1540, and its friendly reception persuaded Copernicus to release his book, dedicated to Pope Paul III, to printer Johannes Petreius. Kepler's 1609 ellipses refined its circles.

sources.title: Wikipedia: De revolutionibus orbium coelestium
'Nicolaus Copernicus', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: Copernicus “probably hit upon his main idea sometime between 1508 and 1514” and wrote a manuscript usually called the Commentariolus (“Little Commentary”). The final version, De revolutionibus orbium coelestium libri vi, “did not appear in print until 1543, the year of his death.” He died May 24, 1543.

sources.title: N. Copernicus, De revolutionibus orbium coelestium libri VI (Nuremberg: Johannes Petreius, 1543), Boston Public Library copy, digitised on the Internet Archive
sources.author: Nicolaus Copernicus
sources.confirms: First edition printed at Nuremberg by Petreius in 1543, with 147 woodcut diagrams and the heliocentric system.

sources.title: O. Gingerich, An Annotated Census of Copernicus' De revolutionibus (Nuremberg, 1543 and Basel, 1566) (Brill, 2002)
sources.author: Owen Gingerich
sources.confirms: Describes all 560 located copies of the 1543 Nuremberg first edition and the 1566 Basel second edition from direct examination.

copernicus-de-revolutionibus-1543.detail: Lutheran preacher Andreas Osiander, supervising its printing, added an unsigned preface calling it mere computation; Kepler later exposed him.

picture.alt: Page from a 1543 De revolutionibus orbium coelestium showing Copernicus's diagram of the celestial spheres with Sun at centre.
picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, Public Domain Mark, via Wellcome Collection

scientific-revolution-era-1543.summary: From 1543 Europeans tested nature by measurement and experiment instead of trusting ancient authors. Historians call this break with earlier natural philosophy across 1500 to 1700 the Scientific Revolution. Its new science departed from Greek traditions, read nature mechanically, leaned on mathematics, and prized gathering and interpreting fresh evidence over reverence for ancient authority. It is often dated from 1543, when Andreas Vesalius's De humani corporis fabrica and Copernicus's De revolutionibus were printed, though some start it with 1572's supernova; it culminates in Isaac Newton's Principia Mathematica of 1687.

sources.title: Scientific Revolution - Wikipedia
Shapin, Steven, The Scientific Revolution (University of Chicago Press, 1996)
sources.author: Shapin, Steven
sources.confirms: The page says that “in the 1600s science emerged from a variety of beliefs, practices, and influences” and calls the 17th century “crucial.” It does not state that change began in 1543, describe measurement and experiment replacing trust in ancient authors, or specify a break with Greek tradition.
sources.qualifies: It supports the broad 17th-century emergence but omits those details.

sources.title: 'Scientific Revolution', Encyclopaedia Britannica
sources.confirms: The page dates the Scientific Revolution to c. 1400-1690 and describes it as a change in scientific thought during the 16th and 17th centuries.
sources.qualifies: It says science shifted toward “quantitative” views and an “experimental, scientific method,” with explanation emphasizing “how” rather than “why.” Copernicus published his heliocentric theory in 1543.

scientific-revolution-era-1543.verification_note: it supports broad 17th-century emergence but omits those details; it says science shifted toward “quantitative” views and an “experimental, scientific method,” with explanation emphasizing “how” rather than “why.” Copernicus published his heliocentric theory in 1543
scientific-revolution-era-1543.detail: Alexandre Koyré used this phrase last century and Herbert Butterfield popularised it. Francis Bacon's calls for progress inspired bodies such as London's Royal Society.

picture.alt: Heliocentric diagram in Copernicus's autograph manuscript of De revolutionibus, written before its 1543 printing, held by Jagiellonian Library, Kraków.
picture.credit: Nicolaus Copernicus, public domain, via Jagiellonian Library (mirrored on Wikimedia Commons)

tanegashima-arquebus-1543.summary: In 1543 two Portuguese muskets reached Tanegashima island, Japan, by chance; within decades Japan made thousands. Its lord, Tanegashima Tokitaka, bought both matchlocks, apparently of a type made at Portuguese Goa, and set swordsmith Yaita Kinbee Kiyosoda to copy barrel and firing mechanism. Most parts posed no difficulty, but drilling barrels helically so that their screw breech plugs fitted tightly was unknown in Japan; a Portuguese blacksmith brought back next year solved it. Guns named tanegashima spread through Japan's civil wars.

sources.title: Tanegashima (gun) - Wikipedia
Lidin, Olof G., 'The Arrival of the Portuguese', in Tanegashima: The Arrival of Europe in Japan (Routledge, 2002), pp. 16-41
sources.author: Lidin, Olof G.
sources.confirms: Chapter landing page shows title and chapter metadata only; bibliographic record only; claim not readable on the opened page.

sources.title: Victoria and Albert Museum, 'Japan's encounter with Europe, 1573-1853'
sources.author: Victoria and Albert Museum
sources.confirms: 1543. The page says Portuguese matchlock guns arrived in Japan and Japanese guns were produced in large numbers within a decade.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Sengoku period'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: 1543. The page supports the broad account that Portuguese firearms and construction knowledge reached Japan and that Japan adopted and produced matchlocks. It does not confirm the record’s specific copying story.

tanegashima-arquebus-1543.detail: Oda Nobunaga's 3,000 gunners fired volleys at Nagashino in 1575, and about one quarter of 1592's Korea invasion force were gunners.

picture.alt: Antique Japanese tanegashima matchlock guns, later photograph of surviving Edo period examples.
picture.credit: pdeaudney, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

vesalius-fabrica-1543.summary: In 1543 Vesalius published the first accurate atlas of human anatomy, from corpses he cut up. Andreas Vesalius, aged 28, published De Humani Corporis Fabrica Libri Septem in Basel: seven books with more than 250 woodcuts. Teaching at Padua, he had broken with practice by dissecting while lecturing; dissection had been left to barber surgeons under a doctor who did no manual work. Comparing what he saw with Galen's texts, he found Galen had worked from dogs and monkeys. Johannes Oporinus printed it, with a dedication to Charles V.

Vesalius, Andreas, De humani corporis fabrica libri septem (Basel: Oporinus, 1543), digitized at BHL
sources.author: Vesalius, Andreas
sources.confirms: Catalogue of the original 1543 Basel edition printed by Oporinus in June 1543.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'De humani corporis fabrica libri septem'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: 1543. The page confirms that Vesalius’s major anatomy work was printed in 1543 and describes it as seminal; it does not call it the “first accurate atlas.”

vesalius-fabrica-1543.detail: He kept some of Galen's errors, such as veins and arteries carrying different kinds of blood. Its woodcuts are now attributed to Titian's studio.

picture.credit: Wellcome Collection, Public Domain Mark, via Wellcome Collection

gessner-bibliotheca-universalis-1545.summary: In 1545 Konrad Gessner catalogued every known author, some 10,000 works, and warned that printing was producing a confusing flood of books. He wrote in its preface of a confusing and harmful multitude of books since printing, and of fear that recent learning could vanish as Alexandria's library had. Authors are entered alphabetically by first name with life details, titles, places and dates of printing, and often extracts or his own judgement. It is counted as the first universal bibliography.

sources.title: Confusa e irritante multidão de livros: relações entre o contexto histórico-informacional da Europa Moderna e a estrutura documentária de Bibliotheca Universalis, de Conrad Gesner
Blair, Ann, 'Reading Strategies for Coping with Information Overload ca. 1550-1700', Journal of the History of Ideas 64, no. 1 (2003)
sources.author: Blair, Ann
sources.venue: Journal of the History of Ideas
sources.confirms: The abstract states the article surveys how early modern scholars responded to what they perceived as an overabundance of books; Blair opens with Gessner's 1545 complaint of a confusing and harmful multitude of books.

sources.title: Blair, Ann M., Too Much to Know: Managing Scholarly Information before the Modern Age (Yale University Press, 2010), ch. 1
sources.author: Blair, Ann M.
sources.confirms: University-press monograph whose first chapter treats Gessner's Bibliotheca universalis as the first universal bibliography and his preface on the harmful abundance of books; publisher record confirmed.

gessner-bibliotheca-universalis-1545.detail: His Pandectae of 1548 and 1549 then arranged the same material by subject. Gessner is called the father of bibliography on its strength.

picture.alt: Title page of Bibliotheca instituta et collecta primum a Conrado Gesnero, Zurich 1574, Simler's expansion of Gessner's 1545 universal bibliography.
picture.credit: Conrad Gessner and Josias Simler, John Carter Brown Library, public domain, via Internet Archive

potosi-silver-1545.summary: In 1545 Spaniards began mining silver at Potosí's Cerro Rico, a mountain whose ores, lake sediments show, Andean smelters worked at scale around 1000 AD. Tradition credits Andean prospector Diego Huallpa with its 1545 discovery. Potosí's silver paid for Spain's wars and swelled Spanish Empire tax returns; production peaked in 1592 after mercury amalgamation arrived in 1572. Earl Hamilton argued in 1934 that American silver drove Spain's 1520 to 1650 price revolution; historians still dispute how much it explains, since prices rose from 1516, before significant American silver reached Seville.

sources.title: Potosí
Tandeter, Enrique, 'Forced and Free Labour in Late Colonial Potosi', Past and Present 93 (1981), pp. 98-136
sources.author: Tandeter, Enrique
sources.confirms: OpenAlex bibliographic record only; claim not readable on the opened page.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Potosi Bolivia'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: 1545. The page says silver was discovered there in 1545 and the city quickly became famous for its wealth, but it does not explicitly say the discovery drove Potosí’s growth.

sources.title: Mark B. Abbott and Alexander P. Wolfe, 'Intensive pre-Incan metallurgy recorded by lake sediments from the Bolivian Andes'
sources.venue: Science, vol. 301, no. 5641, 26 September 2003, pp. 1893-1895; DOI 10.1126/science.1087806
sources.author: Mark B. Abbott, Alexander P. Wolfe
sources.confirms: 'Here, we reconstruct a millennium of metallurgical activity in southern Bolivia using the stratigraphy of metals associated with smelting (Pb, Sb, Bi, Ag, Sn) from lake sediments deposited near the major silver deposit of Cerro Rico de Potosí. Pronounced metal enrichment events coincide with the terminal stages of Tiwanaku culture (1000 to 1200 A.D.) and Inca through early Colonial times (1400 to 1650 A.D.). The earliest of these events suggests that Cerro Rico ores were actively smelted at a large scale in the Late Intermediate Period, providing evidence for a major pre-Incan silver industry.'

sources.title: Kris Lane, 'Potosí', in Mark Thurner and Juan Pimentel (eds), New World Objects of Knowledge: A Cabinet of Curiosities
sources.venue: University of London Press, 2021, Part 1 chapter 3 (open-access edition)
sources.author: Kris Lane
sources.confirms: 'Apparently discovered in 1545 by an Andean prospector named Diego Huallpa, the Cerro Rico, an eroded volcanic plug jutting up 4,782 m or nearly 16,000 feet above sea level, quickly captured the world's imagination.'; 'it was only with the construction of large-scale mercury amalgamation facilities after 1572 that the silver potential of these ores was unlocked'; 'attested to by soaring tax returns and Spanish government spending. Production peaked in 1592, after which the Cerro Rico began to lurch along in stair-step decline'; 'Figure 6. Potosí's registered silver production (yellow) and mint production (red) from discovery in 1545 to 1821.'

sources.title: John Munro, review essay on Earl J. Hamilton, American Treasure and the Price Revolution in Spain, 1501-1650 (Harvard University Press, 1934)
sources.venue: EH.Net, Classic Reviews in Economic History, January 2007
sources.author: John Munro
sources.confirms: 'His object was to validate the Quantity Theory of Money: in seeking to demonstrate that the influx of American silver was chiefly, if not entirely, responsible for the inflation of much of the Price Revolution era, from ca. 1520 to ca. 1650'; 'the Price Revolution had begun as early as the quinquennium 1516-20, long before, decades before, any significant amounts of Spanish American silver had reached Seville'; 'two most important silver mines were brought into production: those of Potosi in "Peru" (modern-day Bolivia) in 1545, and Zacatecas, in Mexico, the following year, 1546.' 'vast quantities of silver (and gold) thus undoubtedly flowed from Spain into the various military theaters, in payment for wages, munitions, supplies, and diplomacy'; 'Published by EH.Net (January 2007)'.

sources.title: Douglas Fisher, 'The Price Revolution: A Monetary Interpretation'
sources.venue: Journal of Economic History, vol. 49, no. 4, December 1989, pp. 883-902
sources.author: Douglas Fisher
sources.confirms: 'This article presents tests of the role of money in the price revolution'; 'The hypothesis is that American specie drove European prices, and that the mechanism was the quantity theory of money buttressed by the specie-flow mechanism.'

potosi-silver-1545.detail: Silver went by llama and mule train to Pacific ports, north to Panama and on to Spain. Spaniards still say valer un Potosí, to be worth a Potosí.

picture.alt: Woodcut of Cerro Rico and Potosí from Pedro de Cieza de León's Crónica del Perú, Seville 1553, eight years after silver was found there.
picture.credit: A.Skromnitsky, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

benin-brass-plaques-1550.summary: In Benin City, palace guild casters produced several hundred rectangular brass plaques, each about 40 by 30 centimetres, cast by lost wax and nailed to wooden pillars in palace courtyards. They show the Oba with mudfish legs holding leopards, warriors in coral regalia, Portuguese traders and court musicians, set against a stippled ground of river-leaf pattern. Kathryn Gunsch dates this series to around 1550 and argues it formed a single planned monument of royal history. Brass arrived as manillas traded by Portuguese ships for pepper and enslaved people. British forces removed them during their 1897 occupation; London's British Museum holds most.

sources.title: Gunsch, Kathryn Wysocki, The Benin Plaques: A 16th Century Imperial Monument (Routledge, 2017)
sources.author: Gunsch, Kathryn Wysocki
sources.confirms: Monograph dating the plaque series to the sixteenth century and treating it as an imperial monument
sources.qualifies: Publisher page shows title, author and dates only

sources.title: British Museum, Collection object Af1898,0115.30: plaque, Benin City, 16th-17th century
sources.confirms: Brass relief plaque of the Oba with mudfish legs holding leopards, made by Edo in Benin City by lost-wax casting, dated 16th-17th century, 38.5 by 32 cm, received via the Foreign Office after the 1897 occupation

benin-brass-plaques-1550.detail: British Museum's record for plaque Af1898,0115.30 gives a sixteenth- to seventeenth-century date, Edo manufacture by lost-wax casting in leaded brass, and arrival in London through the Foreign Office in 1898. Gunsch analysed composition, iconography and nail holes to reconstruct how plaques paired across pillars. Plaque production stopped by around 1700, though Benin casting continued in heads and figures. Restitution of Benin objects has been under negotiation since 2010.

picture.alt: Cast brass plaque with two court figures, Benin, 16th century, Museum of Archaeology and Anthropology, Cambridge
picture.credit: SpeakingArch

leo-africanus-description-1550.summary: In 1550 Leo Africanus's account of Africa was printed; for some 300 years, until modern exploration, European scholars treated it as their most authoritative account of Africa. Al-Hasan ibn Muhammad al-Wazzan, born in Granada about 1494 and raised in Fez, had travelled as a diplomat across North Africa and, around 1510, to Timbuktu in Songhai. Captured by Spanish corsairs in 1518, he was presented to Pope Leo X, freed, baptised in 1520 as Johannes Leo, and known as Leo Africanus. In Italy he wrote, in Italian, an account of Africa's geography, peoples and cities, finished in 1526. Giovanni Battista Ramusio published it in Venice in 1550 as Descrittione dell'Africa.

sources.title: Leo Africanus - Wikipedia
Leo Africanus, 'Della descrittione dell'Africa', in Marvels of the World (Penn Press), pp. 319-321
sources.author: Leo Africanus
sources.confirms: Contents page lists the Description of Africa excerpt; bibliographic record only; claim not readable on the opened page.

sources.title: Encyclopaedia Britannica, 'Leo Africanus'
sources.author: Encyclopaedia Britannica editors
sources.confirms: Descrittione dell’Africa was published in 1550; Leo Africanus completed it around 1526. The page gives 1550 for the work and says his writings were a principal European source for about 400 years.

leo-africanus-description-1550.detail: It was reprinted five times, with French and Latin editions in 1556 and English in 1600.

picture.alt: Title page of Leo Africanus's De totius Africae descriptione, Antwerp 1556, Latin edition of his description of Africa first printed in 1550.
picture.credit: Leo Africanus, John Carter Brown Library, public domain, via Internet Archive

mimar-sinan-suleymaniye-1550.summary: From 1550 Mimar Sinan built the Süleymaniye in Istanbul, a 53-metre dome above schools, a hospital and kitchen. Suleiman the Magnificent commissioned his imperial architect to build it on the Third Hill above the Golden Horn. An inscription dates its foundation to 1550 and inauguration to 1557, though work on parts of its complex probably continued for some years. Like other Ottoman imperial foundations it anchored a külliye, religious and charitable buildings with madrasas, public kitchen and hospital, whose staff and endowment deed served Suleiman's claim to lead Sunni Islam. Its layout deliberately echoes Hagia Sophia, Justinian's church turned mosque and Ottoman symbol of sovereignty.

sources.title: Süleymaniye Mosque - Wikipedia
Necipoglu-Kafadar, Gulru, 'The Suleymaniye Complex in Istanbul: An Interpretation', Muqarnas 3 (1985), pp. 92-117
sources.author: Necipoglu-Kafadar, Gulru

sources.author: Mainstone, Rowland J.

mimar-sinan-suleymaniye-1550.detail: Its dome rises 53 metres, exactly twice its 26.5-metre span. It remains Istanbul's largest Ottoman-era mosque and one of Sinan's masterpieces.

oaxaca-cochineal-dye-trade-1550.summary: Mixtec, Zapotec and Nahua households in Oaxaca, Tlaxcala and Puebla bred Dactylopius coccus on cultivated nopal paddles, shielding egg-laying females in woven nests, brushing mature insects into baskets, killing them in hot water or ovens and drying them into grana. About 70,000 insects made one pound of dye. Spanish merchants shipped grana from Veracruz to Seville from the 1540s; by the 1570s it ranked second to silver among New Spain's exports and dyed scarlet for European courts, Ottoman carpets and later British uniforms. Raymond Lee's 1948 study traced production and trade to 1600; Jeremy Baskes showed how eighteenth-century Oaxacan growers financed harvests through repartimiento credit from Spanish magistrates.

sources.title: Lee, Raymond L., 'Cochineal Production and Trade in New Spain to 1600', The Americas 4 (1948)
sources.author: Lee, Raymond L.
sources.confirms: Indigenous breeding methods, Spanish export trade and cochineal's rank among New Spain's exports before 1600.

sources.title: Baskes, Jeremy, Indians, Merchants, and Markets: A Reinterpretation of the Repartimiento and Spanish-Indian Economic Relations in Colonial Oaxaca, 1750-1821 (Stanford University Press, 2000), ch. 2
sources.author: Baskes, Jeremy
sources.confirms: Repartimiento credit financing cochineal production by Oaxacan households in the eighteenth century.

sources.title: Marichal, Carlos, 'Mexican Cochineal and the European Demand for American Dyes, 1550-1850', in Topik, Marichal and Frank (eds), From Silver to Cocaine (Duke University Press, 2006)
sources.author: Marichal, Carlos
sources.confirms: Export volumes, European demand and the long cycle of the cochineal trade to 1850.

oaxaca-cochineal-dye-trade-1550.verification_note: Cochineal breeding predates 1521; 1550 marks the Atlantic trade's take-off per Lee. Export peaks and insect counts per pound vary by source (60,000 to 70,000 insects).
oaxaca-cochineal-dye-trade-1550.detail: Cochineal breeding predates conquest: Mixtec tribute lists in the Codex Mendoza record bags of grana owed to Tenochtitlan. Spain kept the insect's nature secret for two centuries; Europeans debated whether grana was seed or animal until microscopy settled it. Oaxaca exports peaked near 1.5 million pounds a year in the 1770s before synthetic dyes and Guatemalan and Canary Island competition cut prices after 1850.

picture.credit: José Antonio de Alzate y Ramírez (1737 – 1799)., via Wikimedia Commons

taqi-al-din-steam-turbine-1551.summary: In 1551 the Ottoman engineer Taqi al-Din described, by al-Hassan's reading of his treatise, a spit turned by steam blowing on vanes, a steam turbine for roasting meat. His book Al-Turuq al-samiyya fi al-alat al-ruhaniyya, The Sublime Methods of Spiritual Machines, explains it: steam from its boiler was directed onto vanes, turning a wheel fixed to one end of its axle, so that meat turned without anyone cranking it. Some historians count it as an early step in steam turbine history, though Hill's survey of his treatise mentions no steam. His influence stayed limited: few copies of his works survive, so they reached few readers.

sources.title: Taqi ad-Din Muhammad ibn Ma'ruf - Wikipedia
Hill, Donald R., 'Arabic Mechanical Engineering: Survey of the Historical Sources', Arabic Sciences and Philosophy 1 (1991) 167-186
sources.author: Hill, Donald R.
sources.confirms: Taqi al-Din's al-Turuq al-saniyya, written in 959 AH (1551 to 1552), describes several machines including a six-cylinder water-driven pump.

sources.author: al-Hassan, Ahmad Y.
sources.venue: Institute for the History of Arabic Science, University of Aleppo
sources.confirms: Edition and study of al-Turuq al-saniyya, the treatise in which Taqi al-Din describes his machines.

taqi-al-din-steam-turbine-1551.detail: His book also described four water-raising machines, two driven by animals and two by paddle wheels.

badianus-aztec-herbal-1552.summary: At Colegio de Santa Cruz in Tlatelolco, outside Mexico City, Nahua physician Martin de la Cruz composed a herbal in Nahuatl in 1552 and Juan Badiano, a Nahua scholar from Xochimilco, translated it into Latin as Libellus de medicinalibus Indorum herbis. Its 185 colour paintings show more than 200 plants, each tied to a named ailment and a recipe, from headaches and sore eyes to wounds and childbirth. Sent to Spain for the viceroy's son, it lay unread in Vatican's library until 1929. No earlier medical book written in the Americas by Indigenous authors survives, and none records Nahua pharmacology so fully before Spanish practice displaced it. The Vatican returned it to Mexico in 1990.

sources.title: De Smedt, Johan; De Cruz, Helen, 'Cosmovision as Cognitive Technology: The Case of Mesoamerican Medicinal Knowledge', Topics in Cognitive Science 18 (2025)
sources.author: De Smedt, Johan; De Cruz, Helen
sources.confirms: Confirms Martin de la Cruz wrote the herbal in Nahuatl, Juan Badiano translated it into Latin in 1552 at Tlatelolco, and that it carries 185 illustrations.

sources.title: National Library of Medicine, 'The Badianus Manuscript: An Aztec Herbal of 1552', exhibition text
sources.author: National Library of Medicine
sources.confirms: Confirms the herbal as the first produced in the Americas and describes 204 plants with their uses.

sources.title: Smithsonian Libraries, catalogue record for The De la Cruz-Badiano Aztec Herbal of 1552
sources.author: Smithsonian Institution
sources.confirms: Confirms the 1552 date and the Emmart facsimile edition.

badianus-aztec-herbal-1552.verification_note: Plant counts differ between sources (about 185 paintings, 204 plant names) because several plants share a painting.
